Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

Ever since, the midfielder has enjoyed almost unwavering support. Watzke frequently spoke with him throughout his first season, offering encouragement and reassurance. The same was true of Kovac and other senior figures. Equally important to his breakthrough has been team-mate Felix Nmecha, with whom Bellingham has developed a close friendship and who has become an important source of advice. When time allows, the two enjoy playing padel together. Off the pitch they are opponents; on it they form a midfield partnership.

And while his father Mark was still complaining to club officials around a year ago that his son was not getting enough playing time, the situation has changed dramatically. The Bellingham family are delighted, and his England call-up has provided further confirmation that he is on the right path.

Making the step to the senior team 💪 Thomas Tuchel on Jobe Bellingham 🗣️ https://t.co/kKRR1NcPFR

Fifteen months ago in Austria, Bellingham still needed some convincing before stepping in front of the press. Today, he regularly conducts post-match interviews. He’s leading the way. And in Dortmund they are convinced of one thing: We will be hearing a lot more from Jobe Bellingham.

Very good player, very good season. In the way we play now I don’t see him in a central position in the build-up, more in the finishing position of a No 8 or No 10 and the competition [for those places] is very high in our squad. He is in our squad of 55 and we see his quality. It was close for him.

We were not happy about this. We could understand the disappointment of the fans with what happened before. This is expressed now and should be a closed book.

Everyone can see how Ben presented himself in the March camp. He did excellent and scored for us then conceded a penalty. Not easy for him but when I speak to him I always feel the hunger to come back. He is the stand-out player for Arsenal in a position where we have a lot of problems [with injuries] somehow, a lot of changes. Every time I watch Arsenal I see a very strong Ben White.

He deserves to open a new chapter and receive positive feedback from the crowd.

I think Kobbie has had a difficult spell with his team and club and missed a lot of matches. In the meantime Jobe impressed in that spell. The door is always open for players to overtake and make their mark. That is a sign of the competition for central midfield places.

He is a more defensive player than his brother. Good on the ball, good physique, big body, technical player who can keep possession. It is up to him now. We only have Tuesday and Wednesday to prepare and it will be difficult because [in the last camp] we developed some new patterns, some new behaviours. It will be hard [for him to pick that up in two days] but it is up to him. He is excited, happy and eager to impress which is the best foundation to have a good camp.

It will be Rio [Ngumoha], who played there for Liverpool and impressed in the last camp. Josh [King] can play there. We will try that. And Morgan Gibbs-White. We need runners there and I think we have options. It was a close call not to bring Noni [Madueke]. It was very close since he got his chance when Bukayo was injured at Arsenal, getting minutes and goals. But we stick with the group we have and give them our trust.

The door is always open and nothing has changed. We decided to do this [camp] without him.

It’s an incredible achievement [winning the Ballon d’Or and winning a  record-breaking 126th cap] that these two occasions come together in one week. He wins the Ballon d’Or and deservedly so and now his 126th cap. Incredible achievement that underlines his professional status and his demeanour. His attitude. He is our captain. I cannot find a better frame [he means stage] to celebrate his achievement.

Let’s not forget that it is a crucial match for us. We are desperate to win and have a final in Spain afterwards. The focus is on Croatia and it is a deserved ‘frame’ [stage] and occasion to celebrate his achievement.

Everyone is desperate to play for England and Cole is no exception. We are speaking now about a player who was not in camp and it counts when you miss a camp. As I said last time he misses too many opportunities to impress. It was a long camp, 2½ weeks and the players there used it to build something extraordinary. The credit goes to them and the trust goes to them.

It’s not personal and we will never assume that Cole is not in the mindset or not desperate to play for his country. The competition is on and the players who were in camp used their opportunity and have kept their place.

He has a fantastic character and he impressed us in the US. He gives us a bit of flexibility. We nominated 22 outfield players which gives us flexibility in training. You could call it that he is the ‘extra’ player up front and a young, exciting and flexible player. He can play in the No 10 and No 9 for sure and we would like to see how he can play on the wings. In training [for the World Cup] we tried him at full-back. We won’t try that again!

The attitude, the smile, the positivity and he is difficult to defend against. We hope he can bring that spark to camp.

Lee Carsley is speaking very highly of him for a long time now. He is the captain of the U21s, the stand-out player. I think the door should always be open for the pathway, the door should always be open for special performers over a long period of time and that is what Jobe has done.

He has found his way and his rhythm with Dortmund who have had an excellent start to the season. He is a regular starter there and there is an opportunity because Myles is suspended for the Croatia game.

Jobe comes through the pathway and on his own merit and deserves to make an impression for us. That’s why we are delighted he is with us in camp and we can see what he can do for us.

He misses too many opportunities to impress. The trust is for the players who are in camp. It is not personal and we will never assume that Cole is not in the mindset to come in and play, but the players in camp did an amazing job.

It’s enough No10s and we stick to the guys who were in camp. We were happy with the last two-and-a-half weeks we had together. The impact of the players throughout that camp was immense and that is why we stick mainly with the group. We have Josh King in the group who plays there [No 10] but I want to see him on both wings. He covers all eventualities because Josh can play all four positions. That’s basically the reason.

Jude has previously spoken about his dream to play in the same England team as his brother, who is two years younger than him and has also followed his path by playing for Dortmund. Jobe moved there from Sunderland at the start of last season and finished his first campaign in Bundesliga as a regular starter.

“We’ve played together for so long in the street and to play with my brother Jobe for England would be the biggest dream of my life, that would mean more than any of the trophies, nothing would even get close to that. Nothing,” said Jude two years ago.

Jobe Bellingham’s call-up for the England squad is ahead of Everton’s Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, who has been in eye-catching form for Everton. It also shows that Tuchel is thinking of the future, with Jordan Henderson not picked despite his presence in the World Cup squad.

England checked with Chelsea and were told that Palmer was fit for international duty if selected. “Load management” not an issue this time, then.

He is doing well. The reason why he has been left out, I don’t know. But we are happy with Phil. It is my duty to help him and slowly, slowly he will be back to his best. We are very happy with Phil.

And the message is plain: miss a camp for reasons with which he does not agree and pay the price.

A clear message to the squad 👊 Watch TT's full interview on the official England app ⤵️

I am quite surprised that Noni Madueke has not made the England squad today. He’s on arguably his best run of form in an Arsenal shirt. The winger has started seven of the last 10 matches and has four goal involvements (three goals and one assist) in his last eight appearances. He has been playing well on both flanks, too. Given his importance to Tuchel at the World Cup, it’s a bit of a strange one.

Josh is the pride of her club and our supporters. He came to this club at eight. How he’s playing, how he’s performing, we’re really proud of him. I am so happy for him. He’s a really humble kid. He wants to improve every day, a special day for him and all of us.

He is talented, he can receive between the lines where there is no space, he can dribble, he can run, he can pass. We are working with him on his finishing which is the most difficult thing in the game, to score a goal. But his character, he is so mature. He has everything to become one of the best players in the world.

Lee Carsley has been talking highly about Jobe for weeks and months, that he deserves it if there is a spot and a possibility to join and to make an impression in the first team.

He had good matches and is on a good run of form with Dortmund so he deserves to be with us. We have 21 outfield players for the first match and then possibly 22 for the second match. [Lewis-Skelly is suspended for the Croatia match after picking up two bookings in the opening games].

Thomas Tuchel has Jordan Henderson back fit – and playing well – since the last international break. The last of Henderson’s 91 caps came at the World Cup against Panama, with his tournament effectively ended when he famously broke his arm in the celebrations at the Azteca after Mexico were defeated. From Tuchel’s squad in the summer, Djed Spence has also returned from injury although he is only just back playing for Inter Milan.

Marcus Rashford is set to miss out on England through injury having barely played since the last international break. The Manchester United forward pulled out of the last squad, then returned for his club the following weekend. But he has not featured since the defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League. His absence will open up a space for another wide forward, with Noni Madueke pushing for a call-up with his form for Arsenal.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the announcement by Thomas Tuchel of England’s squad for their remaining two Uefa Nations Group 3 matches against Croatia – them again – at Wembley next Thursday and Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid next Sunday night. England have already qualified for the knockout phase – barring a defeat by Croatia by a margin of eight or more goals – but would need two victories to avoid France and Portugal in the next two-legged phase in March.

Tuchel’s only major injury doubt from the last squad are Arsenal’s Bukao Saka and Como’s Trevoh Chalobah as well as the more long-term absentee Tino Livramento, the man Chalobah replaced in the World Cup 26. Djed Spence has returned to full fitness and played for Inter in their Milan derby defeat last weekend while the head coach’s favourite player, Jordan Henderson, has been passed fit to play for Chelsea at his boyhood club Sunderland on Sunday though at 36 his race may finally have been run at this level despite his unexpected encore in the last 18 months.

For the first time since 2001 England will have the Ballon d’Or winner in the squad and Harry Kane will also become England’s most-capped player – barring some misfortune when Bayern Munich take on Mainz on Saturday – by leading them out at Wembley on Thursday night for his 126th appearance.

Whether he will be joined by Cole Palmer in the squad remains the only significant issue of note. The Chelsea forward pulled out of the last squad as part of his club’s management of his groin injury but he has played in their last four Premier League games, scoring once and being sent off once as well. Kobbie Mainoo is fit again and may be picked to see if his backside has recovered from bench splinters since his summer of exasperation.

The squad will be released at 10am and followed by Tuchel’s explanations, which we will also cover here, an hour later.

#1070. Number of international students arriving in US plunges — worrying scientists

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

International students earn almost 40% of science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.Credit: Bill Pugliano/Getty

The number of international students arriving in the United States in August for the start of the academic year has fallen by 28% since 2024, reaching the lowest level since the depths reached in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Data from the federal National Travel and Tourism Office show that the number of incoming student-visa holders fell from 387,000 in August 2024 to 277,000 in August 2026 (see ‘Students stay away’). The trend has been driven by a decline in the numbers of students from India and China, which dropped by about 50,000 and 23,000, respectively, from 2024 to 2026.

Source: National Travel and Tourism Office (NTTO); Nature analysis.

The number of applications from international students to US PhD programmes has also declined over the past year, falling by 21% from 2025 to 2026, according to a survey of 55 members of the Association of American Universities (AAU), a coalition of research-intensive schools.

These decreases are squeezing already strained university budgets, and researchers worry about the impact on US science. “I can’t imagine a more effective way for the US to cede its dominance in critical scientific fields to China and Europe than by reducing international students,” says Nigel Goldenfeld, a physicist at the University of California, San Diego. In 2024, international students earned 38% of the science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing

The administration of US President Donald Trump has introduced several restrictions on visas and international travel since Trump took office in early 2025. Last month, the administration also attempted to place a US$100,000 levy on science and engineering students enrolling in extended Optional Practical Training (OPT), a work programme used by hundreds of thousands of recent graduates and the largest pipeline of scientific talent into the United States. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which issued the proposal, stated that it is meant to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers”.

Federal judges have suspended the OPT charge and other efforts that the administration made to curb immigration. But higher-education specialists link these attempts to the large decrease in new overseas students, who, they say, can no longer count a US education as a stable investment. “Uncertainty has become policy, and that has registered in the hearts and minds of students,” says Chris Glass, a higher-education researcher at Boston College in Massachusetts.

The United Kingdom, Canada and Australia have also seen drops in enrolment of international students after placing new limits on these populations. But the US policies are especially restrictive, Glass says.

A spokesperson for the White House did not respond to Nature’s request for comment.

#1069. Arsenal wonderkid Max Dowman makes history in England Under-21s win over France

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

England Under-21s bounced back from losing to Portugal on Friday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Max Dowman became the youngest goalscorer in the history of England Under-21s after netting a late winner in a 3-2 victory over France at Ashton Gate.

Lee Carsley’s side continued their preparations for next year’s European Championship, bouncing back from Friday's 1-0 defeat by Portugal despite surrendering a two-goal lead on Monday.

Having produced a lacklustre performance three days ago, England made a lightning start this time. Mikey Moore gave them an early lead on his first under-21s start before Divin Mubama doubled their advantage.

The Young Lions were comfortable, but Tommy Setford made a second mistake in as many games. He let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers to hand France a goal back, before the Frenchman equalised in style moments later.

Carsley handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman, who proved to be the match-winner by tapping home at only 16 years old.

England got off to the perfect start following great work from Ethan Nwaneri down the left. His pass fed Moore, who tucked expertly past Mathieu Patouillet.

The Young Lions doubled their lead in the 29th minute as Nwaneri again provided the assist, lifting a high ball onto the head of Mubama, who nodded back across goal for 2-0.

France did not threaten in the first half but began the second period much more menacingly. Dayann Methalie found space inside the box but fired wide with their best chance to that point.

England almost scored a third down the other end when Nwaneri was denied by Patouillet’s diving save. The ball fell back to the Borussia Dortmund loanee, who saw his follow-up effort cleared off the line by Nathan Zeze.

Setford’s mistake had given Portugal victory on Friday, and he was again at fault when Versini’s untroubling cross slipped through his fingers to make it 2-1.

There was nothing Setford could do about the equaliser, however, as Versini let fly from distance with an impressive strike into the net.

However, England re-established their lead four minutes later when Harrison Armstrong fed Dowman, who was left unmarked inside the box to tap into an empty net for a historic goal.

#1068. Tony Mowbray steps down as Blackburn Rovers manager with immediate effect due to health reasons - two years after bowel cancer battle forced him to leave Birmingham City

Published: 05:25 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 08:02 EST, 17 November 2026

Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role as Blackburn Rovers manager due to ill health.

The 62-year-old, who previously had to walk away from his job at Birmingham City in 2024 due to a battle with bowel cancer, leaves Blackburn with immediate effect.

The Championship side announced his departure with a statement from Mowbray. It read: 'Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as Head Coach of Blackburn Rovers.

'I’m immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I’ve loved working with them.

'Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you’ve given me. It’s been a pleasure working alongside you.

'To the fans, thank you for the way you’ve supported me and the team this season. I’ve always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me.

Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role as Blackburn Rovers boss due to ill health

'I’m grateful to the Owners and Suhail (Pasha, chief operating officer) for giving me the opportunity to lead this great club once again.

Mowbray leaves with Blackburn 13th in the Championship. He took over at the club in June this year having spent two years out of the game following his health issues at Birmingham City.

The veteran manager suddenly stepped down as manager of Birmingham in February 2024 after undergoing surgery for bowel cancer. He had 15cm of his bowel removed during his treatment.

He took a temporary leave of absence after eight games in charge, before officially resigning from the role in May.

Mowbray, who has managed a host of English clubs, opened up publicly about his struggles, telling the Times that his children had feared the worst.

'I had the conversation with my family and you could see they were frightened,' he said. 'Was I frightened? My only thoughts were for my family, my three children and my wife and making sure they were OK.

'I had to put everything in order and I tried to. My wife saw our banking app for the first time in her life. It's little things like that. She understood. This was serious stuff. I felt she needed to know where we had our money, whether it was ISAs or pensions and what was in the bank.'

Speaking on his diagnosis, which came after he collapsed when trying to answer the door, he added: 'My wife put me in the car and drove me back to hospital and they wanted to know why I was collapsing and in the condition I was,' he says. 'They rehydrated me and put me on a drip overnight.

'I remember sitting there in bed and my kids' eyes were watering up. They were scared I wasn't going to live. How old were they? They were 15, 17 and 19. I could see the fear in their eyes.'

Mowbray's comeback story when he was made Blackburn boss in the summer was one of the feel-good moments of the offseason. It has not been disclosed what his current health issue is.

Mowbray leaves Blackburn with the team in 13th place in the Championship table

Blackburn Rovers owner Balaji Rao added his own statement, writing: 'Our thoughts are with Tony and his family as he steps back from his duties to focus on his health.

'Through our many meetings over the years, we’ve come to know Tony well and grown very fond of him. We’ve always admired his professionalism, his dedication and the passion he brings to his work at Blackburn Rovers.

'Tony, please know that you have our unconditional and unwavering support. We send you and your family our love and strength, and we will do all we can to support you through this time.'

Chief Executive Officer Steve Curwood said: 'Tony’s passion for the club and his professionalism are clear to see, but it is his kindness and the care he shows for players, staff and those around him that mean so much.

'Our priority now is to make sure he feels that same care and support from all of us. We will support him and his family in every way we can.

'On behalf of everyone at Blackburn Rovers, I would like to send Tony and his family our very best wishes during this time.'

#1066. Scotland’s miserable night shows Sebastien Pocognoli is already running out of time

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

It remains early days, but there are few signs of progress in Pocognoli’s new approach and the regression Scotland have made in the past 12 months has been alarming. By Jamie Braidwood

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

On Wednesday, 18 November, it will be a year to the day since one of the greatest nights in Scotland’s history: the 4-2 win over Denmark that sensationally sealed qualification to the following summer’s World Cup. The BBC will be celebrating by showing a full match replay on Tuesday and many Scotland supporters who tuned into see a wretched end to their Nations League campaign on Monday evening will have wished they had just waited to watch that instead.

How dramatically Scotland’s fortunes have fallen in the 12 months since, as a miserable 4-0 defeat to a second-string Switzerland side with nothing to play for raised serious questions about the new era under Sebastien Pocognoli. It remains early days –  there have only been six games since the departure of Steve Clarke – but Pocognoli has overseen just two wins, both of which came against North Macedonia. There has been little progress under the Belgian, and the complete absence of a statement result.

On what was a historic night for Andy Robertson, the record-breaking captain offered a damning assessment of their work so far in implementing Pocognoli’s new approach. “I don't think you've got time in international football,” he said. “Are they supporters that have travelled everywhere going to give us time? No. The people inside Hampden, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden that are going to be critical, and rightly so, are they going to give us time? No.”

There were some bright signs in the first half in St Gallen, but then Scotland were the side with something on the line as they chased a victory that could have given them an outside chance of reaching a Nations League promotion play-off. Switzerland, by contrast, were already through as group winners. The World Cup quarter-finalists were missing many of their first-choice team but a much-changed, inexperienced side remained cohesive and took a first-half lead through Lewis Ferguson’s own goal.

Turning into his own net was a horrible moment for Ferguson, but it should not have been a disaster for Scotland. They had time at the break to turn it around. But what was perhaps the most alarming aspect of their surrender to the Swiss was how sloppy they were at the start of the second half, and the way their heads dropped after conceding twice in five minutes following the restart. It did not reflect well on Pocognoli that his players looked as if their confidence was on the floor.

It was notable, also, that Pocognoli appeared to snap at a reporter in response to a gentle pre-match questioning of his tactics and 3-4-3 formation. He wants his team to be front-footed and take the game to their opponents by pushing high up the pitch, but it’s clear for all to see that Scotland are struggling to combine that with being creative from open play and retaining defensive solidity. The mistakes in possession and at the back, once they went behind, suggested a lack of belief in the system they are trying to play. Scott McTominay has been anonymous playing as one of two No 10s, next to John McGinn, in his two appearances under Pocognoli.

Scotland had these issues too under Clarke, increasingly towards the end of his tenure and especially at the World Cup, but in qualifying or the Nations League there was always the sense that the could rise to a challenge when they were being doubted. Scotland may have missed out on the Nations League play-offs even if they had won at Switzerland – as it happens, Slovenia won 3-0 at North Macedonia anyway – but beating even an inexperienced Switzerland side would have been a boost. Collapsing in the manner they did could be even more damaging.

As if to stress Robertson’s point, the Euro 2028 qualifying draw takes place at the start of the December, ahead of potentially staging the tournament on home soil 18 months later. Finishing the Nations League in third place in League B means Scotland will be stuck in Pot 3 of the draw. A potential four-team group could see them land next to Spain and Sweden and with just two automatic qualifying spots available.

And while there are two qualification spaces left in reserve, should any of the co-hosts fail to qualify automatically, there are only two, and they will go to the teams with the best qualifying record: Scotland could be left praying for England, Wales and the Republic of Ireland to coast through.

Should they land in a five-team qualifying group, Scotland could be playing their Euro 2028 qualifiers by as early as the next international break in March. The Nations League carried ramifications but the series of six games across September, October and November where the time for Pocognoli to settle in. Now, there are just more questions than answers, and the clock towards the home Euros ticking while a sense of apathy among the Tartan Army grows.

In that context, Robertson’s message felt even more pertinent. “We've not got time,” he stressed. “The players don't have time. We have to step up. Now we've got a long break until March, which is not a good thing. We really need to step up again because in international football, you don't have time.”

#1065. Jayden Bogle receives threats and racist abuse after Leeds’ win over Tottenham

Leeds and the Premier League are launching an investigation into racist abuse and threats sent to Jayden Bogle’s family.

Bogle escaped a red card in the win over Tottenham after injuring Mathys Tel, with the Leeds full-back receiving the threats via social media.

Should Jason Bogle have seen red for this challenge? 🟥👀 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/fuK42Okkcz

His club have revealed they are looking to identify those who sent messages to the 26-year-old, whose family were threatened in one of the posts seen by Telegraph Sport after the 1-0 victory.

Leeds say they are “appalled at the disgusting, racist social-media abuse Jayden Bogle suffered” and will push for punishments to be taken.

The club added in a statement: “Leeds United condemns this behaviour in the strongest possible terms. There is no place for racism in football or society.

“The club will work with the Premier League and relevant authorities to identify the individuals and push for the strongest possible action to be taken against them.

“Jayden has the full and unconditional support of the club and his team-mates, and we all stand with him at this time. Nobody should ever be subjected to racist abuse.”

Daniel Farke, the Leeds head coach, described Bogle as the “softest player” in the Premier League who would never try to hurt an opponent.

Referee John Brooks did not issue a yellow card, with VAR Tony Harrington sticking with the on-field decision.

“I’m confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There’s a lack of speed going into the challenge and he’s stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge,” Harrington was quoted on the big screen at Elland Road.

Tottenham will make a formal complaint to Pro Ref over the decision not to send off Bogle.

“I haven’t watched the scenes back so I can’t give you a clear opinion, out of the game it looked a handball but the scene with Jayden was not too far away from my bench and it looked a very unlucky coming together,” Farke said.

“Fingers crossed for Mathys that he is back soon, but it looked like there was not much speed in this action, but Jayden Bogle is one of the most fair players in the country, he would never injure or foul a player on purpose because he is such a fair character.”

Tottenham Hotspur’s purple patch of form ended with a worrying loss. Wearing their “Spurple” kit for the first time, Roberto De Zerbi highlighted a lack of character and personality from his players and refused to blame the defeat on referee John Brooks’s decision not to dismiss Jayden Bogle for leaving one of his players injured.

Spurs’ away strip is based on a 1990s design, but this performance was more Christian Gross than Jürgen Klinsmann or David Ginola. Leeds United created the better chances and eventually broke through with 11 minutes remaining when their substitutes combined for Noah Okafor to score the winning goal.

Noah Okafor came off the bench and broke the deadlock just minutes later ⛓️‍💥 What a finish 🎯 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/pnbTQM1YpM

After victories against Coventry City, Chelsea and Crystal Palace, this was a blow for De Zerbi after looking to move Spurs into the European places. Leeds had not scored in 298 minutes of football, nor had they won in five previous matches, yet the Tottenham manager could barely recognise the players who had won three matches in a row.

De Zerbi had warned his team they would face a hostile atmosphere at Elland Road, but instead of rising to the challenge, Spurs were passive until it was too late.

“We didn’t win any duels, we didn’t win any one-to-ones, there was space to play and we didn’t take the right position,” De Zerbi said. “We didn’t show personality, we didn’t show what we are or who we are. It is part of the journey for sure. It can be normal in football but we have to be honest, if you are not honest the future is not good. If you analyse our behaviour we can become a top team.

“We worked very hard this week. We spoke all the days about the intensity, the type of game we would have found in this stadium and the atmosphere, it was not a surprise for us. Sometimes it can happen that we didn’t play the kind of game we want.”

De Zerbi’s honesty shines a light on the amount of work that still needs to be done at Spurs. Even after three straight wins, he has refused to get carried away despite fans looking upwards towards the European places.

Neither did the Italian want to blame the officials for failing to send off Bogle. Brooks has history with Spurs, sending off Xavi Simons against Liverpool last season. Here, he booked De Zerbi for his protests after Bogle’s heavy challenge that forced Mathys Tel off through injury.

Bogle trod on his opponent’s foot before clattering into his knee, forcing the French forward off a few minutes later. “I know that Jayden doesn’t foul out of bad intentions, he is not a nasty player and is one of the softest players in the whole league,” Leeds head coach Daniel Farke said. “I call him my butterfly.”

De Zerbi admitted the injury was “bad” and that Tel would now be scanned to determine the extent of the problem. The Spurs boss was upset that Pedro Porro was later booked for a similar challenge, while Bogle went unpunished – but he said the referee was not the cause of the defeat.

“I was surprised because in the same position in the second half there were two different fouls, the yellow card for Pedro Porro is not possible. I don’t know if it is a red card or not on Mathys Tel but the parameter of the referee was not good enough for this in both situations,” De Zerbi said.

For Leeds, moving into the top half will lift their own hopes of challenging for Europe, such is the congested mid-table.

“For us it has been a difficult period, we are missing key players like Anton Stach, Noah, Dominic [Calvert-Lewin] has not had the easiest spell with several injury problems and it was important to show this unity and commitment to avoid all their individual quality to score goals and reduce them to very little,” Farke added.

“Our final third, the quality was perhaps not there but second half there was no doubt just one team was pushing for that win. Another clean sheet another terrific defensive behaviour.”

Archie Gray will make his first appearance against his old club today after joining Spurs from Leeds in 2024. Dominic Calvert-Lewin is starting for Leeds today, after doubts over a foot issue heading into the Elland Road fixture. He was named in the England squad yesterday, which suggested he was not ruled out of this clash against Spurs

Roberto De Zerbi has kept a settled team as he looks to make it four Premier League wins in a row. Dominic Solanke is dropped to the bench in his only change, with Pedro Porro coming in – so it may be Omar Marmoush playing as a central forward.

There are many processes in [Tottenham’s] build-up. You need players to interpret this and the legs to cover the centre of the game. It is always complicated [tactically against a De Zerbi team], very dominant in possession. You have to find solutions to be competitive in this area.

The most important thing is what happens on the pitch but [we have bought] Sean [in because of the] tactical aspect. He is sop smart, has experience and also the legs to compete. It’s necessary to have a third midfielder on the pitch to control their processes. On the other hand he is sharp on the offensive actions, many times. Lukas [Nmecha] brings the greediness, physicality and can take the attention off Dominic. he has been very sharp in training, scoring many goals and for that he has the chance to shine today.

Dominic is a key player and thank God he was able to join us in team training yesterday. Overall he is in a good position.

The pre-season, it was clear [he is] a special talent. You recognise the special talent immediately and he doesn’t need to show something special, you understand? Everything that he does and he is one of the special talents.

The next step he has to enjoy, he has to follow the older players, the players with more experience like [Andrew] Robertson, [James] Maddison, Ben Davies and to find the time to play.

It is my responsibility because when you manage young players and sucho big talents like Luca, it is a bigger responsibility for me.

He has to be ready when he goes on the pitch. I think it [does] not depend on the result, he can play from the beginning. Before the Chelsea game, I thought to play with him in the first XI, but in the end you have to find the right moment and for them also.

I think the age is not so important. The most important is the quality, personality, the behaviour on the pitch and the qualities. And Luca has all of these qualities.

Leeds United are heartbroken to learn of the passing of supporter Colin Westby at the age of 68. Colin was a long-standing Season Ticket Holder at the club, attending matches for over 50 years. The thoughts of everyone at Leeds United are with Colin's family and friends at this sad time. We will pay tribute to Colin in the 68th minute of our next Premier League fixture with Tottenham Hotspur, on Saturday 7 November.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

Daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. In fairness they played well against the champions for an hour and were deservedly in the lead until Mikel Arteta turnd to his billionaire’s bench and changed the game. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

They never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

Spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.

Tel also scored in Spurs’ home game, a 1-1 draw in May, and then kicked Ethan Ampadu in the head to concede the penalty from which Leeds equalised. I wonder what kind of impact he will have today. Incidentally Roberto De Zerbi on his last visit to Leeds when manager of Brighton in 2022-23 had such a strop on the touchline when the home team equalised that he was within a gnat’s whisker of being sent off.

#1064. Inside Calciopoli, the match-fixing bombshell that brought Juventus to its knees

The 2006 match-fixing controversy exposed corruption at the very top of Serie A – at its centre was one man and his mobile phone

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At the time, it was called “the biggest scandal in the history of European football” – a sporting earthquake that was off the Richter scale. Dubbed by some onlookers as ‘Moggi-gate', it became more widely known as Calciopoli, a match-fixing scandal that dominated Italian football and overshadowed the Azzurri's 2006 World Cup success.

It resulted in Italy's richest and most decorated football club, Juventus, being kicked out of Serie A, despite many saying that, given the club's connection to the powerful Agnelli family – the owners of Fiat motors – such a thing could never happen. Of the other clubs charged with match-fixing, Milan, Lazio and Fiorentina were each deducted 30 points for the 2005-06 season, even if they were allowed to hang on to their Serie A status. The Rossoneri still finished third and qualified for the Champions League, despite their tally falling to 58.

What exactly was Calciopoli and how was it allowed to come about? Who were the power-brokers that made up Luciano Moggi's network? In the months that followed, the scandal left far more questions than answers.

In understanding it all, the logical place to start is with Moggi, the man whose name became synonymous with football corruption. A former railway stationmaster from Tuscany, he was one of the most controversial figures in Italian football for more than 20 years. He started out as a talent scout for Juventus, then had periods as sporting director at Roma, Lazio, Torino and Napoli, before returning to Juve in 1994.

During that period, Moggi began to weave his web of useful contacts. His methods were controversial and he was tagged ‘Lucky Luciano' after surviving a number of investigations, including claims that he laid on prostitutes for referees in UEFA Cup games while at Torino – claims that he denied.

Back at Juventus, the trophies began to pile up, but players and fans of rival clubs suspected that Moggi was using his weighty book of contacts to influence results. Everyone in the game had a story about Moggi, but no-one could prove anything. Moggi himself revelled in the mystique his power had created, sometimes jokingly referring to himself as ‘The Devil'.

The suspicions, it was later discovered, were not completely unfounded. The findings of an Italian Football Federation tribunal claimed that, making more than 400 phone calls a day, Moggi controlled referees, as well as having federation bosses and television presenters in his pocket.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

His downfall came through intercepted calls. The Turin magistrates, who had brought criminal charges against Juve's managing director Antonio Giraudo and club doctor Riccardo Agricola for alleged doping offences (Giraudo was acquitted at the initial trial, while Agricola's charges were later thrown out by the Appeal Court), tapped the phones of the club's directors for 48 days in 2004.

What the magistrates heard was of no use to their inquiry, but they passed the transcripts on to the football federation and to magistrates in Naples, who separately had been investigating links between football and organised crime in the south of Italy. The Naples magistrates tapped the phones of dozens of people from the world of football for the 2004-05 season and Moggi-gate exploded in early May 2006, when excerpts from those two sets of phone taps were leaked to the press.

The selection of referees for games in Serie A was entrusted to two ‘designators': Paolo Bergamo and Pierluigi Pairetto. The names of referees were sorted into groups, according to experience. Then, in theory, they were drawn, lottery-style, and matched up with the weekend's fixtures.

The evidence from the first wave of leaks suggested that not only was the selection of referees for Serie A matches not as random as it should have been but, even more alarmingly, that Moggi held some sway over the choice of refs for Juve's Champions League games via Pairetto, who was also a member of the UEFA referees' committee. Before Juventus travelled to face Ajax in Amsterdam on September 15, 2004, Pairetto phoned Moggi.

PAIRETTO: I know that you've forgotten about me but I haven't forgotten about you.

PAIRETTO: I've put a great referee for the game in Amsterdam.

PAIRETTO: Anyway, it was just to tell you this. You see, I remember about you.

The referee was the Swiss, Urs Meier, most famous in England for being in charge of the Three Lions' quarter-final loss to Portugal at Euro 2004. Juventus beat Ajax 1-0. There has never been any suggestion that Meier was in on the arrangement or acted at all improperly. It was by no means the first time that Moggi and Pairetto had spoken. After Juventus had drawn 2-2 at home to Swedish club Djurgarden in a Champions League qualifier the previous month, in which German referee Herbert Fandel disallowed a goal by Juve's Fabrizio Miccoli, Moggi had angrily disapproved.

MOGGI: What the f**k kind of referee did you send us?

MOGGI: It was valid, it was valid. He can f**k himself. I have to make the return match in Stockholm secure, no? With another like [Fandel], it's going to be a bit difficult, no? You follow me?

Juve won the return leg in Stockholm 4-1, with Graham Poll refereeing. Again, there has never been any suggestion that Poll was aware of the relationship between Moggi and Pairetto or acted improperly. After the match, Moggi clearly had nothing to grumble about, but the appointment of Poll had come as a surprise to him. Two days before the game, Lucky Luciano called the secretary of the Italian football league.

SECRETARY: I've got Graham Poll written here.

PAIRETTO: Well something has happened at the last minute, he was sick or something.

PAIRETTO: Yes, yes. I'll look into it right away.

For domestic games, investigators claimed that by rigging what was supposed to be a random draw, Pairetto and Bergamo could choose from a pool of referees who were considered to be pro-Juventus. Massimo de Santis had been due to officiate at the 2006 World Cup until the scandal broke, after which he was hurriedly withdrawn by the Italian Football Federation.

It was later claimed that the referees in the ‘pro-Juve pool' would give Moggi's men the benefit of the doubt in most situations, award non-existent penalties or deny the opposition blatant ones, and disallow perfectly good goals. They would use different criteria for Juventus and their opponents when deciding what merited a yellow card – most seasons, the Turin club had the lowest yellow cards to fouls ratio.

Sometimes they would be assigned to a game featuring a team that was due to play against Juve the following week. In those games, it was claimed that their job was to book or send off key players so they would be suspended by the time they faced Juventus.

They were not being paid for their favours or receiving lavish gifts. The system was much simpler. Investigators alleged that it was made clear to refs by Pairetto and Bergamo that if they wanted to get on, wanted to take charge of the big games, to have a career, they had to toe the line. Moggi also had a contact on the inside, Italian football federation vice president Innocenzo Mazzini, according to the investigation.

When the Italian federation opened disciplinary hearings, Moggi's network was described as a “sophisticated system which undermined one of the fundamental principles of sport: the independence of referees”.

Investigators alleged that Moggi also controlled what some television programmes said about the referees, to temper any public backlash against controversial decisions that had gone in favour of Juventus. The approach was subtle – the presenters were only to take Juve's side in situations where there had been a close call. If a foul or penalty was obvious to everyone, it would have been counter-productive to pretend it hadn't happened.

The following wiretap conversation, as later translated by a University of Perugia report, was between Moggi and Fabio Baldas, a former referee who was an expert pundit on a television programme called Il processo di Biscardi.

According to investigators, the pair spoke before nearly every programme to discuss what was going to be said, but Baldas received criticism from fans for taking Juventus' side when he analysed a controversial decision made by an official during a match.

BALDAS: I tried to defend myself, but they attacked me from all sides and said I was a Juventus fan!

[Since this article was first published in FourFourTwo magazine in 2006, criminal proceedings against almost all the journalists caught up in the wiretaps were dropped in 2007, although several were suspended by Italy's Order of Journalists]

Lazio and Fiorentina were both run by businessmen who were new to football: Claudio Lotito and Diego Della Valle. The two men sensed there was something rotten in the state of the Italian game from the moment they arrived on the scene. Lotito talked about “moralising” the sport, while Della Valle attacked the system of selling TV rights, which ensured the big three – Juve, Milan and Inter – earned fortunes and everyone else shared the rest.

Key decisions seemed to go against their teams – as the 2004-05 season drew to a close, they were heading towards the trapdoor to Serie B. What to do? Go down with your principles still intact? Get real.

According to prosecutor Stefano Palazzi, phone taps showed that Lotito asked federation president Franco Carraro for help in four end-of-season matches. Carraro told ref designator Bergamo that he should “give Lazio a hand”. Fiorentina asked Mazzini for help in two vital relegation games.

Unfortunately for the two clubs, the federation's sporting code makes no allowance for acting in self-defence. Attempting to alter the outcome of a game is an offence and the two clubs were later hit with 30-point deductions for 2005-06, with more points docked for the following campaign.

They argued that in comparison to Juventus they'd done nothing, but the trio of clubs relegated in 2004-05 – Bologna, Brescia and Atalanta – were unsympathetic. They also knew how the system worked, but asked no favours and went down playing football.

Quite why Milan ever got involved is a mystery. Perhaps they realised what Juventus were up to and felt they were being denied titles that were rightfully theirs. Palazzi accused Adriano Galliani, Milan's vice-president, of backing the dodgy operations of the club's referees' assistant, Leonardo Meani: “Meani was in phone contact with linesmen, who were asked, when in doubt, to favour Milan, and Galliani approved.”

As Milan's links with friendly linesmen became public, the joke within Italian football circles was that Juve controlled the refs and Milan the linesmen, while Inter – perennial underachievers at that stage – controlled the ball boys.

By the end of May 2006, Carraro and Mazzini had resigned from the Italian federation and were joined by Pairetto and Bergamo. On July 14, five days after Italy's victory in the World Cup final, the federation's disciplinary tribunal handed out sentences:

Later, appeals further softened many of the penalties. Juventus remained in Serie B but with only nine points docked. They were stripped of two titles – the 2004-05 Scudetto was not reassigned to another club, but the 2005-06 title was awarded to Inter, making them champions for the first time since 1989.

Lazio and Fiorentina were back in Serie A, docked three and 15 points respectively for the 2006-07 season, plus 30 each for 2005-06. Milan had the same punishment for 2005-06, as well as eight deducted for 2006-07. Carraro's ban was reduced to an €80,000 fine.

The reduced sentences caused outrage. Giovanni Semeraro, president of Lecce, one of the clubs relegated in 2005-06, said: “It's something to be ashamed of, no?”

The verdicts had come against a background of increasing calls for clemency, or even a total amnesty, on the grounds that it wouldn't be fair to punish the clubs that had provided so many of Italy's World Cup winners. Populist politicians from both sides of parliament lined up to argue for mercy, and they were backed by the mayors of Rome, Turin and Florence. A member of the appeals panel admitted that the panel had also been worried about a violent reaction from fans if three teams – Juventus, Fiorentina and Lazio – had been kicked out of Serie A.

There were other factors in the softening of sentences. Lazio's case was strengthened considerably when the club was allowed to call as a witness Daniele Tombolini, the referee who had been in charge of Lazio vs Brescia, one of the games in which the Rome club was alleged to have sought favours. Tombolini told the appeals tribunal that, far from giving Lazio a hand, he'd made mistakes in the game that had favoured Brescia.

Milan appeared to have convinced the appeals tribunal that its referees' assistant, Leonardo Meani, had collaborated independently, and for whose actions the club should not be held directly responsible.

There remained an enigma at the heart of the matter. Moggi was widely recognised as a master of the transfer market. He'd never played at a high level, but had an eye for a player and discovered many who would go on to become legends. At Juve, he finally had the financial clout to hire Italy's best coaches and the world's top players.

By ‘signing up' referees, journalists and federation officials to the club's cause as well, according to investigators, he was admitting that the best wasn't good enough – a surprising lack of faith in his own abilities and an insult to a generation of great footballers, from Alessandro Del Piero to Zinedine Zidane.

Moggi continued to protest innocence, though, seeing himself as a scapegoat who had been ritually sacrificed to pay for the sins of an entire system, with no intention of going quietly.

Bayern Munich CEO Karl-Heinz Rummenigge probably spoke for many in European football when he said in August 2006: “I feel sorry for Juventus, but the important thing is that people like Moggi are not around any more.” Asked whether he would return to football, Moggi told the newspaper Repubblica: “Of course, but this time I'm going to be the guy who breaks everybody's balls. I'll finger them all, by their first names and surnames. I'll break the balls of all the false moralists who think that everything is clean now because they got rid of Luciano Moggi.”

This feature first appeared in the October 2006 issue of FourFourTwo

In June 2011, shortly before the expiry of his five-year suspension from football, Luciano Moggi was banned for life by the Italian Football Federation. Six months after that, Moggi was sentenced to five years and four months in prison for his part in the match-fixing scandal, although that was later reduced to two years and four months on appeal.

The jail term was then cancelled in 2015, when a court ruled that the statute of limitations had expired, though he wasn’t acquitted either.

After being demoted in 2006, Juventus overcame their nine-point deduction to win Serie B at the first attempt, aided by 20 goals from Alessandro Del Piero, who remained with the club. They finished third in their first campaign back in the top flight, before becoming champions once more in 2012, beginning a run of nine successive Serie A title wins.

The stain of Calciopoli never entirely left though – once the world’s finest league, Serie A now trails significantly behind its European rivals.

#1063. Florian Wirtz stars as Germany hammer Netherlands to top Nations League group

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Wirtz scored twice in a thumping 5-0 win as Germany, Netherlands and Greece finished level on 11 points in Group A2

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany hit four goals in 18 second-half minutes to thrash the Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin and reach the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners. Germany, the Netherlands and Greece all finished on 11 points in Group A2 after substitute Giorgos Masouras scored in the 69th minute to give Greece a 1-0 win over Serbia at home.

The Dutch advanced as runners-up and Greece finished third while Serbia ended the campaign without a point. It was the Netherlands' ​first ⁠defeat since Xavi Hernandez took charge in August. The Dutch had beaten Greece 7-0 three days earlier and needed a draw in Berlin to win the ⁠group.

Jurgen Klopp’s side entered Monday’s match third in the Group A2 standings and Derry Scherhant scored his first international goal with a stunning top-corner finish to put the hosts in front at the break. Germany then put in a ruthless second half display as Wirtz bagged a brace, while Nico Schlotterbeck and Brajan Gruda also got on the scoresheet to complete a stunning victory.

"We always hope we can give the fans a lot of enjoyment. And we enjoyed it very, very much ourselves, especially in the second half," Wirtz said.

Donyell Malen had a chance to put the visitors ahead but headed over from close range. Scherhant hit the post at the other end before cutting in from the left in the 41st minute and firing into the top corner for his first international goal. The 24-year-old Freiburg winger grew up ‌five minutes from the Olympiastadion, where he made his ‌Bundesliga debut for Hertha Berlin.

"What can I say? I don't think it could have gone any better. I couldn't even have dreamed of a better outcome. It's truly unbelievable. I had an incredible time out there and I'm just absolutely delighted," Scherhant said.

Wirtz doubled the lead on the hour with a left-footed drive from outside the box that went in off the far post. Schlotterbeck headed in Gruda's free kick five minutes later before Gruda set up Wirtz for a close-range finish in the 71st.

Gruda turned in a rebound in the 77th minute after Scherhant struck ​the post.

Germany's fifth goal secured top spot on head-to-head goal difference. ‌

The Dutch had last trailed by five ⁠goals in an international in 1959, when West Germany beat them 7-0 in ⁠Cologne.

Freddy Adu turned out for 13 clubs during a journeyman career

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the mid-2000s, Freddy Adu was earmarked as the next big thing in world football.

After making his professional debut as a 14-year-old for D.C. United in 2004, he became the youngest ever player to appear in professional sports in the United States. His international debut came at the age of 16, amid reported interest from some of Europe’s biggest clubs.

But the career that followed was a nomadic one, as his progress stalled and Adu would turn into something of a globetrotter in search of fresh opportunities.

This saw the American take in stints in Portugal, France, Greece and Serbia amongst other places, but Adu believes that a key issue with his career was the fact that these teams were often more interested in the marketing buzz that signing him would generate, rather than handing him opportunities on the pitch.

“I’d sign for teams, then you’d find out they were just trying to use you for the marketing part of it, to get eyeballs on their team,” Adu tells FourFourTwo.

“Then when you’re not playing for that team, it’s like ‘Why am I here? I’m living in a different country, I’m trying to get my career going and I’m not getting a chance to play’.

“At some point, you just figure out ‘This isn’t going to work out’.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For Adu, the mixed messages from clubs he signed for would prove to be extremely frustrating at times when he was looking to get his career back on track.

|There were so many different places where the front office wanted you, but the coach had different ideas,” he adds. “I’d been brought in under false pretences.

“Then you go to another team, sometimes you’re playing and it works out at the start, but then it doesn’t work out.

“After a while, it wasn’t fun any more, you start losing confidence in yourself, like ‘How am I here, and how am I not getting a chance to play here?’ You start questioning the reasons why you were brought in.”

For Adu, this cycle began in 2008, when Monaco brought him in initially on loan from Benfica for the 2008/09 season, before declining to make the move permanent at the end of that campaign.

“The whole thing started when I was in Monaco – the president wanted to bring me in, I knew him, I was cool with him, but the coach had different ideas.”

Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

Wales will finish bottom but could dent Portugal’s hopes of topping Group A4

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Wales bid to salvage some pride in the Nations League as they host Portugal in Cardiff.

Craig Bellamy’s team lost 3-1 to Norway on Saturday and will finish bottom of Group A4.

But they are safe from direct relegation and will instead enter the relegation/promotion play-offs in March regardless of tonight’s result.

Portugal are aiming to beat Denmark to top spot, and will be looking to bounce back from their shock 4-2 defeat to the Danes on Saturday.

Portugal were playing for the first time since the retirement of their record goalscorer and former captain Cristiano Ronaldo.

It will be shown live on BBC Two, BBC One Wales and S4C, with kick-off at 7:45pm GMT in Cardiff.

Wales will be without Neco Williams after the right-back picked up an injury in the defeat in Norway, while goalkeeper Karl Darlow is a doubt. Key midfielder Ethan Ampadu is suspended on Tuesday after picking up a second booking against Norway. Centre-back Ben Cabango and winger Sorba Thomas will be available after missing out in Oslo through suspension.

The draw will take place at 11am GMT on Friday 20 November.

#1059. Premier League TV presenter reports WhatsApp 'impersonator' to the police after they contacted a string of sport superstars pretending to be her

Published: 04:43 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 09:33 EST, 17 November 2026

Premier League presenter Ellie Collins issued a warning to her followers after learning that she had been being impersonated on social media.

The 26-year-old has over 58,000 followers on Instagram having built up a loyal fanbase via her work on broadcasters covering the top flight and NFL in the US.

But Collins was forced to make a statement after an imposter was found to have been reaching out to people in her name over a number of months.

'I want to make people aware that someone has been impersonating me on WhatsApp, messaging high-profile athletes, pretending to be me with their username set to my name and a picture of me,' she told her followers on the social media app.

'This has been happening on and off for several months and seems to be upping in frequency more recently.

'I have reported this to the police and they’ve asked that I share it on here to make people aware, particularly anyone I have worked with or connected with in the football/sports world.

Premier League presenter Ellie Collins has warned fans of an impersonator pretending to be her on social media (All photos source: Instagram/Ellie Collins)

The 26-year-old maintains an active presence on the site and has over 58,000 followers

After previously working as a waitress, Collins transitioned into broadcasting four years ago

Since starting her career in the media, Collins has had the opportunity to interview a number of sports stars including Frank Lampard

'If you receive a message from someone claiming to be me... it’s most likely not. If you don’t have my personal number and are unsure, just DM me on Instagram.

'If you receive anything suspicious, please send it to me directly so I can keep a record of it.

'Thank youuu (purple heart emoji, winking emoji),' she signed off.

Collins has worked in the media since joining IMG Media as an assistant five years ago.

Since 2022, the former waitress has served as a presenter for Premier League productions, which has led to opportunities to interview sports stars including Andy Robertson, John Terry, Bruno Fernandes, Conor Gallagher and Cody Gakpo.

Collins has also worked a number of events beyond the domestic league, such as Wimbledon and the 2025 Champions League final.

This year, she also covered the Open for Sky Sports from Royal Birkdale, and racing at York's Ebor Festival with ITV.

The Liverpool legend succeeded Joe Fagan in the Anfield dugout

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By 1985, Kenny Dalglish had already established himself as an all-time Liverpool great.

But after eight years as being the Reds’ talismanic force on the pitch, Dalglish was handed the opportunity to play an even bigger role at the club, when he was asked to succeed manager Joe Fagan.

While Dalglish would excel in his new dual player-manager position, it was not a role he had expected to take on, but he admits he was unable to refuse the offer.

“I don't know why the club asked me to become player-manager in 1985,” the Scot tells FourFourTwo.

“But they did, so I said, ‘OK, no problem for me. If that's what you want, I'll have a go.’”

For Dalglish, it was the structure and culture of the club that made what would be a daunting transition more manageable.

“The people around me were important – there was a vast experience in that dressing room, with the coaching staff, and Bob Paisley came back to help,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“He was fantastic. The people upstairs, the chief executive, they'd do all the negotiations for wages and transfers, I didn't want to be involved in money. It was really well organised.”

This backing from everyone in the club allowed Dalglish to focus on the on-pitch matters.

“They said, ‘All you can do is be your best' – to come out of the dressing room and sit in the manager's office, those were my team-mates and it was tough at times, but it wasn't something that you could turn down,” he adds.

And Dalglish’s best would prove to be more than good enough, as he would win the first of three league titles as manager of Liverpool in that very first season in his new role.
