Wirtz tests Henderson with a whipped attempt following Nyoni’s strong run and Munoz’s lay-off. However, the Palace captain makes a simple save.

Munoz tries to dribble away from Lerma, but the Liverpool substitute dives over the Palace man’s outstretched leg. Mac Allister then unnecessarily squares up to Lerma because of his annoyed reaction to Munoz’s simulation. As a result, all three of the aforementioned players are booked.

Palace can’t find a way past Alisson. Osorio drives down the wing and picks out the unmarked Pino, whose shot is smothered by the Liverpool goalkeeper. Lerma latches onto the loose ball, but Alisson is there once again to comfortably gather the Palace man’s ambitious rebound.

Liverpool continue to protect their two-goal advantage and make another forward change as Ngumoha comes on for Gakpo.

Sage makes an attacking change as Nketiah, who scored the winner against Liverpool at Selhurst Park in September 2025, replaces Strand Larsen up top.

In fairness to Palace, you can’t fault their effort. Liverpool are holding firm and the hosts are lacking end-product. Pino then catches Araujo with a late tackle to pick up a needless booking.

No need to be dramatic, but this does rather feel like the season for Pierre Sage. Losing games you have created the best chances in is a bad look for a manager under pressure, especially in the specific circumstances Palace are displaying. There is enough promise and talent in his team to suggest a different voice could extract more from the group. There is also a dreadful habit of switching off entirely, which might make a chairman wonder if it is time for more of a shouty presence in the dugout. The second Liverpool goal was woeful from a Palace point of view.

Iraola makes a double change as Nyoni and Munoz replace Szoboszlai and Barcola.

Alisson claims Wharton’s cross as Strand Larsen falls on the Liverpool goalkeeper. The Brazilian has been faultless today and looks well on the way to a deserved clean sheet as things stand.

The game has become quite chaotic and Palace’s shape has deserted them. If there’s another goal in this game, then it will be absolutely crucial. The hosts are waiting to craft a notable second-half chance.

Sage makes a change on the hour-mark as Osorio replaces Timber in the game’s first alteration.

Barcola is booked after halting a Palace counter with a forceful challenge through the back of Pino.

That second Liverpool goal has left Selhurst Park very deflated. All the noise is coming from the away fans. Mitchell’s makes a crucial intervention to block Barcola’s cross. Palace look so stretched now.

It’s an excellent team goal as two of Liverpool’s big-money attackers devastatingly combine. Barcola is released down the wing and finds Wirtz with a low, pinpoint cross. The German playmaker then sweeps a composed, first-time effort into the bottom corner, leaving Henderson rooted to the spot. It’s a wonderful finish and credit to Barcola for the assist. Palace are in trouble and have a mountain to climb.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Timber slides a pass in behind Jacquet for Strand Larsen to chase. However, Alisson is alert to the danger and rushes off his line to collect possession.

We are back under way at Selhurst Park. Both sides are unchanged at the break. Can Palace find a way back into this contest?

A thoroughly entertaining first half at Selhurst Park comes to a close as Liverpool hold a slender 1-0 lead over Palace thanks to Mac Allister’s 40th-minute header. Palace struck the bar through Pino and had a Strand Larsen goal ruled out for offside, but Liverpool have also looked dangerous going forward and their opener came as no surprise to anyone. To Palace’s credit, they’ve really taken the game to Liverpool so far, forcing Alisson into a couple of notable saves. However, there was still boos at half-time and Sage has work to do.

Much fury and gnashing of teeth towards the referee Tony Harrington at half time. The tunnel entrance takes players and officials past some of Palace’s most vociferous fans and several were giving him their most strident opinions.

Anger mostly towards the free kick which led to the goal, but it didn’t seem too egregious a decision to me.

Score is very harsh on Palace, though with Kamada, Strand Larsen and Pino all coming desperately close. Exactly the sort of hard luck story you’d expect from a team in trouble.

Palace score but the offside flag is up! Liverpool fail to clear a Palace corner as Mingueza finds Pino with a clipped cross. Palace strike the bar! The hosts make a rare foray forward as Mitchell finds Pino with a pinpoint cross. The Spaniard weaves into some space between two Liverpool defenders and slams a powerful half-volley against the woodwork.

Szoboszlai hangs a deep cross towards the back post. Gakpo directs it back across goal with a first-time volley, but no Liverpool has the attacking instinct to take a chance and anticipate it. Isak was instead loitering near the penalty spot. The visitors are well on top here.

Palace have been careless in possession so far, prompting groans from the home support. Szoboszlai draws a save from Henderson with a bobbling long-range strike, forcing the Palace captain into conceding a corner.

Liverpool are popping the ball around with real intent as Gakpo clips a teasing cross into Barcola. It’s just out of the winger’s reach, with Barcola claiming he was pushed by Mingueza. Fun start. Barcola the first example of a player obeying Iraola’s advice to go down more, collapsing from a gentle push after climbing for a header he was never like to reach. Gets short shrift from the referee and Palace fans.

It’s been a fast-paced and frantic start to this game. Isak’s delightful touch takes him away from Disasi, who pulls the Liverpool forward to the ground, giving the visitors a free kick. The Palace defender is perhaps lucky to avoid a yellow card for that foul.

Mitchell lashes a dangerous delivery across the six-yard box towards Strand Larsen, but solid defensive work from Van Dijk and Araujo allow Liverpool to clear.

Barcola lofts a ball over the top of Palace’s backline for Isak to latch onto. However, Disasi recovers well and blocks the Liverpool striker’s fierce half-volley from a tight angle.

A loose pass at the back from Palace gifts Liverpool an early opportunity, but Henderson does well to get down low and gather Mac Allister’s low, fizzing effort from outside the penalty area.

Liverpool get us under way at Selhurst Park. Can Iraola inflict more misery on Sage?

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Crystal Palace and Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

The pressure is building on Palace head coach Pierre Sage, who desperately needs a win to lift the mood and propel the club out of the relegation zone. Nottingham Forest’s impressive 3-1 win over Manchester City on Saturday evening means that Palace have dropped to a lowly 19th and are two points from safety. To make matters worse, Sage’s beleaguered side have also conceded the most goals in the division (21 in nine games).

On Thursday night, Daichi Kamada’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 home draw in the Europa League against Hoffenheim, after Palace delivered an alarmingly lacklustre performance.

Meanwhile, Liverpool also endured midweek European torment, as Andoni Iraola’s men fell to an error-ridden 3-2 defeat away at Fenerbahce in the Champions League, having previously lost 1-0 to Arsenal in their most recent Premier League encounter on Merseyside last weekend, which has left the club in sixth but just five points behind second-place Man City.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iraola said: “I think that’s the challenge, especially in a club like Liverpool. One week ago in this same press conference, we were on a run, everything was in a good place and we were in a better mood. And now, two defeats, it changes. It has to change and it has to be like this in a club like ours. Now we have to react after two defeats.”

As for Palace’s team news, Jean-Philippe Mateta is serving the first match of a three-game domestic ban after he was sent off for Palace in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham last time out in the league. Liverpool’s long-term absentees include Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong, while Ryan Gravenberch could also miss out after struggling with a heel injury.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news arriving shortly.

Beneath gathering rain clouds and surrounded by thousands of hectares of windswept heathland, FourFourTwo is staring at a 33-foot statue of Vladimir Lenin.

We're not in St Petersburg or Minsk – or any former Soviet nation, for that matter – but Denmark's Jutland peninsula, as it begins to drizzle with rain. It's so wild and remote that old Vlad is one of the few faces we've seen since arriving this morning. Much like the Russian revolutionary – carved in bronze, suspended in mid-air and lying flat on his back, just like at his Moscow mausoleum – we're beginning to wonder what the hell we're doing here.

“We like to imagine that Lenin is contemplating all the terrible things he did in life,” explains Birgitte Damgaard, the proprietor of the land the statue now calls home. Birgitte's father, a local textiles tycoon and art collector, vowed to rescue the statue after watching television footage of it being toppled by Latvians during the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. “It was brought more than 500 miles – first by truck, then by ship,” she tells FFT, after we stop by for a look. “He's been lying here, staring up at the sky, for more than 30 years.”

We're a few miles outside the town of Herning, although our own reasons for being here are more straightforward – we've come to witness a football match between local side Midtjylland and league leaders FC Copenhagen. At first glance, you'd be forgiven for thinking this is a complete mismatch.

From the capital, Copenhagen are Denmark's most successful club, with a record 16 league titles. Midtjylland, meanwhile, were only founded in 1999 following the merger of two second-tier rivals, and hail from a town with fewer than 60,000 inhabitants.

Yet the latter have rapidly grown into one of the country's most formidable sides, claiming four league titles in the past 12 seasons. Last term they won the Danish Cup, and beat both Celtic and Nottingham Forest in the Europa League. When we arrive, they trail only Copenhagen in the domestic league, heading into their table-topping clash. How have they managed it all?

We wave goodbye to Lenin and Birgitte in search of answers, driving through eerily quiet farmland outside Herning, to what appears to be a bunker from 007 adventure GoldenEye. Grey and austere, the building doesn't instantly strike you as welcoming – it turns out we couldn't be more wrong.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“We call this club the miracle from out of nowhere,” beams Midtjylland's bespectacled chairman Claus Steinlein, who shakes our hand enthusiastically before welcoming us into the warmth of the club's Dream 99 training complex. “Allow us to show you why.”

Opened in 2023, Dream 99 boasts a network of pristine football pitches, as well as a spa and gym. Steinlein leads us to a mural depicting the history of the club; a collage of black and white photos resembling newspaper cutouts. It's time for a history lesson.

“Midtjylland were formed from a merger between Herning Fremad and IFS,” he explains, pointing out a photo of the day the clubs came together – the suited, smiling chairmen shaking hands. “The name honours the Jutland province.” Indeed, Midtjylland means ‘Mid-Jutland' in Danish.

“We vowed from the start to become the biggest club in Denmark,” Steinlein adds. “People told us we were crazy. We knew that if we were to prove them wrong, we'd have to be different.”

Steinlein himself saw a way to help the new club stand out. “At that time, no Danish club had its own academy,” he says. “At least not with dedicated programmes. I wanted to be the first.”

Steinlein visited the academy of French side Nantes to learn what he could, returning with a blueprint for success. He asked the board to invest a massive chunk of its fledgling budget – around €800,000 – and, to his initial shock, they agreed. There was just one problem.

“Nobody wanted to send their kids here,” laughs Steinlein. “Children here grow up wanting to play for Brondby or Copenhagen, rather than Midtjylland. Convincing people was the first battle.”

A breakthrough came via Midtjylland's own kit man, who agreed to bring his 12-year-old son with him when taking the job. “It helped that his son was Simon Kjaer,” Steinlein says. “Simon went on to make more than 100 appearances for Denmark.”

Kjaer made a handful of first-team showings after graduating from the academy in 2007, before being sold to Palermo for €4m – a huge sum for a young Dane at the time. Steinlein's academy received a huge financial and reputational boost. “That gave our project the lift-off it needed,” he says.

Midtjylland began painstakingly forming partnerships across the region, more than 100 amateur sides regularly sending their best and brightest for trials. In exchange, Midtjylland provide equipment and tickets to first-team games. “It's about inspiring the next generation,” adds Steinlein.

Neither are Midtjylland's operations limited to the best Danish talent. We're led into an office to meet Jonas Dal, who heads the club's Nigerian academy.

“Every year, more than seven million children are born in Nigeria, compared with about 50,000 here, so the pool of talent is naturally much larger,” says Dal, who was once held at gunpoint during a visit to Lagos, but plays a key role in the Midtjylland project. “We bring over the most promising players. We have to be patient with them, because the weather and culture in Denmark are all very new to them.”

Right on cue, we meet Rilwan Hassan, who joined Midtjylland from the Lagos academy in 2010, before spending close to a decade playing for the club. He's now a coach with the academy. “It was so cold,” he recalls of his arrival as a teen. “But it was a massive opportunity. I was going into the unknown, but I quickly found out that this club was striving to be the very best. Everybody was pulling in the same direction.”

Many of Midtjylland's academy products, either from Nigeria or closer to home, are lured to the club with the promise they'll be sold if a bigger side comes in for them. Indeed, selling players has become a key aspect of Midtjylland's model. “If Liverpool or Barcelona come in for one of our players, that's perfect,” says Steinlein. “It means they've performed well and we can profit. Everybody wins.”

Following their formation, Midtjylland were immediately promoted to the top flight, before cementing themselves as consistent top-five finishers. Yet while results and youth development were impressive, they were beginning to struggle financially. Player sales barely covered the growing cost of operations, especially with European qualification hardly guaranteed each season.

“We'd wanted to become the biggest and best team in Denmark, but we were still some way off that,” winces Steinlein. “That soon changed, though.” The man who would help them take that next step was an Englishman with a physics degree, already making a name for himself at Brentford.

In June 2012, Matthew Benham had taken control of the Bees, then in League One, having made millions as the impresario of Smartodds – a company providing statistical analysis on sporting events to professional gamblers. That data also gave Benham extraordinary insight into how football games are won and lost, where and how goals are most often scored, and which players were being undervalued by the market. In short, a recipe for success.

That same year also saw Benham invite a Danish author to give a presentation to his staff. Benham had become fascinated by Rasmus Ankersen's book The Gold Mine Effect, which looked into cultural anomalies, such as why Jamaica consistently produces the best sprinters. Ankersen was equally impressed with Benham.

“At the time, Brentford were third in League One, and there were a couple of games to go,” the Dane would later recall. “I said to him, ‘What are the chances of you guys getting promoted?' When you ask that question, you expect an emotional yes or no, but he just said, ‘There's a 42.3 per cent chance.' That was when I knew he was a guy who was thinking very differently.”

Benham and Ankersen, the latter a promising player at Midtjylland before injury sent him down a different path, became firm friends. In 2014, the Dane convinced the data guru to invest in a second football club, with Benham paying £6.2m for a majority stake in Midtjylland. He brought with him his legion of statisticians, sports scientists and coaches. It was about to go turbo.

“This club now has tools to evaluate teams and players with much more accuracy using data,” said Ankersen, who was swiftly installed as chairman by Benham. “The model we're using could be applied in any country.”

Midtjylland's strategy was transformed overnight. “Set-pieces then became a fundamental part of the way we played,” Steinlein tells us on the balcony of the training complex, which overlooks the first-team's pitches. “They still are. We boast one of the tallest teams in Europe. We hire the best set-piece coaches and, when it comes to scouting, things like long-throws are key attributes. The approach has been successful.”

In Benham's first year, Midtjylland were crowned Danish champions; their first major trophy. The team finished with a goal difference of plus 15 from set-pieces. “We were finally the best club in Denmark,” grins Steinlein. “A dream come true. Benham's stats and our focus on set-pieces were key.”

We boast one of the tallest teams in Europe. We hire the best set-piece coaches and, when it comes to scouting, things like long-throws are key attributes

Next, Steinlein leads us into the main communal area of Dream 99. Above the only coffee machine in the building, where footfall is at its highest, a chart denoting Midtjylland's historical success from set-pieces adorns the wall. The 2015, 2018, 2020, 2024 and 2025 campaigns are highlighted as being particularly prolific – the Wolves won the league four out of five of those years.

“That one time we didn't win the title still bothers us,” laughs Steinlein. “We want our players and staff to be hurt by that, too. Topping this chart needs to be their motivation.”

Benham sold his stake in Midtjylland in 2023 to better focus on Brentford, though the two sides retain a close partnership. Today the club is owned by fashion tycoon Anders Holch Povlsen, Denmark's richest person, with an estimated worth of more than £12bn.

Ankersen has also departed, though his influence is still felt. A school called Guldminen, named after his book, was built into the Dream 99 complex. It aims to nurture both the best young sporting and academic talent in Denmark. FFT learns that students are given free rein of the building, meaning it isn't unusual for first-team players and schoolkids to share meals.

“We have a word for the environment we've fostered here: ‘sammenhold,'” says Steinlein. “It literally translates to ‘unity club', but it means so much more than that. It's about every person, from the kids to the first-teamers, coaches and cleaners, feeling part of something bigger. We are one entity. That's what sammenhold is, and it's our way of life.”

Overwhelmed by the scale and passion behind the Midtjylland project, FFT waves goodbye to the dream factory and makes our way over to the MCH Arena for tonight's crucial showdown against FC Copenhagen.

Inside the 12,000-capacity stadium, opened in 2004, FFT catch up with fans who are noisily drinking beer out of plastic cups and watching Brondby's early fixture on a big screen. Ahead of kick-off, we chat to lifelong Midtjylland fan Thomas Schouv Jacobsen. “My father is from Ikast, one of the two clubs that merged into Midtjylland,” he says. “Supporting this club since the start has been an extraordinary ride. The jump from winning a few silver medals to actually taking our first ever title in 2015 was indescribable. Seeing my father's face when we scored the decisive goal in the decisive match against Copenhagen is something that I'll never forget.”

Midtjylland's record against title rivals Copenhagen is certainly impressive.

Going into this game, the latter have won just twice in their past 14 meetings, with Midtjylland winning seven. Tonight, however, there's a fear that the league leaders might be too strong, especially given that regular Midtjylland defenders Rasmus Kristensen, Magnus Jensen and Martin Erlic are all out injured.

“We've had terrible setbacks in defence this season,” Jacobsen laments. “But, come May, we should have a very good chance of taking the championship. I think we have the best squad and the ability to come out successful.”

FFT also catches a moment with a Copenhagen fan. “We're massively important to Danish football because we have the biggest fanbase and play European football every year,” says lifelong supporter Kevin Willendrup.

“We're the flagship club. Our games against Brondby are by far the biggest in Denmark. There isn't the same level of hatred between the Midtjylland and Copenhagen fanbases – they've become extremely good in a very short space of time. Along with us, they're favourites to win the league every season. It's great that another team has emerged with so much quality.”

Yet there's no doubt in Willendrup's mind who'll emerge victorious tonight. “Copenhagen will win here for the first time in a long time,” he says. “We're on an incredible run under Bo Svensson and we're starting to look like a championship-winning team.”

As fans around us drain their beers and head inside, FFT does the same. We emerge onto the terraces to a magnificent sight. It's a record crowd, as flags swirl from the melee behind either end of the field. To our right, the home fans bellow into the evening sky and beat war drums. Off to our left, the white-clad Copenhagen fans are making their own thunderous racket.

Pitchside for the warm-ups, we see some familiar faces, including former Bournemouth beanpole Philip Billing, now at Midtjylland, and the ex-Cardiff targetman Andreas Cornelius, who is among the visitors' line-up. Curiously, Midtjylland's warm-up routine involves pain-staking set-piece practice; coaches repeatedly whipping vicious free-kicks into a packed box of giants.

As the players head inside to make their final preparations, we brush past former Everton and Real Madrid hard man Thomas Gravesen, who has presumably been loaned to a Danish TV outlet by the poker tables of Las Vegas. “Should be a good night tonight, guys,” he winks. “This is one of the biggest games of the season.”

The players emerge before kick-off to a deafening roar – the tifos, flags and rhythmic beating of drums providing an epic backdrop – before getting the game underway beneath the floodlights.

Copenhagen swiftly take charge but their dominance doesn't last. In the 12th minute, Midtjylland win a free-kick high on the left, not far from the corner flag. As Billing fizzes it in, FFT remarks that it's silly he isn't in the box himself given his size. He quickly shows us what we know, planting a ball squarely on to the head of onrushing Nigerian forward Friday Etim, whose effort crashes into the net to make it 1-0. Recorded wolf howls are played over the PA system as the roof comes off the MCH Arena.

Copenhagen dust themselves down and settle back into their rhythm, knocking the ball around menacingly, but they're unable to find a way through as Midtjylland's makeshift defence, marshalled by the imperious Andreas Maxso, clear everything.

Such low-block defending inevitably leads to mistakes, however, and one arrives just after the break, as wing-back Kjell Watjen fells Copenhagen skipper Thomas Delaney just inside the penalty area. The referee points to the spot and former Southampton star Mohamed Elyounoussi slots in an equaliser. The Copenhagen fans go wild.

The visitors take their possession up a notch. Robert Silva slaloms down the left and into the Midtjylland box, but his cutback is prodded away before the rebound is fired wide. Surely it's just a matter of time before they score again.

Then the unthinkable happens for the league leaders in the 62nd minute. Under very little pressure, Copenhagen goalkeeper Diant Ramaj passes straight to opponent Etim, who rounds the shot-stopper and shapes to pull the trigger, only to find his path blocked by recovering defenders.

As an entire stadium holds its breath, Etim squares the ball to Denil Castillo, arriving in support. The Ecuadorian fires low and hard into the Copenhagen net, and Midtjylland are in the lead once more, courtesy of a horrific error. Clearly shaken, Copenhagen never recover their rhythm. When the final whistle blows half an hour later, it's pure ecstasy for the Wolves supporters.

FFT rush onto the field to join the Midtjylland players as they celebrate in front of the frenzied home end. Arm in arm, players and coaches bounce in front of the melee, as we grab a word with Billing. “It's amazing when a result like this comes off,” he yells above the bedlam, with a huge smile on his face.

“We knew they'd play nice football, but that we could win it with our set plays and our physicality. We had to cope with a lot of injuries today, so the fact we came out of this game with a win is massive for us.”

When the players are finally separated from their adoring public, we're invited to join them inside. The dressing room is packed as victorious manager Mike Tullberg delivers a rousing speech in front of players, board members, staff and children. This must be what Steinlein meant by sammenhold. “I'm proud of you today, guys,” he says, singling out Maxso and his fellow defenders for an extraordinary performance. “There's a long way to go but we've given our ambitions a huge boost.”

A post shared by FourFourTwo (@fourfourtwouk)

Castillo, scorer of the winning goal, is also singled out in surprising fashion by the boss. “You've recently surpassed 100 games for us and what a way to cap it off,” Tullberg enthuses. “You keep playing like that and you won't be here for another 100.”

The whole room then erupts into an obscure song – a tradition that also sees players dancing and banging their lockers to the beat (watch the video above). It's a joyous scene. Afterwards, we head into chairman Steinlein's personal office, resembling a wood-panelled smoking room. The likes of Kenny Dalglish and Louis van Gaal have been guests here before us.

Drinks begin flowing and, at some point, FFT is only vaguely aware that the night is coming to an end. When we finally head back out into the cold Scandinavian air, it's with a sense that we've witnessed something truly spectacular – a wonder from nowhere.

With this result, there are just two points between Denmark's leading sides – one of them a traditional giant from an illustrious European city, the other a motley crew of dreamers and disrupters who refuse to accept the status quo.

It's the sort of revolution Vladimir Lenin, now lying flat on his back on a rain-soaked heath in our rear-view mirror, might have approved of.

Ed is a staff writer at FourFourTwo, working across the magazine and website. A German speaker, he’s been working as a football reporter in Berlin since 2015, predominantly covering the Bundesliga and Germany's national team. Favourite FFT features include an exclusive interview with Jude Bellingham following the youngster’s move to Borussia Dortmund in 2020, a history of the Berlin Derby since the fall of the Wall and a celebration of Kevin Keegan’s playing career.

#1039. Juventus midfielder admits Mauricio Pochettino could sign United States players at Man United

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Weston McKennie has suggested several USMNT players could follow the Argentine to Old Trafford

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie has suggested several US players could follow outgoing boss Mauricio Pochettino to Manchester United, after the Argentine succeeded the sacked Michael Carrick as head coach.

Pochettino has remained with the USMNT squad for their Nations League fixtures in this international window, both against Haiti, before he heads for Old Trafford.

And McKennie suggested several players could potentially follow the manager as he sets about a rebuild of the struggling side, who are currently in the Premier League relegation zone.

Speaking at a press conference, McKennie said: “USMNT players at Manchester United? I think that, obviously, the time Pochettino spent here allowed him to appreciate this squad and see the quality it has to offer.

“And yes, I think it's a possibility. We have a lot of guys on this team who will probably make a move soon or within the next year. So I think the links are somewhat inevitable.

“At the end of the day, though, you never know what's going through a manager’s head or what kind of players he's looking for.

“Still, I think you could see a few of us linked with United, and maybe it will actually happen.”

Pochettino is taking several of his staff with him to United, with goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez, assistant Jesus Perez and fitness coach Sebastian Pochettino having already left for England after the US’ 6-0 victory over Haiti on Saturday.

Assistant coach Miguel D’Agostino, fitness coach Sylvia Tuya Vinas and analyst Alex Scott will follow them after Tuesday’s second leg of the quarter-finals.

Pochettino said on Monday: “That was the plan when we agreed terms with Manchester United and with the national team. They are preparing all there because Wednesday when we arrive, it’s going to be nonstop, and then start with playing games. We are focused here into finishing the best way.”

For his part, the former Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea boss refused to be drawn into speculation over whether he will sign some of his former US charges in the winter transfer window.

He said: “All the good players always have dreams to reach the (highest) level, and United is one of the teams in that level.

“In case some decisions need to be made, we are going to pay attention to the players we know really well.”

The former Inter and Argentina great has played with some of his era’s best players

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Javier Zanetti spent more than two decades playing against and alongside the planet’s very best footballers.

It’s therefore fair to say that the former Inter Milan and Argentina stalwart knows a thing or two about identifying world-class players.

Despite this, two of the entries in his all-time XI that he has given to FourFourTwo may raise an eyebrow among Manchester United fans.

The first is Juan Sebastian Veron, who arrived at Old Trafford in 2001 with an enormous reputation and a hefty £28million price tag, having impressed in Serie with Sampdoria, Parma and Lazio.

And while the midfielder would fail to reproduce his best form in England, Zanetti remains convinced of his former Argentine teammate’s ability.

“A box-to-box midfielder with enormous quality,” he tells FourFourTwo. “He could dictate play like no one else, mixing short and long passes with that wonderful right foot of his.”

Zanetti also highlights just how complete Veron’s game was.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I rarely saw him give the ball away… He also had a ferocious shot from distance, we're talking thunderbolts. He was a magnificent midfielder.”

While Veron’s qualities were immediately apparent, Zanetti believes that another former Argentina and Manchester United star did not always get the recognition he deserved.

The Red Devils broke their transfer record to sign £59.7million Angel Di Maria in 2014, but like Veron, was unable to recreate his best form at Old Trafford.

“Going forward, he is a nightmare for defenders, always creating danger,” Zanetti insists.

“But people forget just how hard he works without the ball and how much he does to keep the team balanced.

“He has been essential in every final Argentina have played, the 2008 Olympics, the 2021 Copa America, the 2022 World Cup.”

In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

The future Liverpool legend was born and raised in Glasgow

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During his 22-year playing career, Kenny Dalglish became one of the greatest players in British football history.

After winning no less than four Scottish titles and another four Scottish Cups with Celtic, Dalglish made the move south of the border in 1977, where his achievements with Liverpool outstripped even those he accomplished at Celtic Park.

But it was in Glasgow where the foundations of this great career were laid, from Sunday morning kickabouts and makeshift goalposts and onto amatuer football and apprenticeships.

“My dad took me to the football when I was a wee boy, so I started to get into it and we had a bit of grass in the back garden, six-by-six – after the game, I'd go back and have a kickabout there with my dad,” Dalglish reminises to FourFourTwo. “He was a Rangers fan, so he took me there – my first hero was a player that no-one would have heard of now, a centre-forward named Don Kitchenbrand. I thought, ‘He must be good, he scores goals all the time!'

While Dalglish would end his career with almost 350 goals, he started further back on the pitch.

“When I was seven, I played as a goalkeeper before moving outfield – one of the boys' dads must have been a plumber, because they used to get these wee poles and fit posts onto a crossbar, then got nets from somewhere,” he continues.

“That was our wee team on a Sunday. “Why did I become a good player? I never thought I was that good – it was for other people to think that. A lot of people help you on the way – the most important person is the one who starts you off, and that was my dad. I'd play for school on a Saturday morning, then my amateur club in the afternoon. Mum was there too – there was never enough money, so if there was a tear in a sock, the mothers were there with a knitting needle. They took turns washing the strips as well. It was really communal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“When I was 14, we moved to high-rise flats near Ibrox. I was about to leave school – you left at 15 then – and I'd been playing football with the school, as well as an amateur club, Possil YM. I got into the Glasgow Schools under-13s, under-14s and under-15s teams – I could have gone to a new school near the flats we moved to, but thought, ‘I've been to my school since I was young, I don't want another one to get the credit.'

“It was only right that the school where I was educated – supposedly! – was where I got into the Scottish squad. “The guy who took the Glasgow team was very prominent with the Scottish schoolboys – they got beat once, so he said, ‘This boy could come and play.'

“Then when you're leaving school, they put a piece of paper in front of you and say, ‘Get yourself a job.' That was a very limited choice for me, but my first job was as a van boy, delivering school books – they were educational books, but I never read any of them!

“At my amateur club Glasgow United, we had a really good team and you could join a professional club at 15 as an apprentice, but I thought it would be more advantageous to try to get a trade instead. At a club, all you were doing in the summer was painting the crossbar or the terraces, doing something to help the groundsman.

“I thought it would be a good idea to have a trade, so I got a job as an apprentice joiner. At that point, I was training twice a week with a semi-professional team, Cumbernauld United, but if I wasn't going to be a footballer, at least I'd have had something to fall back on.

“I’d be a tradesman. It's just as well as football worked out for me, because I wasn't much cop with a saw and chisel…”

#1036. Chelsea handed huge Emi Martinez injury boost with keeper to make Argentina return

Martinez has not played a minute since suffering a fractured jaw in Chelsea’s win over Everton last month

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Emi Martinez is poised for a return to action on Tuesday night in a huge boost for Chelsea.

The 34-year-old goalkeeper underwent surgery after fracturing his jaw during Chelsea’s 2-0 win at Everton in October, though manager Xabi Alonso revealed he was ahead of schedule in his recovery when he returned to training earlier this month.

Despite not playing a minute since suffering the injury, Martinez was called up Lionel Scaloni for Argentina’s November internationals.

And after not featuring in the 2-1 defeat to Uruguay on Friday, Scaloni confirmed that Martinez will be start in between the sticks for a friendly against Costa Rica in Cordoba.

“Emiliano is going ⁠to play in goal, he'll be there," Scaloni told reporters.

"Maybe he was fit for the previous match, ‌but it was a risk, ​and since we trust ‌Gero [Geronimo Rulli], Juan [Musso] ⁠and Santi [Santiago Beltran], we ⁠chose to look after him. An extra ‌three ​days was a ‌prudent choice."

Martinez was in contention to feature for Chelsea in their last match before the international break, but Alonso opted for deputy Mike Penders as the Blues lost 1-0 to Sunderland in contentious fashion.

Chelsea have won one and lost three during 21-year-old Penders’ run in goal, though the highly-rated Belgian keeper did impress in a 2-0 win over Manchester United at the end of October.

Martinez’s return to action will likely spell the end for Penders’ stint, though, with the Argentinian now on course to start for Chelsea when they host Leeds on Saturday.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For many, Peter Schmeichel was the greatest goalkeeper of his generation.

The Dane enjoyed a trophy-laden career with Manchester United and also played a huge part in helping his country to a remarkable European Championship victory in 1992.

Schmeichel would eventually be succeeded as Denmark’s No. 1 by Thomas Sorensen, with the former Sunderland stopper able able to benefit from training alongside his legendary compatriot.

“There was nothing better than watching him train,” Sorensen tells FourFourTwo. “It was great because you could see him firsthand and get a lot of experience.

There were times, however, when Schmeichel’s formidable reputation came to the fore at training.

“It was also pretty intimidating,” Sorensen adds. “He could be quite rough sometimes. He’d put me in my place. One day he’d be my best friend and the next he wouldn’t even say, ‘Good morning’ to me.”

But as the pair have got old, this relationship has mellowed.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“He was a strange character in some ways, but I’ve gotten to know him a lot better over the years and I’m still good friends with his son Kasper,” he adds. “He’s totally different now than he was in his playing days.”

Schmeichel called time on his international career in 2001, leaving Sorensen with the somewhat tough task of replacing an all-time great in the Danish team.

“It wasn’t just me – there were a few of us dubbed ‘The next Peter Schmeichel’,” Sorensen recalls.

“I ended up being the winning horse. From the outset, I knew I was different from him and wanted to do it my way. He was very loud, outspoken and aggressive on the pitch. I was a little bit calmer.

“I came in at the right time because I’ve spoken to a lot of goalkeepers who were in his shadow for years and never got the chance. It probably wasn’t as hard as people think. We had success as a team and I played some good games. That always helps.

“He wasn’t forgotten, but that changeover was accepted pretty quickly.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1033. Fan who racially abused Kylian Mbappe at LaLiga match avoids prison time

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The fan abused Mbappe during Real Madrid’s win at Real Oviedo in August 2025

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A fan who racially abused Kylian Mbappe during a LaLiga match last year has been handed an 11-month suspended prison sentence after being convicted of a hate crime.

The suspension of the sentence is conditional on the unnamed fan not attending football stadiums for any official sports competitions for two years.

The individual has also been handed a fine along with “various disqualification penalties”, Real Madrid said in a statement.

“This ruling adds to the criminal convictions already issued for racist insults against Real Madrid players at the Mestalla, Son Moix, Vallecas, and José Zorrilla stadiums,” the club statement continued.

“Real Madrid, which has acted as a private prosecutor in this case and continues to do so in others involving similar incidents, reaffirms its commitment to combating racism and eradicating any racist behavior in football and sports.”

The incident occurred during Real Madrid’s 3-0 win over Real Oviedo at the Carlos Tartiere Stadium in August 2025, during which Mbappe bagged a brace.

Vinicius Jr, who has been persistently targeted with racist abuse at multiple stadiums in Spain as well as online, also scored in the match.

After the match, LaLiga reported alleged racist chanting towards Mbappe and Vinicius to Spain’s National Police, with the league alleging that chants imitating monkey sounds were heard on multiple occasions.

In March 2024, Vinicius broke down in tears during an emotional press conference as he bemoaned that racism was getting worse as perpetrators were going unpunished.

“I just want to play football but it’s hard to move forward… I feel less and less like playing (due to the racist abuse),” he said.

#1032. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

Sunderland have a throw inside the Chelsea half - this is about game management for the side in dire need of a win now...

Angulo nrings down his man after a poor pass from Sadiki. The visitors with a free-kick inside their own half.

Emegha drifts past Mukiele before he feels the full force of a Luke O’Nein tackle. It looks as though he gets the ball but the ref awards the free-kick. It’s in the final third, can Chelsea create anything from this?

In short ‘yes’, Estevao delivers a peach of a ball and Welbeck gets on the end of it. BUT his header is over, when it seemed easier to hit the target.

Sunderland in Chelsea half, they’re looking for a free-kick as Angulo goes down. The referee isn’t having any of it...

Sunderland break at pace (only the second time this half) Isador finds Talbi who is free before cutting inside and unleashing a shot from outside the box. It’s just wide, don’t think it was too far away though.

Talbi is off for Angulo, Rigg on for Le Fee for Sunderland, and for Chelsea, Henderson makes way for Emegha.

For all their possession this half Chelsea have not forced Roefs into a meaningful save. The west Londoners are again dominating possession in and near the hinterland of the Sunderland box, but it’s all a bit after you Claude and ultimately Roefs gladly picks up an anaemic cross. That sums up Chelsea as an attacking force today.

Chelsea corner after Geovany Quenda gets in a shot from the left-side of the area that gets a tiny hint of a deflection. Roefs punches away the set-piece and Sunderland breathe a sigh of relief.

Better from Sunderland, there are spaces in behind Chelsea as the visitors go in search of the equaliser and over the past few minutes the hosts have found them.

Lovely ball from Reinildo finds Sadiki in space on the left, they keep the ball brilliantly before Le Fee plays in Isador, it’s a one-on-one and all the Frenchman has to do it dink it over the on-rushing keeper. He goes low, however, and Penders makes a fine save - that was the game for Sunderland there...Penders has kept Chelsea in this.

Brobbey may have been tiring but without him Sunderland cannot keep the ball. Sadiki earns a free-kick which takes a bit of pressure off the hosts.

Palmer pulls back for Gusto whose dinky, cheeky chip tries to find Roefs off his line. He doesn’t succeed and the Dutch goalkeeper claims with ease.

Chelsea still seeing plenty of the ball, Sunderland may well be tiring. It’s hard to keep up that intensity for 90 minutes, hence Isador on for Brobbey, but they are struggling to keep the ball at the moment.

The first half was lively and entertaining, this half has been lively and lacking in anything that could be remotely described as a spectacle...

Rogers tries to find Palmer, but the ball is too long and Roefs gobbles up with ease.

Meanwhile, Hume looks injured and Chelsea do not give the ball back after Sunderland kicked it off. You won’t be shocked to hear that the home fans are not happy with that...

Change for Sunderland, Brobbey off for Isador. The Dutchman has been brilliant today, he might have scored a couple of goals, but despite not finding the back of the net he has proved a handful for the Chelsea backline. I would have kept him on for longer...

Chelsea looking better this half, they’re seeing plenty of the ball but have not had a shot on goal since the break. In fact there have only been two touches in either box this 45...Sunderland won’t mind that at 1-0.

ON - Welbeck and GustoOFF - Neto and Palestra

So Alonso has opted for a physical presence up front.

No sooner had I pressed send on that last post than Chelsea break through the middle but some great last-ditch defending from Muenier prevents Estevao from getting a shot at goal.

Chelsea haven’t been able to play through Sunderland and you think they’d need to bring on a physical presence up front if that’s to change.

Another chance for Sunderland - they break down the right before Hume sends in a low ball to the penalty box, it’s met first time by Le Fee, I think, and Penders saves low to his right. To state the obvious, the hosts would love a second to give them a deserved cushion. As I typed that last but the linesman has his flag up, it wouldn’t have counted, promising signs nonetheless.

Pressure from Sunderland. A good bit of possession ends with Mukiele swinging in a lovely cross from the right which Chelsea are forced to head clear for a corner. Nothing results from the set piece, but things still looking promising for Sunderland who look as energetic and ‘at it’ as they did in the first half.

Rogers picks up the ball in the middle just inside the Sunderland half and is immediately pick-pocketed by one of three Sunderland players. The Chelsea men have not been allowed to settle when they have a sniff of a mini counter.

Good, feisty opening to this half, Chelsea look more up for it, though to be fair they couldn’t look any more insipid than they did in the first 45. Meanwhile, Brobbey shoves Lavia and earns a yellow. Think that’s three yellows for the hosts now.

It is going to be fascinating to see how a team with well known - and long standing - disciplinary issues copes with a pressurised pursuit of an equaliser. There have already been a couple of flash points that Chelsea’s players have reacted to and it wouldn’t be the wildest thing to predict referee Jarred Gillett brandishing a red card before the end of the game. Watch it unfold with interest.

Brobbey lays the ball off for Meunier in the final third, it’s asking a lot of the Belgian but his compounds the Dutchman’s error with one of his own - stretching for the ball and taking out Caicedo. Something for which he earns a needless yellow card.

There’s a bit of argy bargy on the pitch, not sure what started that but the referee Jarred Gillett has to have a word with several players. All a bit of handbags really.

They’re back under way on the banks of the Wear. Chelsea have been insipid and you imagine they won’t be as bed these next 45 minutes. Can Sunderland play with the same aggression and energy? We’re about to find out.

Changes Estevao on for Colwill, interesting substitution to say the least...

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The half ends with an audacious attempt at goal from Rogers, a full 40 yards out from a free kick. It’s catching practice for Roefs and that sums up Chelsea as an attacking force in the first 45. Sunderland are well worth their lead.

Rogers has a shot-cum-cross from the left and it sails high, wide and not so handsome. He’s been on the periphery this half, as has Palmer and that explains as much as anything why they are behind. Sunderland have cut out the supply to him and Roefs has had little to do as a result.

Approaching half-time and save for the contentious VAR call when he wanted a penalty, Cole Palmer has done absolutely nothing. The talk of him being in the England squad, on this evidence, is for the birds. Sunderland are full value for their half-time lead. Chelsea, like Palmer, have been absolutely insipid.

There will be five minutes added time in this first half.

Something I’ve not written much this half ‘chance for Chelsea’. Neto works a bit of space in the inside-right channel outside the box, but his shot is easily saved by Roefs.

Talbi attacks down the left but cuts in when he would have been better served going wide.

Chelsea have seen plenty of the ball but they’ve been way too slow and cumbersome with it. It’s been in front of the Sunderland back lines and easy to defend against. The hosts are letting the visitors have the ball wide and with Neto in the middle, it’s been too easy for Le Bris’s men.

Brobbey wants the ball at every opportunity and Sunderland would be well advised to give it to him. Colwill is has his hands full.

Sunderland have kept the aggression and energy throughout the half - and kept Chelsea quiet as a result. As I type that the hosts give Lavia too much room 25 yards out and his shot is well wide of the left-hand post.

The lead is no more than Sunderland deserve and that means, as the table stands, Manchester United are bottom of the Premier League. Fair play to Enzo Le Fee for keeping his nerve in a pressure situation. Sunderland needed him to be cool.

First chance of the game for Chelsea and, as with Brobbey 10 minutes ago, it should have found the back of the net. Rogers is the culprit - he sends his header wide of the right post after a grade-A cross from Palestra.

One-all in terms of great chances...but the score remains 0-0.

Sunderland have looked the better side so far and have had the better chances.

Neto is in the Sunderland half but three Sunderland players snap at his heels like a hyperactive dog after a bone. Chelsea haven’t been allowed to settle yet. Plenty of time to go though...

Chelsea with the early possession, but they go backwards and the hosts are up and at them with the press and the visitors have to go back to Penders in goal.

As the Stadium of Light remembers all those who lost their lives in war.

Xabi Alonso has confirmed he has been picked because of the quality he provides, rather than any sentimental value, and Regis Le Bris revealed ahead of the fixture he tried to bring the England international home during the summer window, when Chelsea attempted to sign Granit Xhaka.

“Jordan is a great player, first of all,” said Le Bris. “For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo [Ghisolfi, director of football] and Kyril [Louis-Dreyfus, the Sunderland owner], they had conversations.

“I thought that it could have been a good signing for the club, a good symbol, a great player, a great leader. But the market is the market.”

Has just said that Sunderland, and in particular Brian Brobbey, can ‘get at’ the Chelsea defence of Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria. I am not sure he has seen much of the Sunderland attack this year, but Brobbey is a handful for any defence.

“We have to stay consistent and true to our identity. It’s always difficult to predict what the other side does but you have to focus on yourself and connect with the fans and impose our ideas.”

On whether they can get a result today...

“I hope so... I see the players every day, they care and sometime its hard to understand the unforced errors.”

“He’s loved by fans and team, so we know the situation at beginning of season. He is an important player for us and didn’t start for various reasons, but has qualities run in behind and finish - he’s excited worked and has worked hard.”

I mentioned earlier that Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season. But the manner of the victories revealed more than the scorelines. In both matches, especially the second, the west Londoners looked somewhat lightweight and easily bullied.

This season Xabi Alonso has been determined to ensure that that is not the case this season.

In the land of the Premier League giants, Chelsea have been on the small side in recent seasons. But they are no longer being looked down upon and are finally showing signs of being capable of going toe-to-toe physically with opponents.

Sunday’s opponents Sunderland ran Chelsea off the park twice last season. Only once, in the 36th Premier League game of the campaign against Liverpool, did Chelsea cover more distance than their opposition.

Here’s Matt Law’s article on Why Chelsea have gone from pint-sized players to taller trees...

SUNDERLAND XI TO FACE CHELSEA: Roefs, Meunier, Mukiele, O’Nein, Reinildo, Xhaka, Hume, Le Fee, Talbi, Brobbey.

Subs: Ellborg, Danso, Methalie, Rigg, Tutierov, Ahoka, Fofana, Angulo, Isador

Regis Le Bris makes two changes from the sorry defeat at Coventry City. Nordi Mukiele returns to the centre of defence and there’s a start for Chemsdine Talbi  – Chris Rigg and Nilson Angulo are the ones to make way.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE SUNDERLAND: Penders, Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria, Henderson, Lavia, Caicedo, Neto, Palmer, Rogers.

Subs: Sharman-Lowe, Gusto, Anselmino, Nicoll-Jazuli, Barco, Quenda, Estevao, Welbeck, Emegha.

Xabi Alonso also makes two changes – Pep Chavarria and Jordan Henderson start today. Estevao Willian drops to the bench while Josh Acheampong is a somewhat surprise absence the 20.

Goalkeeper Mike Penders continues in goal with Emiliano Martinez deemed not ready to return having fractured his jaw against Everton.

That Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season.

A last-minute winner from Chemsdine Talbi grabbed the points at Stamford Bridge, before Sunderland won 2-1, without breaking sweat, at the Stadium of Light on the last day of the campaign.

Those victories, and the manner of them, underlined what a season it was for Regis Le Bris’s men. How they wish this campaign started as that one ended.

RLB's XI to take on Chelsea! 📝👊 #SUNCHE https://t.co/1XWyHk0x56

Your Chelsea side today! ✔️ #CFC | #SUNCHE https://t.co/ciaILJeAuu

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

The hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume said.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”

#1029. Jeff Stelling: We’d have two or three beers the night before Soccer Saturday – it was brilliant

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Stelling speaks to Will Castle about his Sky Sports exit, his relationship with old Soccer Saturday colleagues and the new age of punditry, spearheaded by Jason Cundy and Jamie O’Hara

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

There is a changing of the guard in football punditry and the 17th floor of talkSPORT Towers provides a snapshot of its evolution. Listeners, pick your poison.

In the morning, you can tune into the veteran of sports broadcasting. Jeff Stelling, once the voice of our Saturday afternoons, hosts your breakfast show alongside Ally McCoist from Mondays through to Wednesdays. It’s classic stuff. While most of his Soccer Saturday colleagues have since been consigned to the scrapheap, Stelling still very much has his foothold in the industry and as such brings us a taste of the ‘good old days’.

However, his old-school bread-and-butter style admittedly feels like it’s on its way out, for better or worse. Because in the dark of the night, during the prime-time slot, things go a bit blinky-eyed manic. The seat occupied by Stelling earlier that day is now filled by a man in a mask, shouting into a microphone. Jason Cundy and Jamie O’Hara are changing the pundit’s playbook with The Sports Bar; it’s chaotic, it’s crude and it does millions.

Never one to be behind the times, Stelling recognises the market for football media based largely on mockery nowadays. But don’t expect him to follow suit.

“I think there’s a place for it... not on one of my shows!” Stelling tells The Independent, who will not be showing up to work with a Derek McInnes mask any time soon.

“But Cundy and O’Hara, I think at that time of night... it’s irreverent to say the least. Obviously they take the mickey out of each other mercifully, Cundy with his Ange mask and so on. And they take the mickey out of callers as well. I think it works perfectly well at that stage. But you can’t have that all the way through.”

Pundits increasingly find themselves leaning into their club loyalties for the sake of entertainment, when purists would argue that the position should be neutral. Stelling, admittedly, was never completely down the middle; he was and still is known for his die-hard fandom of Hartlepool United, where he serves as honorary president. It’s fuelled his love of non-league, which is why he found himself at Woking FC on this grey October afternoon, fronting Enterprise’s Local Legends campaign which strives to celebrate the volunteers that keep clubs like his alive.

But in the context of ‘Cundyism’, Stelling feels his Hartlepool ties benefited him in during his three-decade stint in front of the cameras.

“It’s one of the things that has helped me in my career, being a Hartlepool fan, because if I were a Liverpool or Man United or Tottenham fan, I’d have found things much more difficult,” he adds. “People would never have accepted that I was neutral, which I’ve always tried to be. People say, ‘Who’s your Premier League team?’ I say, ‘I haven’t got one,’ and I genuinely have not got one.

“But the growth of that [less neutrality in punditry], everybody seems quite happy now. They shout from the rooftop who their team is. Football is incredibly tribal, and I think that’s sometimes one of the problems.”

Stelling brought his legendary stint with Sky Sports to an end over three years ago, presenting his last Soccer Saturday in May 2023 after 29 years behind the desk. He was the last of a banished era, with the show’s once-regulars - Charlie Nicholas, Phil Thompson and Matt Le Tissier - all axed by the broadcaster following sweeping personnel changes in 2020. Chris Kamara, of “Unbelievable Jeff!” fame, followed out the exit door two years later amid his deteriorating health, diagnosed with speech apraxia - though he has since made a remarkable recovery after undergoing experimental treatment in Mexico.

Stelling, however, called time on his own accord after simply falling out of love with the job. “It was fully on my own terms,” he says. “ I had been intended to leave when Phil Thompson, Charlie Nicholas and Matt Le Tissier were sacked, but I was asked to stay on for another year to help bed in the new boys, then  I actually stayed longer than that for all sorts of different reasons. But I felt the time had come.

“I was finding that it had become, to a degree, a chore. I used to love going out there, loved working on Soccer Saturday, used to love building up to it, doing statistics and stories at home. And being there on the Saturday, the best day of the week, every week.

“I'd lost that feeling. And because I'd lost that feeling, I'd done it for 30 years, I thought it was time maybe to see what life outside Sky was like.”

Stelling was anxious about his own health during his final days at Sky, but got out before the “mental toll” became too much. “It was a mental stress and I feared if I carried on, it would make me unwell,” he admits. “But I was never physically unwell. I just got to the stage where honestly, I didn’t want to go in and do it.”

Even the idea of the show doesn’t make him long for the days of old. “I don’t miss it,” Stelling asserts. But he can still cherish the memories with the old Soccer Saturday crew, especially those outside of the studio.

“We used to get together on a Friday night and I’m not ashamed to say we’d have two or three beers, and it was brilliant,” he says. “They were just great, great nights.”

Holding celebrity value in their own right, the odd notable name from the world of football would join the party. “I know [we went out with] David Moyes once, Delia Smith, Chris Wilder - happy to spend time with them,” he recalls. “But it was the company of the boys, really.”

A group that made the 3pm blackout not just tolerable but enjoyable, hearts broke when the clock ran out on Stelling’s cohort. Fans of that time may therefore find solace to know that, to buck a time-old trend of television, their friendship has survived beyond the screen.

“We live all over the country so it’s difficult to get together, but we do get together from time to time, and bump into each other at various events and things,” he says. “We’re all in touch. We were all best mates, really. We still are.”

#1028. Chinese scientist sacked after child died in gene-editing trial

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chinese authorities have sacked the researcher who led an experimental gene-editing trial that resulted in the death of a child. An investigation into the trial by the Shanghai municipal government found that the researcher and his team failed to follow regulations and overlooked warning signs in a safety report. Several others involved in the case have also been punished.

Two children died from gene therapies in China: where the field goes next

Two children died from gene therapies in China: where the field goes next

In July, the journal Science and the website Retraction Watch jointly reported that Zilong Qiu, a neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, led a team that developed an experimental gene-editing therapy for a six-year-old girl with a rare neurodevelopmental disorder called Snijders Blok–Campeau syndrome. The therapy was carried by a viral vector that was injected into the girl’s spine and then travelled to her brain. The girl died of medical complications after receiving the therapy at Xinhua Hospital, also in Shanghai, in March 2025.

The institutions involved in the trial — Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Xinhua Hospital — have also been reprimanded and instructed to examine their own practices. “I expect the action to send a big warning to research institutes and hospitals across the country,” says Jiayou Shi, a lawyer at the National Research Center for Civil and Commercial Law at Renmin University of China in Beijing.

The trial was conducted under China’s fast-track pathway, called investigator-initiated trials (IITs). IITs allow researchers and biotech companies to test therapies quickly in hospitals without supervision from the country’s regulators. The Chinese government increased oversight of these trials in May, which Shi says should prevent similar cases in future.

Lizzi Lee, who studies China’s economic and technological policies at the Asia Society Policy Institute, a think tank in New York City, says the trial is “a cautionary tale” for the country’s rapidly growing biotechnology industry. There is real momentum in the industry in China, but clinical oversight hasn’t always kept pace, Lee says. “The investigation is quite candid about what went wrong,” adds Lee.

According to a statement released through China’s state-run media on 13 November, the Shanghai government’s investigation found that Qiu was the main person responsible for the research. He has been sacked from his position as the deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institution, which is affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. Another member of Qiu’s team, a deputy researcher at Xinhua Hospital, has also been dismissed. Both researchers have been barred from leading or participating in science projects for five years and have been added to a national database of people and organizations that have committed serious breaches of research integrity.

About a month before the girl received the experimental therapy, Qiu’s team received results from a preclinical toxicology study showing that monkeys sustained liver damage, according to Science and Retraction Watch. Investigators found that Qiu’s team failed to inform the researcher in charge of the clinical research at Xinhua Hospital in a timely fashion about the results of the primate experiment, which meant “the early warning signal” in the safety report was not “given high attention”, according to the statement. The clinical researcher has been removed as head of research at Xinhua Hospital. Qiu did not respond to questions about the investigation report.

Shi says the trial in the girl should not have gone ahead if the therapy showed evidence of harm in animals.

The investigators also found that Xinhua Hospital failed to conduct sufficient scientific assessment for the clinical trial. According to the statement, although the hospital’s ethics committee asked the research team to submit extra materials when safety evidence was lacking, it approved the trial without receiving those materials. In addition, the consent form given to the children’s family did not mention death as a risk of taking the therapy. Two members of the hospital’s ethics committee were given penalties.

Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Xinhua Hospital did not respond to questions about the investigation report.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03752-2
