#1026. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

But analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Lammens’s only positive contribution was to come up for the late corner from which Dorgu scored, possibly getting away with a sly nudge on Villa’s Zion Suzuki.

What a start for Aston Villa! 🔥 Alysson fires home to give the the visitors the lead https://t.co/F0nfSRMWRa

Then Lammens conceded a second as he fumbled a shot from Alysson, after the Brazilian was again teed up by McGinn with Nicolas Jackson tucking home the rebound. It followed a poor defensive header from Leny Yoro. It would not be his last one.

Nicolas Jackson has made it 2-0 to Aston Villa after just 4 minutes and boos ring out around Old Trafford 🤯 https://t.co/G7oWDNMjGS

At that point, even so early, it felt over. For United. For Carrick. Then it got complicated. In fairness, United responded brilliantly. By half-time it was 2-2 and a potentially mutinous situation, with the fans on edge and unfurling new banners attacking the hierarchy – including one which read “your funeral not ours” – had turned and were raucous in a positive way.

Matheus Cunha, with a sharp turn and run into the Villa penalty area before being brought down, earned the spot kick from which Bruno Fernandes pulled back the first goal. Former Villa midfielder Youri Tielemans drew them level with a first-time shot. Not just that but they peppered the Villa goal.

Youri Tielemans against his former club! 😱 Manchester United are level just before the break! https://t.co/8kFOQkl814

Then they conceded two more in quick succession with a ridiculous trip on Alysson by Diogo Dalot, who was given the runaround at left-back until he was substituted to cheers. McGinn scored from the penalty. It was 4-2 when Yoro inexplicably headed a McGinn free-kick goalwards, Lammens tipped it on to the crossbar and Leon Goretzka eventually bundled the ball in.

Tellingly, the United supporters appeared too stunned to protest. The game meandered to what felt like an inevitable conclusion, petering out much like, surely, Carrick’s time in charge.

But, football, bloody hell. As someone – who was appointed United manager 40 years ago last week – once said. Dorgu made a difference. As did Joshua Zirkzee, another substitute, as the pair became United’s unlikely saviours, the striker sweeping home the full-back’s cross in the 92nd minute, with six added on.

Then a corner was won. The roar went up – as did Lammens. But it was Dorgu who met the delivery from close range to salvage a point. But the big question is: did he also salvage Carrick?

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

"That's not going to happen" 🗣️ Michael Carrick responds to the notion that he could resign as Manchester United head coach 🔴 https://t.co/q1fBKSXL7l

Asked later if he had seen enough to turn the situation around, the United head coach added: “Yeah, 100 per cent. I think there’s more than enough. Goals change games and you’ve got to deal with it, and it’s part of something we have to improve on drastically, but there’s more than enough.”Carrick scoffed at talk of United being in a relegation battle. “We’re in November,” he said. “I don’t like this situation where we are and where we’re at. But we can do something about it.”

Roy Keane, the former United captain, likened Carrick to a “politician”. “It’s hard to believe what’s coming out of the United camp because we can’t even be sure they’re being honest with themselves. It’s just words,” he said. “It’s obviously difficult for the manager. Under pressure, no doubt. He talks a lot but doesn’t say much. I don’t know if that’s a tactic. Like a politician.

“He keeps saying we need to tighten up and there’s things we need to work on. But they better get moving on that.”

"Should be banging heads!" 😡 Roy Keane discusses how Manchester United can improve their form https://t.co/r7JZzj62LD

Diogo Dalot’s second-half substitution was cheered by the home supporters and the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe again came under fierce attack from fans, who held up a banner in the Stretford End that read: “We don’t want a new stadium. We want new owners.” It is understood the banner was later confiscated by stewards.

Carrick defended Dalot’s contributions after another dismal showing from the Portugal defender and claimed the fans were “right behind” the players, despite growing discontent in the stands.

“I understand the frustration, I understand the disappointment of the supporters, so I get it. We’re all frustrated, we’re all disappointed,” Carrick said.

“Diogo, he gives absolutely everything. He’s played in different positions, he’s played left-back, he’s played really well at times. He gives a penalty away today, he knows that. Maybe he can do a little bit better, he’s made a mistake, but he cares an awful lot and he’s giving everything.

“I like what he brings to the team, I like what he brings to the group, I like what he brings to the whole environment and the culture that we’ve got.”

Asked if Dalot needed taking out of the team for his own good, Carrick: “Picking a team and who plays the next game, that’s a whole different decision, but it’s a whole different game that we’ve got to look forward to now.

“They [the fans] are desperate to get behind us and for us to give them something to go on and shout about. There’s frustration and disappointment at times, we all feel that. But they are right behind the boys and were at the final whistle as well.”

Unai Emery stormed straight down the tunnel before the final whistle, furious at his team’s failure to see out the game.

“We are disappointed, frustrated because in minute 90 we are winning 2-4,” the Villa manager said. “We will accept the result because we have won three and drawn three in last matches and we’re doing well. But today we have lost two points.”

There’s been too many – that is clear and we know that. Something we have to put right.

I liked the character, the quality of football. We had most of the game, attacked the box we had shots and created chances. We have a lot of inexperienced players but a lot of talent and that’s why we score goals. It doesn’t matter if United are low in confidence, you’re always up against it. The third goal was really poor and gave them a lot of encouragement to score.

We lost two points. We threw it away. The last five minutes were just madness. It’s going to sting.

The manager is a winner; he’ll be hurting the way we are. We go play international football but he’ll dwell on it for two weeks.

A very difficult match. We competed well and we struggled in the first half after our two goals. Second half we had good balance to try to win the match. Manchester United will spend the international break in the relegation zone and are winless in their last eight Premier League games, but it could have been so much worse.

Nobody in Old Trafford knows what to think, apart from Villa fans who must devastated that they chucked it away. Twice.

The question now is whether United showed enough to spare Carrick the sack.

The game has just restarted with 98 minutes on the clock.

And United are on the attack again through Fernandes, who feeds Mount on the left but his low cross is in front of everyone.

With Lammens up for the corner, Suzuki makes a mess of it in the six-yard box and grasps fresh air, allowing Dorgu to nod home an improbable equaliser. Villa will be sick, they have thrown this away.

Emery marches straight down the tunnel. How important will that be for Carrick? Answers on a postcard.

Dorgu is proving a weapon for United down the left, and Villa are having to defend their box.

Lacey then whips a really dangerous cross in from the right, and Harwood-Bellis clears at the back post at the expense of a corner.

Was that the chance for United?! Maatsen’s defensive header from a Dorgu cross lacked power, and Mount was unmarked at the edge of the box, but he skewed his left-footed half-volley over the bar.

United have hope again, but it is diligent defending from Hemmings to intercept and attempted one-two between Mount and Fernandes.

One of United’s best efforts of the second half, with Mason Mount helping on a chipped miss on the volley but the shot clipped the top of the crossbar. United needed that one to go in.

Resignation around Old Trafford now, and Madjo has just replaced Jackson up front for Villa. Emery has a really exciting battery of attacking options to choose from, they should always carry a threat no matter how well they are playing as a team.

Neat passing football out from the back from Villa, with Barkley turning in midfield and playing a searching pass towards Hemmings. Dorgu slides in to concede a throw deep in United territory.

Another throw of the dice from Carrick: Mbuemo off, Zirkzee on but it feels as if the air has gone out of the balloon at Old Trafford. Villa just need to stay professional and avoid any unforced errors.

Villa enjoying a strong spell of possession in United’s half now, Mbaye proving an outlet down the left since coming on as a substitute.

Barkley then spreads play to Hemmings on the break, and Fernandes finds himself in the left-back zone and trips the winger.

Villa looking comfortable now, and some United fans are heading for the exits.

Emery with another double change: Mbaye and Gomes replace Goretzka and Manzambi. Villa’s manager is very good at pacing his team through these matches and adding pace and power from the bench at the right time.

Shea Lacey earns United a corner from Maatsen, an attacking full-back who tends to give wingers a chance. The ball flicks off Hemmings at the back post and goes for another corner. Taken short, but Kamara blocks a tame Fernandes shot.

“It’s a long way to London when you’re s---,” is the latest chant in the repertoire of Villa’s away fans. Fernandes and Mainoo are trying to force passes forward but Harwood-Bellis and Torres are reading their intentions and intercepting.

Stoppage in play after a hefty challenge on Manzambi from Yoro, but there was nothing malicious in the tackle. Some groans from the Old Trafford crowd when play resumes as Fernandes slices a pass high into the sky. Villa happy for a few more minutes to tick by.

Goretzka with a really poor square pass inside his own half, and Kamara cannot make a challenge against Cunha, but his shot from a tight angle is straight at Suzuki. Fernandes then lifts a cross over the bar.

Emery’s turn to make changes: McGinn and Alysson off, Barkley and Hemmings on.

Mbeumo shoots just wide of the far post from 20 yards out, not a bad effort. Villa are not impregnable, but they are managing this half’s two-goal lead better than the first. A touch more compact, and winning fouls to halt any nascent United momentum.

Triple sub by United: Dalot, Amad and Tielemans the players off, replaced by Dorgu, Lacey and Mount. Hearty cheers from Lacey from the United fans, the young attacker who set up Cunha’s winner against Roma.

Huge cheers when Dalot is substituted from the United fans followed by boos as he left the pitch. Shades of Zirkzee against Newcastle.

United work a free-kick short, and Fernandes’s shot from the edge of the box deflects wide. Bodies fall like skittles from the corner, but VAR decides there was nothing sinister in Villa’s defending. Alysson then bodies Mbuemo but the referee waves it away as the home crowd appeal for a decision.

Tielemans slices a left-footed shot over the bar from distance, but both teams are still finding it easy to progress the ball and create half chances. There are surely more goals on the way if it carries on like this.

McGinn with a teasing delivery from the free-kick, and but his cross evaded everyone. Mbuemo then tests Suzuki with a snap shot, but the flag was up for offside against the Manchester United forward in any case.

Attack, or counter-attack, might prove the best form of defence for Villa because Alysson is tearing it up down their right flank. Heaven hacks him down at the expense of a yellow card, and the forward requires some treatment.

Chaotic defending from the free-kick, with Yoro losing his bearings and heading against his own crossbar from a few yards out. There ensues a goal-mouth scramble, but Goretzka was on hand to make sure from a few yards out. United two goals down for the second time in the game. Can they do it all again?

Good work in midfield from McGinn to protect the ball not once but twice and buy a foul from Fernandes, who throws his hands up at the decision. That is the name of the game for Villa: if they can keep the ball for longer spells, chances will open up around the edge of United’s box.

Mazraoui with a misdirected cross that drifts behind for a goal kick. Old Trafford is quiet again, save for the Villa fans in the corner. Maguire has his critics, but his half-time departure has not helped United’s cause. Their defence was flimsy enough with him there.

Just like in the first half, Villa have an early goal. Unerring finish from the spot from McGinn, plenty of power and sending Lammens the wrong way. Can Villa keep their foot on the pedal this time?

United on top now and have a little momentum after that shocking start. The crowd have also lifted noticeably.

United are certainly in the ascendancy now, Villa allowing too much space around the edge of their box. From there, a Fernandes shot deflects off the boot of John McGinn and loops not far wide of the post. Suzuki palms the ball behind for another corner.

Villa trying to restore some order with considered passing from deep, but Maguire steps in well to take the ball off McGinn. Mbemo is the flagged for offside. United are the team with bigger problems, but Villa do not look wholly trustworthy themselves.

#1025. Hiding remotes and unplugging TVs: How Celebrity Race Across the World cut Jeff Stelling off from football

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Exclusive interview: Former Soccer Saturday host Stelling is a contestant in the latest series of the hit adventure travel show which will see him traverse South East Asia

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Jeff Stelling has revealed that producers would unplug televisions and hide remotes during filming of Celebrity Race Across the World, which left the veteran sports broadcaster completely cut off from football and his beloved Hartlepool United.

Stelling is taking part in the latest series of the hit adventure travel show, teaming with his son Matt in a 4,660-mile race from the Malaysian city of Kuching to the finish line in Melbourne, Australia on a budget of £26 a day.

The former Soccer Saturday presenter, who ended over 30 years of service with Sky Sports in May 2023, is a passionate lifelong Hartlepool fan and serves as honorary president of the National League club.

But as he traversed the depths of South East Asia with no phone and limited technology, he was left completely in the dark about the club’s performance at the tail-end of the 2025/26 season.

“We couldn’t get any football scores at all because we’ve got no way [of finding them out],” Stelling told The Independent.

“If you’re within your checkpoints, if there’s a TV in your room, they [the producers] make sure it’s either disconnected or else they don’t give you a remote, so they make sure that that’s taken away. You’ve got no contact.”

The fourth series of the show, which aired its first episode on Wednesday, was filmed from February to April earlier this year.

During that time, Hartlepool experienced a mixed bag of results - going on their joint-best win streak of the season with three consecutive victories, only for that run to be ended by their heaviest defeat of the season: a 7-0 hammering at Wealdstone at the end of March.

Stelling says he was out of the loop for all of this, however, which allowed him to let his dreams run wild as the National League season approached its climax.

“For me, it meant I could fantasise that we were winning every game,” he added. “And then when we finished, I found out the truth that we hadn’t been winning every game.”

Hartlepool ended last season in ninth, 12 points adrift of the National League play-off places.

His agony without any knowledge of the Pools’ performance was not a shared experience with his youngest son, though, with Matt a Brighton supporter.

“Well obviously, my relationship with this son’s a bit stressed because he’s a Brighton fan!” Stelling joked, whose older son meanwhile follows his father’s lead in supporting Hartlepool.

“No, we’ve always gotten on really well,” he continued, “but it’s sort of challenging for both of us, but probably more for him, that you are going to spend six weeks, 24 hours a day, with your dad - often sharing a bed or sharing the same floor.

“Different generations have got different views of things, so inevitably, over that period of time, in the sort of intense situation that you’re in, there are inevitably going to be occasions when you’ve got to bite your tongue, on both sides.

“But it was brilliant. As I say, we were close before. We’re probably even closer afterwards.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former England and Chelsea star Joe Cole has highlighted the vital importance of protecting grassroots pitches across the capital, warning "you can’t produce any footballers without football pitches."

The 45-year-old enjoyed an illustrious playing career, which included three Premier League titles at Stamford Bridge and 56 caps for the Three Lions, and London’s local playing fields played a pivotal role in shaping his journey to the top.

Established in 1890, the charity works to safeguard the capital’s green spaces, inspiring future generations to follow in the footsteps of sporting greats. Speaking exclusively to FourFourTwo, Cole admitted the nomination means a great deal to him.

"London and football are two of the things most dearest to my heart," Cole said. "I’m a London kid. I was born in Camden Town, and obviously football is my passion, so the two things together make perfect sense, and they do a great job there.

"We need to protect the green space, not just for football, but for every sport, for kids to play, particularly in London. We have a rich history of producing footballers. You can’t produce any footballers without football pitches – whether that be five-a-side, seven-a-side, 11-a-side, cricket pitches, anything for young people to go out and be active. It’s about keeping them off the developers and making sure there’s room for kids to play."

Renowned throughout his career for his street-footballer flair and close control, Cole honed his trademark skills growing up in north London during the 1980s, making the most of whatever space was available.

"I lived in a ground-floor flat with a tiny garden, so London was my back garden," Cole recalled. "There were no boundaries. There was a bit of grass right outside my house, a wall, and over the back end there was a little concrete seven-a-side pitch.

"You had to be imaginative. I used to walk to Market Road, which was one of the first AstroTurf pitches in the country. London is just a city riddled with little areas to play. I love London, I really do, and I can’t ever see myself living far from it."To learn more about the London Playing Fields Foundation visit lpff.org.uk

#1022. Andorra owner Gerard Pique says Jesus Owono doesn’t deserve ban after footballer’s death

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Owono has been suspended for 12 matches after colliding with De Miguel during a Spanish second-tier match

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Andorra owner Gerard Pique believes that goalkeeper Jesus Owono does not deserve the 12-match ban he received following the death of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel.

Owono collided with De Miguel in stoppage time of a Spanish second-tier match on 2 November, with De Miguel subsequently rushed to intensive care before passing away the morning after in hospital.

Owono, who was sent off for the foul before the match was abandoned, said he was going through “the most difficult days of my life” in the aftermath of De Miguel’s death.

He has since been hit with a lengthy suspension for violent conduct by the Spanish football federation (Rfef), with its disciplinary committee saying he used “excessive force” in the collision.

This has drawn the ire of former Barcelona defender Pique, the majority shareholder of Owono’s club Andorra, who feels the Equatorial Guinea stopper is being punished for the consequences rather than his action.

"Players, ​former ⁠players, coaches, goalkeepers, everyone has called it an accident," Pique said in a video posted on social media ⁠late on Monday.

“I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened.”

Pique says there is inconsistency in the punishment, citing Albacete winger Jose Corpas’ three-match ban after his high challenge on Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed left him hospitalised.

“Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches,” he added.

“With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?”

Andorra general manager Jaume Nogues told Andorra Radio and Television on Tuesday that they would not be appealing the disciplinary committee's decision, but that their resolution on the case was "not done well".

Nogues said an appeal would be "frowned upon socially", adding that Owono was also not in favour of launching an appeal.

Meanwhile, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera ‌did not agree with Pique's evaluation.

"He has to defend his players and his club, and he clearly believes thats what hes doing," Cervera told a press conference on Tuesday.

"I do think the action [Owono's ⁠challenge] could have been avoided. I don’t believe this is the kind of action ⁠we see every day, despite what he seems to be suggesting."

Spanish police opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter.

Under Spanish law, deaths from non-natural causes, including accidents, are subject to judicial investigation, though prosecutors have said that criminal proceedings are unlikely.

Andorra coach Carles Manso said it will be up to Owono to decide when he feels ready to play again, with Pique stating that Owono will live with the repercussions of the incident for much longer than the duration of his 12-game suspension.

“Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete,” he said. “No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us.”

England's next generation came of age at the Metropolitano on Sunday night

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Succession planning is one of international football’s trickiest arts, especially when replacing a goalkeeper who has laid claim to the No. 1 shirt for nearly a decade, or trying to fix a left-back spot that has become something of a revolving door.

For Thomas Tuchel, though, the answers to two of England’s biggest long-term headaches have been forged at Elland Road and St James’ Park.

On a thrilling Sunday night in Madrid, as 10-man England stunned reigning world champions Spain 3-2 to snap La Roja’s 43-match unbeaten run, Leeds United’s James Trafford and Newcastle’s Lewis Hall announced themselves as the next generation of Three Lions stalwarts.

For almost 10 years, Jordan Pickford’s status as England’s undisputed No. 1 has been largely uninterrupted, stretching from the 2018 World Cup to last summer’s semi-final run in North America. It left little room for an understudy to build experience or a case for selection.

Moving on from a 94-cap mainstay is never straightforward, which is why Trafford’s decision to swap Manchester City’s bench for regular Premier League football at Leeds in August has proven so vital for Tuchel. Playing week-in, week-out has helped the 24-year-old develop into a ready-made alternative capable of taking the gloves whenever Pickford eventually hangs his up.

Handed a rare start at the Metropolitano and given the chance to test his temperament and big-game mentality against elite opposition, Trafford watched as goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White fired England into a 3-0 lead.

But when Elliot Anderson saw red in the 62nd minute, Leeds’ No.1 was faced with a relentless Spanish siege. Spain racked up 23 shots, seven on target and 2.73 Expected Goals (xG), yet Trafford refused to buckle.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Leeds stopper made five crucial saves - repelling Fermin Lopez from close range, recovering well to deny Lamine Yamal and Marc Cucurella, and producing an outstanding stoppage-time double save to thwart Yamal and Aymeric Laporte - all the while impressing Tuchel with his composure during build-up.

At left-back, Tuchel’s gratitude to Newcastle should be equally clear. Since Euro 2024, England have cycled through 10 different players in the role, experimenting with the likes of Nico O’Reilly and Myles Lewis-Skelly, right-footed deputies such as Djed Spence, and stopgaps. This is largely because nobody had convincingly locked down the position consistently at club level.

Many felt Hall was unfairly overlooked when Tuchel left him out of the 2026 World Cup squad, a tournament in which England’s left flank seemed to lack balance. But the 22-year-old’s emergence as an indispensable starter for Newcastle, particularly this season, has finally given Tuchel a specialist he can rely on.

Against one of the most dangerous wingers on the planet, Lamine Yamal, Hall was excellent. Defensively, he registered five clearances and two vital first-half interventions inside his own box to snuff out Yamal and Mikel Merino, before drawing two late fouls to relieve pressure in the dying seconds.

In possession, he was just as accomplished, completing five dribbles in the first half alone - more than Spain’s entire 10 outfield players combined. He found a teammate with 30 of his 34 passes (88 per cent accuracy), providing natural left-footed width that facilitated Anthony Gordon's strong performance, too.

Pickford’s experience ensures he won't be surrendering his place without a fight, and Tuchel insisted afterwards that no permanent changing of the guard has taken place. International bosses are ultimately reliant on club environments to forge their stars, so by entrusting Trafford and Hall with pivotal Premier League roles, Leeds and Newcastle are doing the heavy lifting for future tournaments.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#1020. Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

This would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

That was a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, he can still bend the game to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

This was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great banner on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

That was a nod to Modric, a second-half substitute at the age of 41 and now on 207 caps for Croatia and almost 1,200 senior games. This Croatia team still seem unable to part company with their greatest player, despite his struggles against England in the seven-goal defeat in Rijeka. On this occasion, Croatia were much better.

The win means that England’s game in Madrid on Sunday against Spain, who beat the Czech Republic and lead the Nations League group by three points, has some bite to it. Another England win would mean they would overtake Spain on goal difference and win the group ahead of the Nations League quarter-finals in March.

This was one game when the players might have wondered if they were due more from a Wembley crowd that went through the motions in the first half and scarcely returned for the second. England manager Thomas Tuchel, speaking to ITV: “Good win. We wanted this win desperately and I think we deserved it. I think it was hard work against a good opponent. It took us a while to grow into the game but after 15 minutes I think we did OK, got the goal and got better and more confident and had some good actions and good chances, good half-chances.

“Got a little bit sloppy at the very end of the first half, started the second half very good, didn’t score the second goal, conceded from a set piece, and then showed a good reaction.

“We got the job done and it was important because it was a special occasion for Harry [Kane] and he scored the winner, so perfect evening.”

On whether England were sloppy when they conceded: “It was maybe only three or four minutes before we gave passes away and especially in a moment when we were clearly the better team, we came with a very strong reaction after the half-time, had a beautiful chance created from Declan Rice and they blocked it on the line. It was like our third goal was coming and we had some easy ball losses in our own half that killed our momentum.

“An awkward moment in our box can always happen. It’s important to react and we did it.”

On his defenders: “Good. It was demanding for Dan Burn and also for Jarell [Quansah] because they [Croatia] play with a back five and have two number 10s in between the lines.

“It was a lot of work to do, a lot of communication but they did very well.”

On what will be better against Spain on Sunday: “I don’t know. Everything will be different. Completely different scenario, completely different setup, but I’m very positive that we will get what we want.”

England put in an the-Lord-Mayor’s-show performance following their 7-0 victory over Croatia. But it was still good enough to beat the same opponents 2-1 on the night Harry Kane celebrated his 126th record-breaking cap at Wembley.

Kane capped the night with the winning goal from the penalty spot, but a poor second-half showing – after Morgan Rogers had opened the scoring in the 24th minute – allowed Petar Sucic to equalise, aided by a dreadful mistake by Jarell Quansah.

England captain Harry Kane, speaking to ITV: “An incredible gesture, reception at the start of the game. Once the game starts, it’s about getting the win, getting the three points. We’re playing against a tough team, a team that wanted to prove something tonight.

“I think for large spells of the game we done well. Got a little bit tired towards the end but overall a really great win and sets up a great game on Sunday now.”

On how he was feeling as he stepped up for his penalty: “Same as ever. I missed my last one for Bayern, so I think it’s always important to try and bounce back with the next one. Try to not miss two in a row but executing. I practised yesterday like I always do and it’s just about going out there and doing it out on the pitch.

“I think we gave away a few too many easy balls, especially in our own half, which killed the momentum a little bit. I think we had enough chances to score two or three but we’re playing against a good team.

“We’re in the midst of a run of tough games for club and country, so you can’t always expect things to be perfect. Of course, we know we can improve on a few bits and we will need to if we want to win on Sunday, but ultimately it’s about getting a win tonight.”

On aiming to beat Spain and top the group: “100%. After the first game when we lost here against them, we knew we left a bit out there. We knew we could’ve done a bit better. We said to ourselves let’s win every game until the next one and see what happens. It’s the perfect opportunity now on Sunday to try and prove ourselves.”

Thomas Tuchel tells ITV: “A good win, we wanted this desperately, we deserved it. It was hard work against a good opponent.” We will bring you more from the England head coach shortly.

Harry Kane has told ITV that it was an “incredible reception” for him at the start of a “really good win”. We will bring you the captain’s full quotes shortly.

While top spot in the group is still up for grabs, England have booked their place in the Nations League quarter-finals, which will take place in March 2027.

The winners of those ties progress to the Nations League Finals in June.

Harry Kane has now scored 92 goals in 126 appearances for England.

Thomas Tuchel has said he has “unfinished business” with England and will remain in his position for the Euros in 2028, but did say that he would return to club football after seeing out his contract.

“I signed the contract, I want to stay until the Euros,” he said this week. “I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.”

But he added: “I miss the 50 matches [a season].

“I miss the two minutes when everything is done. You go out two minutes before the whistle goes, it’s like the best two minutes, everything is done and you’re in a full stadium, lights are on and you’re just so excited and you’re part of it.”

Shortly before kick-off, Croatia captain Luka Modric will present England captain Harry Kane with a special gift from the Croatian Football Federation (HNS), marking his Ballon d’Or win and his achievement in becoming England’s all-time record appearance holder with 126 caps.

Modric is not in the starting line-up but the 41-year-old has 206 caps for his country and will present Kane with a specially crafted replica of the first football ever brought to Croatia, which English industrialists introduced to the town of Zupanja in 1880. This event is regarded as the beginning of organised football on Croatian soil.

England’s 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic last month left them on nine points after four Nations League group games.

It came after a 2-0 win in the away contest, a 7-0 thumping of Croatia and a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

A draw tonight will be enough for Thomas Tuchel’s side to book their place in the quarter-finals of the competition.

The eight teams to finish in the top two of the four League A groups will play in the knockout rounds that start in March 2027.

The two worst sides to finish bottom are automatically relegated, while the other bottom sides and third-placed sides are at risk of relegation via a play-off.

Few expect Jobe to be better than his older brother. While Jobe will make his England debut just two months after turning 21, Jude’s first cap came aged 17. By the time that he was Jobe’s age now, Jude had already thrived for England in two international tournaments. But Jobe has one major sporting advantage: he is the younger sibling.

Younger siblings have significantly more chance of becoming elite athletes. If two siblings both become professional, the little sibling is significantly more likely to enjoy the better career.

Jude and Jobe Bellingham could become the first brothers to start for England since Gary and Phil Neville took to the field together 19 years ago, with Jobe included in his first senior squad.

Jack and Bobby Charlton are the only other brothers to play together for England in the post-war period.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the FA’s England app as he discussed his call-up.

“It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great. To be called up for England is a dream itself and I’ve been so proud to have the opportunity to represent England at every age group.

“I always enjoyed coming away with England, I love competing against top players at whichever age group. But to have that chance of an opportunity to represent England with my brother, it’s really hard to put into words.

“I don’t have the words, really. I think it’s only emotion that could describe it, and, hopefully, if that time does come, you’ll see a lot of emotion from people, and definitely from my family.”

There will be a special pre-match presentation to honour Harry Kane becoming England’s record appearance maker, with 126 caps, overtaking Peter Shilton. Shilton has held the record since 1989.

The goalkeeper is at Wembley to formally mark Kane’s achievement. The England captain will also show the Ballon d’Or trophy he won last month.

Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph from last month will also be celebrated tonight before kick-off, along with his record appearance.

“I think I maybe underappreciated how big it was going to be, how big the reaction was going to be,” he told the BBC.

“It’s just been crazy, whether it’s messages on my phone or on social media, or people calling me, and just being in the street and everyone congratulating me.

“I think the actual moment when Ronaldo said my name, it’s strange, it’s almost like a movie.

“In the moment, it was like in slow motion and the confetti was supposed to fall and all this, but when I watched it back, I had my hand to my mouth and maybe a couple of seconds and I was out, but in the actual moment, it felt like I was doing it for a minute.

“It was a really unique feeling because it is different to playing a game or scoring a goal, because it is so individual, it is nothing you can kind of do.

“Your mind is playing games with you the whole night, whether it is going to be you or not.

“So, when he actually said my name, it was just a crazy emotion.”

To the exclusive club of Billy Wright, Sir Bobby Charlton, Bobby Moore and Peter Shilton, the name Harry Kane will be added on Thursday night. It is only the fifth time that a new men’s England international appearance record has been set in the post-war era, with Kane preparing for his 126th England match to surpass a landmark that has stood for 36 years.

“I’ll be the first to congratulate him because I think he’s done it the right way,” says Shilton, who will be back at Wembley to metaphorically pass on the baton.

“He’s not coming on as a substitute; he’s been out there every game, doing his job. Records are there to be beaten and I couldn’t think of anybody better than Harry, not just on the pitch but off the pitch. I am very proud of the record and handing it to Harry makes it not quite as bad.

“I think striker is the hardest position to play and goalkeeper is the second hardest because of the responsibility you’ve got. But scoring goals is the most difficult thing and Harry’s record in the modern game is there to be seen.”

Thomas Tuchel has said Harry Kane was the deserved winner of the Ballon d’Or, with the England head coach describing the striker as “an extraordinary player”.

“He wins the Ballon d’Or, and deservedly so, and in the next game for England he gets the all-time record with 126 matches,” Tuchel said when announcing the latest squad.

“Thursday is a deserved occasion to celebrate an extraordinary player.”

Kane said: “It’s not about me – it’s about the team. I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

Harry Kane starts for England in what will be a record 126th appearance for his country.

Thomas Tuchel makes three changes from last month’s win over Czech Republic, with Dan Burn, Declan Rice and Anthony Gordon replacing Marc Guehi, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Eberechi Eze.

Harry Kane will become England’s record appearance maker this evening, with the 33-year-old set to earn his 126th cap.

The striker started his international career against Lithuania in March 2015, scoring just 79 second after replacing Wayne Rooney at Wembley.

Eight years later, Kane surpassed Rooney as the country’s record goalscorer, netting his 54th England goal in an away contest with Italy.

He equalled Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps last month against Czech Republic as he scored his 90th and 91st international goals.

England will be hoping for a repeat of their fixture against Croatia last month, with Thomas Tuchel’s side producing an emphatic 7-0 victory in Rijeka.

England were 4-0 up at half-time of the Nations League contest, which was attended by 6,000 schoolchildren and 100 visiting fans, with Croatia supporters sanctioned over previous bad behaviour.

England’s front four of Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka were all on the scoresheet in the opening period, with Kane and Saka doubling their tallies in the second half before a late seventh from Morgan Rogers.

The last time we met Croatia in the Nations League 👊 https://t.co/b07QcUSlPI

Good evening and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of England vs Croatia in the Nations League, with the hosts’ captain Harry Kane set to become the country’s most-capped player.

The 33-year-old has enjoyed a memorable few weeks, becoming the first English Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years and following it up with a new Bayern Munich contract, and an appearance at Wembley tonight will take him clear of Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Kane scored twice in his record-equalling appearance against Czech Republic at Wembley last month, extending his international tally to 91 goals – a total that is unrivalled for England.

“It’s not about me – it’s about the team,” Kane said before tonight’s landmark moment. “I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

The 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic left England on nine points after four Nations League group games, with a 2-0 win in the away contest and a 7-0 thumping of Croatia coming after a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

Thomas Tuchel will be hoping that his side can inflict another heavy defeat on Croatia this evening, but a draw will be enough to book their place in the quarter-finals, with the group’s top two teams progressing.

While Kane will collect plaudits for his 126th cap, attention will also be on a potential first, with Jude Bellingham’s younger brother, Jobe, included in a senior England squad for the first time.

The two Bellinghams appearing together in a senior match would be a new experience for them, while it would be the first time that brothers have taken to the field together for England in 19 years.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the Football Association’s England app. “It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great.”

#1019. Thomas Frank explains why Crystal Palace job was ‘too good to turn down’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Frank was appointed Palace manager after Pierre Sage’s sacking

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Frank decided the Crystal Palace job was “too good to turn down” after talks with chairman Steve Parish.

The 53-year-old Dane, out of work since being sacked by Tottenham in February, has spent the last nine months travelling, spending time with family, and reflecting on his career.

He takes charge of what he believes is an “iconic” English club, but one with plenty of work to do if they want to escape the Premier League relegation battle.

“You know, honestly speaking, I was a little bit, ‘When do I want to go back in? Is it now?’ Then this opportunity came up,” Frank told PalaceTV.

“I was thinking, this is probably too good to turn down for various reasons.”

Frank’s strong admiration for Eagles supporters – he was at Wembley when Palace lifted the FA Cup – was a contributing factor.

He added: “The second part of it was the very good conversation with Steve Parish. He’s been around, he knows what’s happening, he knows how to run a football club.

“You always say you need to do your due diligence about the one who takes the decisions, and everything I’ve heard about Steve, everything I knew, it was positive, and then on top of that the conversation with Matt Hobbs, Iain Moody, was big.

“So all that adding up, looking into the team that I see is extremely exciting, good potential, or just thinking, ‘Hmm, this is interesting’. And when I’m sitting here, walking around the training ground, it was just, ‘Ok, you’re back’, which scared me a little bit, but it’s good.”

That Hobbs and Moody helped convince Frank to sign a two-and-a-half year deal will, for Palace fans, carry hope that the new boss will be backed in the January transfer window.

The Eagles lost a number of key personnel in the summer from their Conference League-winning squad, including Daniel Munoz to Nottingham Forest and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea.

Their absence has been felt on a side that has conceded the most goals, 24, in the Premier League.

“To state the obvious, we need to stabilise things,” said Frank, who pointed to defending, set pieces in both boxes, and defensive transitions as priorities to address, beginning with Saturday’s trip to Coventry.

“We need to bring energy, we need to bring belief, we need to bring confidence, because this is a very, very good team with very good players, but they need to believe in themselves.

“We need to balance a lot of things with aiming high in Europe, two fantastic cup tournaments, but of course the Premier League is the most important if we need to prioritise, but we would like to compete in all things.”

Frank, who was sacked by Tottenham after a run of only two wins in 17 matches, said he needed to “re-energise” after that disappointment.

He travelled to Japan and Australia with his family, spent a rare summer in Denmark, reflected on a relentless decade of work, and started speaking to people to get inspiration. Then, Palace called.

“Timing is everything in football,” he added. “Coming back to the convincing conversation with Steve, Matt and Iain convinced me that this was the right time to come back.”

Jordan Pickford has a fight on his hands to retain England's No. 1 shirt

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Since succeeding Joe Hart as England’s No. 1 in the 2017/18 season, Jordan Pickford has seen off significant challenges from Aaron Ramsdale, Nick Pope and Dean Henderson with other keepers like Jack Butland, Fraser Forster, Sam Johnstone, Tom Heaton and Jason Steele also involved in squads.

He’s used to competition. But Pickford’s age, 32, and the quality of his main challenger now, 24-year-old James Trafford, means he knows he’s now in the biggest fight of his England career to remain No 1.

This is not to call time on Pickford’s England career. It’s actually more to celebrate that England have two exceptional goalkeepers who have huge respect for each other and will push each other.

Pickford still has a role to play. It was only back in March that we were lauding Pickford for keeping a clean sheet for 923 minutes, comfortably an England record. He then conceded only eight goals in seven World Cup games - and was unbeaten in the two Florida warm-ups. Writing Pickford off is premature.

What Sunday night’s epic events in Madrid confirmed is that Trafford is Pickford’s obvious successor and the changeover may be quicker than anticipated.

Trafford is probably now favourite to start for England at Euro 2028. Such headlines will drive Pickford on even more. The Wearsider is very proud, very patriotic, is understandably determined to reach a century of caps (he’s six shy) and he’s always felt slightly under-appreciated.

Pickford deserves more respect. He’s played in the semi-final of two World Cups and in the final of two European Championships. Pickford helped England overcome their fear of shootouts.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

He saved five penalties in shootouts at four different tournaments and even took one – and scored. Such service to his country cannot be dismissed lightly.

I’ve watched Pickford closely in training, hearing the impact as he throws his body around, leaping up, often slapping his gloves together in approval at a save or simple self-encouragement.

His language is very lively at times. During one session filmed by the media at Euro 2024, Pickford was heard half-laughing, half-concerned that one failed save attempt would end up all over the internet.

Pickford is far more emotional and vocal than Trafford, partly rallying his defence but also charging himself up. He needs that adrenaline charge. Get the rave on, to quote one of his sayings.

Trafford, who grew up on a farm in Cumbria, helping his dad herd sheep, is more sanguine, more controlled, and that may appeal more to Thomas Tuchel. He’s less hyper than Pickford. He also offers more of what Tuchel wants in distribution. Growing up at Manchester City, Trafford was coached to pass out from the back. Pickford launches his booming deliveries downfield but not always accurately. Trafford is more precise, picking out his wingers well. He can be vulnerable to the quick press, though. Trafford’s still developing.

But if Trafford’s time has truly come with England, he will reflect on successfully negotiating difficult times. Re-signing for Man City after a successful two seasons at Burnley should have been a re-start, embedded as No. 1, but then Gianluigi Donnarumma arrived, and Trafford was benched. Moving to Leeds United proved inspired.

It’s impossible to say that Trafford came of age in Madrid as he has to deliver week after week, minimising mistakes and improving decision-making. He’s 24, playing regularly, and will mature even more into a fine goalkeeper with great shot-stopping strengths and sound distribution.

Trafford certainly impressed against Spain, making reflex saves from Fermin Lopez and then the follow-up from Aymeric Laporte. It is these double saves where Trafford most impresses. Late on, protecting the 3-2 lead, Trafford watched like a hawk as Lamine Yamal glided in from the right. A keeper has to make so many decisions in such short, intense passages of play, perhaps lasting only a few seconds but demanding total concentration and swift reactions, mental and physical.

Yamal could have whipped an early shot to the near-post, so Trafford had to guard that. He then stepped across as Yamal, using Anthony Gordon and Myles Lewis-Skelly to try and mask his intentions, targeted the far-post. Trafford was equal to the threat, dropping smartly to his right, pushing Yamal’s curling strike away. He remained alive to the continued threat. Marc Cucurella now had the ball.

All those drills in training, the reflex save and then jumping up for the follow-up developed the muscle memory for Trafford. Cucurella’s driven return was complicated further by a slight deviation off Ben White. Trafford readjusted in a split-second and pushed the ball around the post. Trafford truly saved the day.

England’s No. 1 shirt is up for grabs now. The Nations League quarter-final in March will clarify who is the owner. If Trafford keeps delivering for Leeds, the smart money is now on him to retain it. One thing can be stated for certain: England have two very good goalkeepers.

Henry Winter is one of football's most popular and respected writers. Previously the Chief Football Writer for The Times and a Football Correspondent for The Daily Telegraph, his work now primarily features on his Substack. He has also lauched his own podcast 'The Winter View'

#1016. England stun world champions Spain in one of their greatest victories

Thomas Tuchel may not have planned it this way, but in one night he gave us all the rich history of the England team at once: some glorious attacking football, some self-sabotage defending, a red card, a late siege and a fight.

This was the beguiling story of Spain 2 England 3, an evening that began with the world champions parading the World Cup trophy and ended with 10 Englishmen defending a lead with their last breath. England beat the world champions in Madrid, and for more than 30 minutes including injury time they did so with 10 men, Dan Burn heading the last ball out as per the tradition of a defensive rearguard action.

This was the game that had it all: including a substitute, in Djed Spence, who had already picked up a yellow card on the bench before he came on. It was a coming-of-age performance in goal for James Trafford. So too for Ben White, the 2022 World Cup departee who scored the third and lunged with astonishing effect in the 84th minute to block a Nico Williams shot.

Trafford again! 👊🏻 An excellent double save from the Leeds United keeper 🙌 https://t.co/L27oQFQO1J

This was a performance good enough to win a World Cup final, never mind Nations League Group A3 – just a shame England neglected to get to that World Cup final in the summer. The fight in question was at half-time as the players came off and White and Fabián Ruiz first tangled and others dived in.

There was so much to admire. England began the night testing Spain’s first-phase passing to breaking point. They began the second half counter-attacking Spain for two goals from Ezri Konsa and White. Then after Elliot Anderson’s red card, this was a different England. With Trafford in inspired form, they held off the relentless Spain for long enough.

Harry Kane scored his 93rd England goal from the spot and was replaced before the end so that Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy could give the midfield one more lease of life. By the end, the excitement meant that Kane was unable to take his seat on the bench, and he stood alongside Tuchel in the technical area, cajoling and advising.

England have beaten Spain on Spanish territory in recent times, but it was the nature of this performance, its many qualities when the moment required them, that made it so significant. This was the end of a 43-game unbeaten streak for the European and world champions, and it was ended by an England team in their best form in recent years.

Only three who started this game – Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice – started the final of Euro 2024, lost to Spain. Tuchel’s pool of talent is deeper than it was for his predecessor but there is also a greater maturity to the way they play. The England manager called it the greatest performance of almost two years in charge “given the circumstances… who we play, where we play” and as ever for England just slightly too late.

The defeat by Argentina in the semi-final in Atlanta just stings that little bit more when one considers the craft and resilience England showed on this night. They were under the hammer after Anderson threw an arm over the shoulder of Lamine Yamal and was dismissed before Mikel Oyarzabal converted the penalty that followed. “Thirty minutes against Spain in Spain feels like three hours,” Tuchel said, although Spain had a long way back after the blitzing they took at times in the first hour.

They all had their moments. Anthony Gordon had a strong first half. Morgan Rogers was central to the two goals England scored in the 10 minutes after the break. Anderson demonstrated that he is one of the best midfielders in the world in the hour before his red card. Spain were without Rodri and in his absence his Manchester City successor was in control.

Tuchel encouraged his players to mount a ferocious press against the best first-phase passing team in the world. Brave, but it worked beautifully and for an absorbing opening 10 minutes, Spain looked all at sea. Such was the pressure, the Spain goalkeeper Unai Simón abandoned the usual build-up strategy and launched his goal-kicks to the halfway line.

Even when Spain finally found their rhythm at the mid-point of the first half, England adapted. It took them a while to manage the discomfort of being denied the ball, and the familiar rapid incursions and switches of play. The counter-attacking switch from the early period pressing Spain in their own area yielded the penalty from which Kane scored the first.

Tuchel and Declan Rice revealed they had both believed England would end Spain’s long unbeaten streak, and their confidence proved well-founded.

“This was of course a statement victory,” Tuchel said. “I’m happy the players felt so confident. I felt it as well. I also had the same belief [that England would win]. I think we felt it from each other.

“The result followed the performance. I think it was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness and it was on the highest level football-wise, in all aspects of the game.”

Tuchel described the nature of England’s win as “the Azteca reloaded” in reference to the World Cup victory over Mexico, but felt the win in Madrid was the best of his reign as head coach.

He said: “Yeah [it was the best performance of his reign so far], given the circumstances and the pressure and the quality and where we played and playing against the reigning world champions. They were unbeaten in 43 games. So putting a performance out there in Madrid, in this environment, that was a very complete performance and the best I’ve had so far.

Thomas Tuchel will speak openly to England’s players about what they should do if they encounter racism in the Nations League Group 3 decider with Spain.

This is the first time England have faced Spain in Madrid since November 2004 when they were beaten 1-0 in the Santiago Bernabéu, a game that was ravaged by obscene chanting. The nations were supposed to play a fixture in the Spanish capital in 2008, but the Football Association insisted it be moved to Seville instead.

Earlier this year, Spanish supporters brought shame on themselves again after a flurry of anti-Muslim chants marred a friendly against Egypt; they were fined $20,000 by Fifa and must play their next friendly in a partially closed stadium.

There will be a full house in the Wanda Metropolitano on Sunday night, as the reigning world and European champions aim to defend their extraordinary unbeaten run of 43 games, and England head coach Tuchel is adamant the atmosphere will be in keeping with the occasion.

The German has, however, made it clear he and his staff will use their platform before the contest to remind England’s players of the steps they should take if the worst scenario unfolds.

Asked about incidents that had pockmarked this fixture before, Tuchel said: “I think I hear it the first time that this happens. I think it’s unacceptable. In any stadium, not even in stadiums, we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of England’s final Nations League Group 3 decider as Thomas Tuchel’s side take on Spain at Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

Although both countries are safely through to the quarter-finals, England will seek revenge on Spain, who beat them in the Euro 2024 final and in their previous Nations League face-off on September 26 at Wembley. That day, Luis de la Fuente’s men profited from Harry Kane’s uncharacteristic penalty miss, England’s general wastefulness in front of goal and some seriously lacklustre defending to earn a chaotic 3-2 comeback victory after falling 2-1 behind at half-time.

Since that defeat, England have won four successive Nations League fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia by an aggregate score of 14-1. Last time out, they beat Croatia on Thursday, earning a 2-1 win as Kane, who became England’s most-capped men’s player with 126 appearances, dispatched a second-half penalty to seal the three points. Spearheaded by the Ballon d’Or holder’s brilliance, England must win this evening in order to overtake Spain and top the group.

Speaking ahead of the match, Tuchel said: “I think we are ready to win. Now it’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength. I think that’s what we want to see. And then you can never predict the result in football, never. But it’s important that we show the mindset that you speak of and the spirit, and we will. I’m very confident about that.”

Meanwhile, fresh from lifting the World Cup in the summer, Spain have a 100% winning record in this season’s Nations League. They currently boast a staggering 43-match unbeaten run in all competitions, since losing a friendly to Colombia back in March 2024. England’s task is daunting, but not impossible.

#1015. Lionesses announce squad for Women’s World Cup play-off including uncapped duo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Wiegman has also recalled Chelsea striker Aggie Beever-Jones for the matches against Ukraine

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Sarina Wiegman has recalled Chelsea forward Aggie Beever-Jones and handed two players their first England call-ups ahead of the Lionesses’ World Cup play-off matches against Ukraine.

Beever-Jones, 23, was left out of England’s previous camp in October, when the Lionesses overcame Greece, but she has earned her place back in a 25-player squad named on Tuesday morning.

Injuries to regulars Alex Greenwood and Lauren James have forced them out of the team while forward Isobel Goodwin and goalkeeper Katie Cox have both been handed maiden senior call-ups.

On London City Lionesses star Goodwin, Wiegman said: “I think she has done well. We always know she’s a huge talent, high potential. She showed that over a couple of games. So we want to see her in our environment.

“She has some different qualities. She’s really fast too. She has length, she can head and she can score goals.”

Grace Fisk, Freya Godfrey, Erica Meg Parkinson and Lexi Potter all made their debuts in October’s 8-1 two-legged round one rout over Greece and have kept their places in the squad this time.

London City Lionesses left-back Poppy Pattinson, who made her debut against Ukraine in March, has been recalled.

Arsenal forward Chloe Kelly continues to miss out and there is no place for Lucia Kendall while Manchester United’s Ella Toone keeps her place in the squad after she originally missed out on being named in October’s internationals.

Speaking on Toone, Wiegman said: “She responded really well, working really hard.

“She came in our camp and was ready also straight away. Going back to her club, she’s done well too and that’s what has been fed back to me.”

Wiegman’s side are just one step away from securing their place at next summer’s World Cup in Brazil, needing to beat Ukraine in round two of the play-offs.

England will travel to Murcia on Tuesday 1 December for the away fixture before they host the second leg at Wembley Stadium four days later.

The upcoming fixtures will be England’s first since head coach Wiegman signed a contract extension until the conclusion of Euro 2029.

Tottenham Hotspur have interest in Eli Junior Kroupi - but the move for a striker is shaping up for January

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tottenham Hotspur are to move for a new striker, as their search for goals intensifies.

The Lilywhites endured a terrible start to the season under manager Robert De Zerbi and were the last team in the Premier League to pick up a win – but after encouraging signs in recent weeks, it appears that they may have turned a corner.

With Tottenham struggling to score goals, however, a new forward has been earmarked for the January transfer window.

Spurs were said to be interested in Bournemouth forward Eli Junior Kroupi over the summer, but with the recent France international picking up a foot injury in preseason, any move to a bigger was put on hold.

De Zerbi instead brought in Omar Marmoush from Manchester City, with the Egyptian job-sharing the No.9 role with Dominic Solanke – though the pair have just two league goals between them this term.

With the North Londoners lacking a reliable hold-up man who can also offer threat in behind, attention has turned to Igor Matanovic of Freiburg.

Speaking on the Market Madness podcast, transfer expert Ben Jacobs claimed that the Croatian is an option for a loan move in January that Spurs could explore, with Bournemouth closing the door on Kroupi leaving midseason.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Cherries sold Semenyo to Manchester City in January – though the Ghanaian international only left when his release clause was triggered – and the south coast outfit are determined not to see another talent leave in the same way this campaign.

“If [Spurs] can’t find the right target, or maybe someone with a bit more experience within the Premier League, then they can reassess in the summer,” Jacobs claimed.

“What they won’t want to do is necessarily go all in and panic buy in January for someone on a long-term contract, instead of just biding their time and waiting it out.”

Tottenham spent around £400 million in the summer building a side that finished 17th two years running, smashing their transfer record twice and recruiting seven new faces.

Every one of De Zerbi's signings over the summer – including youngsters such as Cole Ramsey and backup goalkeeper Martin Dubravka – was signed from an English side.

Matanovic is worth €30m, according to Transfermarkt. Tottenham take on Ipswich Town when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

Liverpool will not look to the transfer market to replace Virgil van Dijk in January - or next summer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool are accused of having an unbalanced squad this season, however, the club will reportedly resist the urge to recruit a new centre-back during the January transfer window.

The Athletic claim that adding to the heart of the defence is 'not a priority' for the Reds, ruling out investment in the position for both the upcoming winter market and the summer of 2027.

Instead of turning to the transfer market to silence critics, the Liverpool hierarchy is placing its trust in the crop of emerging defensive talent to eventually succeed 35-year-old Virgil van Dijk.

Liverpool's decision is largely down to the impact Jeremy Jacquet has had since arriving at Anfield. Behind him, Anfield still has high hopes for a trio of highly-rated youngsters: Giovanni Leoni, who is nearing a return to fitness following an ACL injury last year, Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who is currently on loan with Levante in Spain, and teenage prospect Mor Talla Ndiaye.

Opposition supporters and media pundits have spent much of the season pointing out a lopsided squad that is forcing Iraola into tactical compromises on a weekly basis, as well as Van Dijk's advancing years.

The primary target of this criticism is the club’s full-back situation with Conor Bradley sidelined and Jeremie Frimpong unfancied in a traditional back-four system.

Iraola has been forced to deploy centre-backs, most notably Ronald Araujo, as makeshift right-backs. And while the Uruguayan has brought physical solidity and aggression, asking a traditional central defender to provide the overlapping width hasn't always had the desired effect and on occasion left Liverpool looking somewhat asymmetrical in possession.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Square pegs in round holes is never a sustainable fix, and coupled with a lack of midfield depth, squad planning is never far from the Anfield conversation.

If Liverpool are officially ruling out central defensive reinforcements, even with Virgil van Dijk entering the twilight of his career, funds and focus can theoretically be redirected toward the squad’s weaknesses.

In FourFourTwo's opinion, their January priority must be identifying a specialist right-back and a dominant midfield presence, although Trey Nyoni's emergence as a water-carrier of sorts makes up for that to an extent. The lasting message from the corridors of power at Anfield is that in the centre of defence, Liverpool consider themselves already locked down for the foreseeable future.

#1012. Uefa announces candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino for Fifa presidency

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Gianni Infantino is seeking a fourth term as Fifa president despite criticism from governing bodies including Uefa

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Gianni Infantino will face a challenge from French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo in next year's Fifa presidential election.

National association representatives on Uefa's executive committee have invited Diallo to stand and given him their unanimous backing.

Uefa said Diallo will stand and this was formally ratified following an executive committee meeting at the French Football Federation’s headquarters in Paris on Tuesday. The move follows Arsene Wenger ruling himself out of a challenge to Infantino over the weekend.

Uefa pledged in August to identify a credible alternative candidate to Infantino. That pledge came after the body said it had lost confidence in the Swiss over his plan to seek private investment in a company to run the commercial aspects of the World Cup and other Fifa competitions.

A Uefa statement said: "Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of Fifa, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community.

“They also called for a Fifa that places the development of the game in every region of the world at the heart of its mission, upholds the highest standards of governance and works in close partnership with its member associations, confederations and football stakeholders. They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition.”

Diallo, who said he wasn’t initially intending to enter the presidential race, says he wants to restore what is now “broken” trust in football’s governance after Infantino seemed to act alone in his privatisation plans, while the creation of a peace prize for US president Donald Trump and the Folarin Balogun red card debacle also sparked huge concerns.

“It created a situation this summer whereby the trust placed in Fifa and it’s president was broken," Diallo said. “They have damaged the image of football and have introduced the poison of division.”

Diallo faces a tough challenge to unseat Infantino, who will be standing for a fourth term as Fifa president.

Infantino appeared to be on the ropes in August when his private investor plan was rejected by three continents and a number of key allies expressing their concern at how it had been developed.

He has since rallied support, however, and is expected to receive strong backing in Africa, Asia, Oceania and South America.

Japanese FA honorary president Kozo Tashima had earlier declared his intention to stand, as has former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega.

Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp has called for a change of leadership in Fifa, claiming Infantino compares unfavourably to his predecessor Sepp Blatter, who resigned in 2015 amid allegations of corruption.

In quotes reported by the BBC, Klopp said: "I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense.

“I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that.”

Klopp added: “Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job.”
