#958. Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson

In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers

Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S

Although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling.

The United States’ interest in Pep Guardiola, and his talks with Italy earlier, have me wondering – what separates club and international management? Could Pep, as successful as he’s been, do well in either? – Joe P

International and club management seem to me related but essentially different jobs. It’s one thing to have the players every day and be able to drill them over and over to impose a philosophy; quite another to pick them up for perhaps a dozen training sessions over a calendar year, plus major tournaments. International football is necessarily less sophisticated than club football, more based on individual excellence or heroism. Guardiola, you suspect, would be able to adapt, but it’s not certain. Plus there’s the fact that at major tournaments players are with their manager for a month or more, cooped up in the same hotel with no release. With the more intense coaches, such as Marcelo Bielsa, that seems to become problematic. And it’s notable that at the last World Cup the nations with the big-name managers – England, Brazil, the United States, Germany – fared less well than those who had appointed technocrats from within.

Michael Carrick’s firing highlighted the lack of top-class English managers. Why has an Englishman never managed a Premier League club to a title? – Ricky M

I think there are two related issues here. Are there any good English coaches? To which the answer appears to be that there are nowhere near as many as there ought to be. The various changes in player development enacted by the elite player performance plan and the England DNA project have, over the past 10-15 years, led to the development of far more technically proficient English players than there have ever been before, which has been reflected in the uptick in England’s performances at major tournaments. St George’s Park was supposed to be about developing coaches as well as players but, as yet, that seems not to have happened.

That said, it’s probably also the case that it’s very hard for British coaches to be appointed to top Premier League jobs. Say they get their start at a mid-sized Championship club and win promotion; they then have to amend their approach in the Premier League to scrap for points in a relegation battle. If they fail they are written off as not good enough for the top division; if they succeed, they’re seen as not playing the right sort of football for an elite club. It’s happened to Scott Parker … even the likes of Gary O’Neil or Eddie Howe seem somehow not quite right for the elite who, perhaps understandably, prefer to turn to somebody with experience of European competition.

Is there any part of you that feels sympathy for the current Man City players, who will presumably have to play out a “lost season” thanks to actions they had nothing to do with, and which probably happened long before their time at the club? – Jason D

To an extent, yes, but they’re pretty naïve if they didn’t realise the potential issue they were walking into. I have far more sympathy for those players who played for clubs who were denied success by City’s cheating. It’s not just the teams who finished second in the league, lost to City in cup competitions or missed out on European qualification because of City; it’s those teams, most obviously Arsenal and Aston Villa, whose development was derailed by City taking their best players, offering wages and transfer fees that it turns out they had no business offering.

Italy have gotten some big results in the Nations League. Are they back? – Nicholas A

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

This question, to be fair, was sent in before the 4-1 defeat to Belgium on Sunday. But anyway, beating France at home may be a big result, but that and two wins over Turkey seems limited evidence to say they’re back. They have definitely looked sharper under Roberto Mancini than they have probably since winning the Euros under him five years ago, but that’s a long way from being back. Even if they were to win the Euros in 2028, it wouldn’t alter the fact they haven’t qualified for three World Cups in a row. They need to qualify for 2030 and then probably get to at least the quarter-finals before you can start to say they may be back. And even then, Serie A is way off what it was at its peak – and how many of this squad would get in a Spain or England squad? Even being generous, probably no more than four or five.

#957. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:

Matheus Cunha (Manchester United - red card suspension)

Former Chelsea captain John Terry has become an investor in MatchWornShirt

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sports memorabilia platform MatchWornShirt has secured new backing from a group of active and former footballers, alongside North American sports investors.

Announced on Tuesday, the funding round is led by Gamma Waves Partners, a global sports and technology investment platform founded by former Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini, Andrea Agnelli and Rocco Benetton.

Former Chelsea and England captain John Terry and current Tottenham Hotspur defender Tosin Adarabioyo have invested individually. Premier League brothers Jurrien Timber (Arsenal), and Quinten Timber (Crystal Palace), have also joined the round through Joyned Capital, a private investment club for professional athletes.

Outside football, the investment group includes basketball player Kevin Durant and Rich Kleiman’s 35V, along with the ownership group behind the NBA's Indiana Pacers and WNBA's Indiana Fever.

The capital injection follows a year in which MWS expanded its physical presence in North America ahead of the 2026 World Cup and agreed inaugural partnerships in the NBA, WNBA, NFL and NHL.

MWS were founded in Amsterdam in 2017 by brothers Tijmen and Bob Zonderwijk, the idea initially coming about during a search for an Ajax shirt for their father.

The company now partners with more than 450 clubs worldwide to auction authentic, game-worn items.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I first got involved in match-worn shirts by selling them for charity, seeing the unique emotional value these items hold for fans,” Chiellini said. “Today, it is exciting to see the category evolve, as collectors increasingly recognise the significance and value of these pieces of sporting history.

“MatchWornShirt is building the infrastructure to connect fans and collectors with authentic moments from sport, while helping sports organisations unlock new value from their intellectual property. We are excited to support the company's next phase of growth.”

MWS co-founder and CEO Tijmen Zonderwijk said the incoming shareholders align with the platform’s long-term strategy.

“The scale of the names and businesses involved in this group of investors demonstrates a collective passion for what we have already built here at MWS, and for that, we're incredibly proud,” he said.

“It also represents a shared vision for the future, and we're excited to accelerate the growth of the business whilst remaining true to our values.”

The individual size of Terry and co's investment has not been disclosed at this time.

#955. Football Daily | England’s Nations League triumph in Spain sparks familiar rush to glory

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

Glory. Imminent and near-enough-guaranteed glory. That, surely, is what we’re looking at from the giddy heights England reached in crushing Spain 3-2 on Sunday. “If we can find that first hour consistently, we are a genuine favourites for the next tournament,” roared Steven Gerrard, a statement he believed in so much he then said it again using different words: “The first 60 minutes told me, from watching it, that we’re capable of winning the next tournament. That’s the big thing to take away.” Thomas Tuchel reckoned England had reached the “highest level football-wise in all aspects of the game”. This is the kind of positivity engendered in visiting international teams when they romp to victory in Madrid. Just listen to what the England captain said on the flight home: “You play like that and you’ve got a chance against anyone, anywhere. You get 11 fellows who can play a bit – and let’s face it, they’re not going to be there in the first place if they can’t – and you get them running themselves off their feet, working themselves into the ground for an hour and a half, and you’re odds on before you start, aren’t you.”

You’ll have worked out from the use of the word “fellows”, which dropped out of common parlance long before Harry Kane was born, that the person who said that wasn’t England’s megastar marksman. In fact it was a chap called Bobby Moore, after England had prevailed 2-0 in Madrid in December 1965. “If we got to the World Cup final and we went out and played like that, I’d fancy myself. No trouble about that,” Moore concluded. Seven months later England got to the final and went out and played like that, with glorious results. And what’s happening seven months from now? Only the actual Nations League final. Get those red and white ribbons ready, Monsieur Ceferin, it’s coming home.

Sure, winning in Madrid in the 1960s wasn’t exactly a guarantee of success – before England, the last team to win there had been Scotland, who on the back of a 6-2 victory in 1963 proceeded not to qualify for any major championships for another decade – but, as time passed, the achievement became rarer and the Spanish themselves stronger. So much so that before Sunday night no team had done it for 39 years, eight months and 28 days. And that was England too. In fact England have won on four of their nine visits to the city, a 44.44% rate, while everyone else in the world has emerged victorious seven times in 63 attempts, a meagre 11.11% ratio. Since that Scotland game in 1963 Spain have lost there just five times: to England (in 1965), England (in 1968), West Germany (in 1982), England (in 1987) and England (on Sunday). Madrid, it’s fair to say, is ours (sadly this has not been an exchange arrangement, Spain having won three and lost one of their last six visits to Wembley).

So, how much of our life savings should we all be putting on England to win the next [insert tournament of choice]? Well, hold your horses. In 1987, the last time they (or anyone) won in Madrid, everyone went a little over the top. The Express declared England were ready to win the World Cup. According to Gary Lineker, scorer of all four goals, “after the game Andoni Zubizaretta, the Spain goalkeeper, came into the England dressing room, walked over to me and said in a perfect cockney accent: ‘[Effing] hell.’” The following summer England headed to the Euros as second favourites. “England are quite capable of reaching their first final in a major tournament since 1966,” declared David Lacey in Big Paper’s big preview. Turned out they were even more capable of losing every game and being knocked out inside a week. The lesson: winning in Madrid might not mean anything, but it’s still good fun when it happens.

#954. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#953. Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football

Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous

It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it.

The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous?

This year clubs from the south coast to the north-east have reported disorder caused by supporters under the age of 18, some seemingly as young as 10. In February, Aldershot Town experienced a series of disorderly incidents involving young people that included brawls outside the ground, behaviour the club described as “wholly unacceptable and [which] will not be tolerated”. In August, Enfield Town said they were “concerned and disappointed” by young fans at a fixture in Lewes. Two weeks ago, a Gloucester City fan was hit by a rock thrown by teenagers at Redditch United during an FA Trophy tie. Even Soham Town Rangers of the ninth-tier Eastern Counties League urged parents to ensure their children make “sensible choices” ahead of a match against Mildenhall Town.

Hednesford have experienced consistent trouble for a number of seasons and in August their owner and chair, Craig Gwilt, attempted to face it down. A rising tide of disorder was harming the club, he said, behaviour that included “pitch invasions, fighting, abuse directed towards players, missiles being thrown at opposition goalkeepers, flares entering the field of play and even interference with players’ water bottles”. He called on fans to improve their behaviour or risk permanently damaging the club. The plea was not immediately heard. Three weeks after Gwilt’s statement the club banned 20 young supporters from attending matches after there was action away at Telford.

Hednesford is a town of 19,000 people on the edge of the protected landscape of Cannock Chase. The town centre is neat and tidy, a well-maintained monument to the Stafford regiment at its heart. On the way to the ground you can get a pint at the Cross Keys where Dick Turpin reputedly rested his head. It’s a town seemingly at peace with itself and the club is at the heart of the community. But both are struggling to get to grips with an issue that leaves people scratching their heads.

This season the club have introduced measures to prevent under-16s from entering without an accompanying adult. There is also extra security on matchdays, ostensibly to manage car parking. These interventions appear to have contained any trouble in and around the stadium, but now gangs of up to 50 youths will gather post-match at a safe remove to look for trouble or, more likely, save their energy for an away fixture. Like the one at Chester, for example, when the schooligans were removed from one train for antisocial behaviour and were drinking alcohol throughout their journey up. Encountering such groups on a Saturday will be familiar to many rail passengers.

The schooligans, whose nickname was coined by Hednesford’s security staff, “baffle” the club’s chief executive, Marvin Robinson, who would rather be spending his time modernising a club that have had back-to-back promotions. “I’m not really sure I understand why it seems to be a trend,” he says. “It’s a wider social issue but what is it and what will it become? Is it a social media thing? Is it about notoriety or becoming known for something? The adult response online has been almost to normalise it. I don’t agree with that.”

Go on TikTok and the picture does start to become a little clearer. From aggregator accounts to individual semi-anonymised accounts belonging to the teenagers, there is a wealth of posts celebrating the behaviour of “top lads” who “mooch” to the ground before “running” the opposition out of town. Often set to a backing of euphoric electronic dance music with a layer or two of visual effects and captions such as “this weekend’s got me feeling like a little kid at Christmas”, the posts are celebratory and almost nostalgic in tone. In recent weeks TikTok has begun appending disclaimers to them that read: “Participating in this activity could result in you or others getting hurt.” TikTok removed an account named “NLN [National League North] gimps and chants”, when alerted to it by the Guardian, for contravening guidelines that do not allow content that glorifies violence.

The mythology of old-school football hooliganism appears to be well‑known among these groups, with references to the 2005 film Green Street commonplace. But the schooligans of 2026 don’t behave like the firms of the past. For a start they rarely, if at all, arrange to fight their rivals. Instead they use the mapping feature on Snapchat to alert opposition to their presence on the day, and take it from there. The concept of rivalry itself is fluid. In the West Midlands, for example, teens from Hednesford will band together with those nominally affiliated with Redditch or Cannock Town. When there was trouble recently at Hednesford’s fixture at Hereford, local police said the majority of disorder had been caused by Redditch fans chasing supporters from Solihull Moors. It isn’t just local either. Children as young as 12 have been detained in the north-west having travelled from the south coast, a distance of more than 200 miles.

The chair of Redditch, David Faulkner, is still dealing with the fallout from the Gloucester tie two weeks ago. He says the fluid set of alliances between ultra groups has created a “travelling circus” and that no one knows where it will turn up next. Branding himself “the non-League chair”, Faulkner has started posting videos on YouTube drawing attention to the disorder and calling for collective action.

“People think of non-league football as one man and his dog, but we need to catch up with the fact that it’s massive now,” Faulkner says. “Some clubs have attendances bigger than in League One but the regulations were put in place decades ago. We need that extra regulation, that support, so we can get the funding to put things like CCTV and more stewarding in place. Because the other way this could go is that [change only happens] when someone gets seriously hurt. I haven’t got metal detectors on our gates to stop kids bringing knives in. None of that stuff. I’d rather take action before something happens.”

The Football Association says the behaviour of fans is primarily a matter for clubs and relevant authorities but that it is working to develop policies that welcome young fans safely to National League grounds. The UK Football Policing Unit, meanwhile, is working alongside leagues and the Crown Prosecution Service to develop new policies around “youth risk”, which are likely to include an extra focus on education via schools and community work.

“It’s probably the most important area of football policing that we’re focused on,” says Mike Ankers, the deputy director of the UKFPU. “We are seeing children as young as 12 or 13 engaged in antisocial behaviour at best, but also actual violence and that’s up and down the country, with some travelling hundreds of miles. There comes a great risk and a great safeguarding issue with regards to that. In terms of our focus, we are making sure that we bring the right people together to have a solution. It’s not just the policing, it requires a more holistic view.”

Ankers says he supports Faulkner in speaking up on the topic and believes many more adults need to take responsibility. “These children need a strong adult role model,” he says. “I would very much question that if your 12-year-old is going out to follow football and is being detained, perhaps 200 miles away, then you need to look at how they’ve been able to travel and have those conversations. I think there’s very much a role for parental responsibility.”

The Hednesford schooligans, having been deposited on the platform at Chester by police, made their way home by train, only to find themselves stuck in a combination of Halloween revellers and national signal failure. Constrained, they hunched over their phones viewing footage from different teenage firms and discussed the day’s events. In the end, they concurred they had got the best of it. After all, said one: “What experience do you get from chasing a taxi?”

TikTok and Snapchat were approached for comment.

#952. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

Manchester City star Josko Gvardiol could be about to leave, with the Citizens' closest rivals playing a part

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Talks have started over Manchester City star Josko Gvardiol's exit from the Etihad.

That's according to one report, which says that the Croatian defender's departure may have begun as early as the summer, with the future of the Citizens uncertain and a potential points deduction coming after an independent commission found the club guilty of over a hundred charges of financial rule-breaking.

Manchester City have launched an appeal – but an exodus could well be on the way, with Gvardiol the first domino.

January isn't the optimal time for transfer business, but Barcelona have interest in Gvardiol, as per AS via Sport Witness, with Hansi Flick wanting to improve his defence if he's to land a sixth Champions League title in Catalonia this season.

The report states that the Blaugrana asked about taking the 24-year-old along with Rodri while negotiating a move for the 2024 Ballon d'Or winner – but that the deal is “almost impossible” this winter due to the La Liga champions needing to raise funds to secure a major new signing.

That's where Manchester United come into play, with the Red Devils languishing in the relegation zone and having just hired Mauricio Pochettino to turn fortunes around.

United have an interest in Alejandro Balde, with the La Masia graduate failing to get the requisite playing time under Flick, and should Pochettino request a new full-back, the signing could well bolster the coffers for Barça to pursue Gvardiol.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Gvardiol is said to be wanted by Flick for his athleticism and his ability to play both centrally and at left-back, but having signed a new deal at the Etihad Stadium over the summer, he may be completely unattainable now.

City maintain their innocence over the 115 charges, but should the club face a serious penalty, Gvardiol would surely reconsider his future, despite his recent contract extension.

The Athletic have noted that RB Leipzig’s Castello Lukeba is an option for Barcelona – as is United's own Lisandro Martinez, who fell out with club hierarchy recently over comments aimed at his team's recruitment over the summer.

The same report also mentions that United made a “deadline day check” on Balde but decided not to go any further with the deal.

Gvardiol is worth €75 million, according to Transfermarkt. City face Fulham when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

#950. Who is NFL MVP favourite? 'He’s head and shoulders above the rest’

Sky Sports NFL presenter Neil Reynolds explores his favourites to win the 2026 MVP award, tipping Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow as his favourite to claim the individual honour; tune into Sky Sports NFL at 5.30pm Sunday for Week 11 of the season on the road to Super Bowl LXI

Who is leading the NFL's MVP race? Sky Sports' Neil Reynolds explores his frontrunners heading into the second half of the 2026 season on the road to Super Bowl LXI...

When I was asked to write a column about the frontrunners for the Most Valuable Player award in the NFL this season, I thought it might be quite fun to compile such a list and look at the leading players in the NFL.

But the reality is this could be a one paragraph feature, because I believe Joe Burrow of the Cincinnati Bengals is head and shoulders above what is also a very good group looking for that prestigious prize.

Burrow is enjoying the form of his life for the 7-2 Cincinnati Bengals, as he demonstrated on Sunday Night Football, delivering a devastating performance to dismantle the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Burrow threw for over 300 yards and three touchdowns in the first half alone before Cincinnati called off the dogs in a 38-18 win. Burrow ended that game with more than 400 passing yards, four touchdowns, no interceptions, and the praise from future Hall of Famer Aaron Rodgers ringing in his ears as he said 'you put on a clinic kid'.

So I think with Burrow at the helm, the bar is as high as you can imagine or dare to dream about for the Cincinnati Bengals.

In the 2021 season when fully healthy, he took Cincinnati to within five minutes of winning the Super Bowl. And a year later, down to the wire at Arrowhead Stadium against the Kansas City Chiefs in the AFC Championship game before coming up just short. So with Burrow leading the way, the Bengals are genuine Super Bowl contenders.

But he does headline a really good group with Brock Purdy also in the mix as the quarterback for the San Francisco 49ers.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Burrow is the highest rated quarterback in the NFL of any passer who's played in at least nine games with a rating of 117.7. Purdy is right behind him with a rating of 115.2.

He processes so well in Kyle Shanahan's attack and is the perfect quarterback for the San Francisco 49ers, who boast the best record in the NFL at 8-1. Purdy's 20 touchdown passes and five interceptions speak to his efficiency and his ability to run that offense.

You've also got to look at Jahmyr Gibbs who leads the NFL with 1,384 scrimmage yards. Gibbs has already put together a complete season rushing for a thousand yards and 11 touchdowns and also contributing through the air, and that's in just nine games. He's explosive, he's powerful, he's the heartbeat of the Detroit attack and I think he remains a key player for them the rest of the way.

Another player who has put in a season's worth of work in 10 games is Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the wide receiver of the Seattle Seahawks. He's caught 79 passes for more than 1,200 yards and 10 touchdowns and he still has seven games left in this season. JSN is not the fastest, he's not the strongest, he's not the most explosive but put it all together and he's pretty much uncoverable.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He will get open on every play, he will run away from defensive backs, he'll run over them if he has to. You're talking a complete football player and he doesn't look anything like him in terms of how he plays but the production reminds me of Jerry Rice.

The greatest wide receiver in NFL history was dubbed too slow coming out of Mississippi State and all he did was run away from defensive backs for his entire career. The stopwatch is not that important in the NFL, it's what you do when you put on the helmet and shoulder pads.

I think any list has to involve Josh Allen of the Buffalo Bills because he is so vital to that team but I think just 13 touchdown passes on the season kind of holds him back even though he added 11 rushing touchdowns. Ironically, and this perhaps plays into the MVP award debate, if you took one player out of every NFL team, the two teams that would arguably suffer the most from losing their quarterback would be the Bengals without Joe Burrow and the Bills without Josh Allen.

So his value to the Bills is extreme but I just think he falls behind some of these other guys around the league as does Jordan Love, who leads the NFL with 2,838 passing yards. He has 20 touchdowns but there have been seven interceptions and a lot of sacks taken for the inconsistent Green Bay Packers, so Love is prolific in terms of yardage but he's not quite there yet in this conversation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

And finally, the last time a quarterback failed to win the MVP ward it went to a running back in Adrian Peterson. Defensive players winning the MVP award are very rare, the last one was Lawrence Taylor for the New York Giants back in 1986.

So this is a long shot but the leading defender for me in the NFL this season is Xavier McKinney, the safety for the Green Bay Packers. It's hard to get interceptions in the NFL and he has six of them leading into the second half of the campaign, making him a danger to every quarterback he faces.

That's an impressive list but again I'll go back to what I said at the start of this column. Joe Burrow is way out in front in my mind in this race to be named the MVP of the 2026 season.

#949. Bone broth, sweets ban and acupuncture: Harry Kane’s road to record England cap

Obsessive attention to detail is helping striker to reach new heights – and a 126th international appearance on Thursday

It was Harry Kane’s dirty little secret. Something the England captain got up to after matches. He felt he deserved the indulgence. Yes, it can be revealed, Kane loved to reward himself after a gruelling 90 minutes with a bag of sweets. “I do like a Haribo,” he said with a smile after the Nations League win against Czechia in Prague at the end of September.

No more. At the beginning of last season, Kane took the decision to cut out the naughty treats. After a while, he noticed a difference. He felt sharper; able to sprint more, make a greater number of accelerations. Was it down to this latest entry on the list of personal sacrifices? Or was it a consequence of his broader health regime, the scope of which is mind-blowing?

The bottom line was that there was a gain. So Kane did what he has always done – he leaned into it. Strongly. As the goals flowed as never before, he said it became “addictive”. The 33-year-old striker finished the season with 61 goals for Bayern Munich and 12 for England. According to data from Gradient Sports, his sprints and accelerations per 90 minutes for Bayern were up significantly on 2024-25. This season, he has 10 goals for Bayern and six for England. Again, his sprint and acceleration statistics have improved.

It is a window into Kane’s mentality, the insatiable quest for self‑improvement, the fixation with details large and small, which was the basis for his Ballon d’Or coronation two weeks ago. It is why, as he prepares to make his 126th England appearance against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday night and overtake Peter Shilton as the nation’s most capped men’s player, it is hard to argue that he is not getting better with age.

Kane is the ultimate modern‑day professional, who controls everything he can control. The no‑sweets choice is the most recent on a dietary journey that started more than 10 years ago when he began to work with the nutritional specialist Dan Sargeant.

Kane had his meals prepared by Sargeant, who believes that everyone has a different reaction to food and analyses everything from bone broths to the white bits on oranges to tailor individual plans. Kane has not worked directly with Sargeant since his transfer from Tottenham to Bayern in 2023 – he has a different chef in Munich – but he continues to follow his advice.

It is common knowledge that Kane is teetotal during the season, albeit he had a few drinks as he celebrated his Ballon d’Or triumph. It was the first and almost certainly the last time he broke his rule. Similarly, everyone is aware of Kane’s obsession with recovery after games; his use of ice baths and infrared saunas. He also places great store in the quality of his sleep.

Less well-known is the depth of his relationship with his private doctor, Alejandro Elorriaga Claraco, who specialises in electrical neurofunctional acupuncture. Kane started seeing the Spaniard on a recommendation from the golfer Justin Rose after sustaining a severe hamstring tear playing for Spurs in 2020.

Claraco is based in Canada but travels to see Kane and spends at least a week every month with him. During that time, he will treat Kane on a table for four to five hours each day, getting his muscles pumping with acupuncture needles hooked up to a small battery. Claraco has been fundamental in helping Kane to understand his body; what he can and cannot do, plus how he gets over injuries.

Kane is hurtling towards his record-breaking England cap. He is in better shape than ever; mentally, as well, because he has grown so much as a leader and public speaker, particularly over the past few years of his England captaincy. He was given the armband on a full-time basis by Gareth Southgate in 2018, the fulfilment of a boyhood dream.

Kane has never hidden the fact that England is his priority, mainly because he was such a fan of the national team as a boy. It will be an emotional occasion for him against Croatia and his journey will flash before him. It began with the goal on his debut against Lithuania in 2015, 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for Wayne Rooney, and it is worth dwelling on the numbers.

Of Kane’s 91 goals – an England record – 21 have come at major tournaments: 14 at World Cups, seven at European Championships. Only two European players have more combined goals at World Cup tournaments and European Championships: Cristiano Ronaldo (25) and Kylian Mbappé (23). Kane has scored 12 times in the knockout rounds. As an aside, he has 21 assists for England, which puts him joint‑second on the all-time men’s list with Steven Gerrard, behind David Beckham (39).

The best moments? Kane is very fond of the Lithuania goal, not to mention the last-gasp winner against Tunisia in the 2018 World Cup group stage and the clincher against Germany in the last 16 at Euro 2020. He always says that one of his best England performances was against Ukraine in the quarter-final of that tournament, when he scored twice. More recently, there were the two goals that saved the day against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 of the World Cup last summer.

Kane’s penalties are a major part of his England story. His record shows 26 successes and five misses, although he scored on the rebound against Denmark in the Euro 2020 semi-final. His conversion against the Netherlands in the Euro 2024 semi-final involved withstanding incredible pressure. Ditto the one against Mexico in the last 16 of this past World Cup. The scar that will never heal was the miss in the 2-1 World Cup quarter-final defeat by France in Qatar in 2022. Was it the low point of his career? Kane is on record as saying the World Cup semi-final exit against Argentina in the summer was worse.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

He was never supposed to make it this far; to reach the Hollywood moment of winning the Ballon d’Or, receiving the trophy from the Brazilian Ronaldo and giving an acceptance speech that tugged hard on the heartstrings. His voice wobbled as he paid tribute to his mother, Kim, who had tears in her eyes, and his father, Pat.

Kane was never a wonderkid at Spurs; he had difficult loans at Norwich and Leicester. He was doubted. It is true to say he has wrung every last drop from his talent; the dedication has underpinned everything. And yet the raw ability was always there, something often overlooked.

Harry Redknapp, the manager who gave Kane his Spurs debut in 2011, tells a story from the player’s formative days. It involved a behind-closed-doors game at the training ground against Birmingham, whose centre‑half Scott Dann was on the verge of a move to Arsenal. Birmingham included Dann in their team as he returned from a minor injury and Arsenal asked Redknapp whether they could come along to watch.

“I got a call from Pat Rice [the Arsenal assistant manager] and Steve Rowley [the chief scout] and I said: ‘Of course, no problem, come over,’” Redknapp said. “Arsenal were signing Scott Dann, they just wanted to check his fitness. So they came to watch and I think Harry scored four goals that day and Arsenal didn’t sign Scott Dann. Harry absolutely ran amok that day.

“We always felt Harry was going to be a player. No one could come here now and say we knew he was going to be England’s all-time record caps holder, record scorer and Ballon d’Or winner. Anyone who says that is talking rubbish. But we did think there was a player there. How good he would be, no one was ever sure.”

Kane was breathtaking when he broke through for Spurs and England in 2014-15 and there were people who thought that would be it; he was tagged as a one-season wonder. He has been a wonder in every season since, the dynamics finessed, perhaps, by the sense that nothing has been given to him; his humility, too.

There has never been the hint of scandal about Kane and it is perfectly possible that Haribos may be his biggest vice. The Ballon d’Or is the Boy Next d’Or and there was genuine happiness in all quarters when he won the award – not only among his friends in the game. That said, the reaction of his former Spurs teammate Son Heung‑min, who is at Los Angeles FC, was gold. He tore off on a goal celebration‑style run at his club’s training ground when he heard the news.

Where can Kane take this? When will it end? Nobody knows but two things are clear. He is equipped to keep pushing for a good number of years and it has long since passed the point where it is reasonable to doubt him.

Leeds United's Tarik Muharemovic ranks alongside Virgil van Dijk and Gabriel in Premier League centre-back data

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Leeds United defender Tarik Muharemovic has emerged as one of the Premier League’s most complete centre-backs this season, ranking alongside Arsenal’s Gabriel and Ezri Konsa, and Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk.

Data published by football analytics platform Ballity Insight Lab evaluated 54 qualifying Premier League centre-backs across the opening 10 league games of 2026/27, plotting each player’s percentile rank across two criteria: front-foot 'stopper' centre-backs and the more disciplined 'covering' centre-backs.

In the model, a stopper is measured by their ability to step out of the defensive line and win the ball, encompassing tackles, aerial duels, clearances and interceptions. Conversely, a covering centre-back is judged on positional security and composure, factoring in ball retention, recoveries and an avoidance of errors.

Out of the 54 central defenders assessed, only four sit inside the top-right quadrant reserved for players who excel at both covering and stopping. Alongside established title contenders Van Dijk and Gabriel, as well as England international Konsa, sits Elland Road favourite Muharemovic.

The numbers underline just how consistently the Bosnia-Herzegovina international has performed at the heart of Leeds’ backline. Muharemovic sits comfortably around the 77th percentile in both the stopper and cover pools, demonstrating an ability to step aggressively into challenges while also sweeping up danger in transition.

Stopper or Cover? Premier League centre-backs 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 🛑 Stopper CB: steps out and wins the ball. Tackles, aerials, clearances, interceptions and duels. 🧠 Cover CB: rarely beaten and keeps the ball. Dribble avoidance, ball retention, recoveries and few errors. Formula in the comments 👇 🇳🇱 Van Dijk, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Konsa, 🇧🇷 Gabriel and 🇧🇦 Muharemović do both to some degree. 🇸🇪 Lindelöf, 🇵🇹 Dias, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Guéhi and 🇳🇱 Van de Ven cover, but don’t stop. Needs a stopper as a partner 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Hill, 🇳🇱 Botman and 🇧🇷 Murillo stop, but don’t cover. Needs a cover as a partner.November 16, 2026

He keeps elite company at the top end of the chart with Liverpool skipper Van Dijk still leading the cover metric near the 98th percentile while posting around an 80th-percentile stopper score.

Konsa hovers near the 92nd percentile for covering and 88th for stopping, and Arsenal’s Gabriel posts roughly 83rd-percentile marks across both categories.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Just as striking is the calibre of Premier League defenders who fall outside that dual-threat bracket. Several household names are classified as being better covering central defenders than stoppers, meaning they thrive at reading the game and keeping possession, but rely on a more aggressive partner to engage attackers directly.

Manchester City’s Ruben Dias and Marc Guehi, as well as Tottenham Hotspur’s Micky van de Ven all fall into that zone.

Muharemovic’s capacity to bridge both roles has proven invaluable for Leeds so far this season, and the Whites have established themselves as a tricky team to beat.

Whether it be winning first contacts against physical Premier League strikers or dropping off to snuff out balls over the top, the Bosnian's balanced skillset allows Leeds to pair him flexibly across their central defensive trio.

In a division where most central defenders lean heavily toward one side of the game, rubbing shoulders with Van Dijk and Gabriel is a ringing endorsement of Muharemovic’s rapid acclimatisation at Elland Road.

Muharemovic is valued at £33.3 million by Transfermarkt.

#946. US Supreme Court rebuffs White House effort to cut research grants

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Max Kozlov is a senior reporter with Nature in Washington DC.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

The Supreme Court’s decision not to take up a dispute over federal research grants hands a win to scientists.Credit: Kevin Dietsch/Getty

The US Supreme Court has dealt a blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to terminate research grants it deemed at odds with its political priorities.

The court said today that it would, for now, not intervene in a landmark legal battle over the cancellation of research grants by the US National Science Foundation (NSF) and four other federal agencies. The court’s decision leaves in place several lower-court rulings that came out this year and last and required the reinstatement of hundreds of cancelled awards while a lawsuit brought by a group of scientists against the government proceeds.

Since early 2025, US President Donald Trump’s administration has cancelled thousands of grants from agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the NSF. Many of the cancelled grants were for studies that contained terms that the administration said ran counter to its priorities, such as “climate change,” “equity” and “gender”. In response, a group of University of California researchers whose grants had been terminated sued the administration. Lower courts have repeatedly sided with the scientists, finding that the government had penalized academic researchers based on their viewpoints and that this likely violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech and other activities.

Judge rules against NIH grant cuts — and calls them discriminatory

Judge rules against NIH grant cuts — and calls them discriminatory

The Supreme Court’s refusal to hear the case is a relief to scientists whose work was left in limbo, and leaves protections for their reinstated funding in place. “The denial is terrific news,” says Claudia Polsky, a lawyer for the University of California researchers. The denial came only three days after the case was considered on 13 November, and none of the nine justices publicly dissented from the decision. “Those are all of the best signs one could have that the Supreme Court really did not buy the government's argument,” Polsky says.

The White House referred Nature to the US Department of Justice, which said that it would “continue to litigate” the order by one of the lower courts that “currently prevents the cancellation of certain federal research grants supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives within the University of California system”.

The Supreme Court’s decision not to take up the case now is not the final word on grant terminations. The lower courts found that the researchers were likely to succeed, rather than issuing a final judgment. Once a final ruling is issued, it could be appealed, potentially bringing the case back before the Supreme Court.

The case kicked off in June 2025, when Neeta Thakur, a physician who studies marginalized communities, and five other researchers at the University of California who had had federal grants terminated sued the Trump administration. The researchers argued that the cancellations were arbitrary and unlawfully penalized scientists whose work clashed with the White House’s political agenda.

The same month, judge Rita Lin at the US District Court for the Northern District of California ordered the NSF, the Environmental Protection Agency and the National Endowment for the Humanities to reinstate the University of California researchers’ grants. The plaintiffs had a “substantial likelihood that their funding was terminated based on the viewpoint expressed in their grant proposals”, Lin wrote.

Can NIH-funded research on racism and health survive Trump’s cuts?

Can NIH-funded research on racism and health survive Trump’s cuts?

In August 2025, the Supreme Court issued a ruling in a separate case about the termination of around 800 NIH grants. The court ruled that federal district courts — such as the one that originally ruled in favour of Thakur — cannot reinstate cancelled grants by invoking a law called the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires federal agencies to follow proper procedures and justify their decisions. Some lower courts had used this reasoning to reinstate terminated grants.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03765-x

#945. Pochettino’s Chelsea maelstrom the best yardstick for what lies ahead at United

Argentinian oversaw high-scoring games in his one Chelsea season and Opta predicts his Manchester United side will move upfield quicker than that team

Among the 20 managers with more than 290 matches in the Premier League, only the five “big beasts” of Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, José Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola have better points-per-game averages than Mauricio Pochettino. He is an elite manager.

Pochettino took over Southampton midway through their first season back in the top flight (2012-13) after the club spent seven years in the lower leagues. In his only full campaign, they finished eighth. He led Tottenham to second in 2016-17, third in the seasons either side, and reached the 2019 Champions League final. His presence lifted those clubs.

However, the Argentinian has competed in only one of the past six Premier League campaigns. Winning Ligue 1 and the Coupe de France in an 18-month spell with Paris Saint-Germain tells us little. His most pertinent recent experience for the Manchester United job is the 2023-24 season he spent at Chelsea, a campaign that left more questions than answers.

The club had finished 12th the season before, in the first year of the Todd Boehly/Clearlake Capital era. Pochettino was always likely to take Chelsea higher. And he did. But his influence is harder to judge. Opta predicted Chelsea would finish sixth in 2023-24, a forecast that proved correct. By this measure Pochettino hit par though, as Transfermarkt rated the market value of his squad as the third-highest in the Premier League in October 2023, perhaps he fell short.

The squad value grew thanks to remarkable investment. Chelsea spent more than any other club in Europe’s big five leagues in each of the three transfer windows from the summer of 2022 to the summer of 2023. Working for Boehly will have provided a good primer for the madness of Manchester United, even if the spending won’t be as generous.

Assembling a winning team from a rapidly evolving squad is not easy. Pochettino crafted a side that delivered the fifth-most expected points in 2023-24. Chelsea’s 63.4 was a fair way shy of Arsenal (81.2), Manchester City (79.3) and Liverpool (76.2) but it was a decent first season.

Chelsea conceded 63 league goals, the club’s worst figure in the Premier League era. Yet only twice have they amassed more than the 77 goals they scored. They were a little above their expected goal figures at each end but the bulk of their large goal totals was reflected in the underlying data.

But even the xG numbers raised questions, because Chelsea benefited from 12 penalties, the joint-second-most in the past 10 Premier League seasons. Chelsea have had 14 in their 86 league games since Pochettino left. They conceded five penalties and committed the joint-most Opta-defined defensive errors leading to shots (22) in Pochettino’s season.

Across three matches in April 2024 they drew 2-2 with the bottom side Sheffield United, thumped Everton 6-0 then lost 5-0 at Arsenal. They endured a similar seesaw sequence earlier in the campaign, losing 4-1 at Tottenham and Newcastle, with a 4-4 draw against Manchester City in between. Chelsea also set the record for matches in which a team score and concede at least two goals in a 38-game Premier League season (12). How do you assess a manager’s performance in that maelstrom?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

If the low point was not the Arsenal loss, it was being called “billion-pound bottle jobs” by Gary Neville after losing the 2024 Carabao Cup final. Never mind that Chelsea had enough chances to win, Pochettino had to answer for the defeat. Less than three months later, he was gone.

The Premier League has evolved in Pochettino’s relatively brief absence. Arne Slot arrived, won the title and left, while Guardiola’s departure leaves no big managerial beasts remaining. There have been tactical shifts, with increased man-to-man marking across the pitch, and set-piece skirmishes have decided more matches than feels healthy.

Opta’s data shows Pochettino’s probable new side move upfield more quickly but press less intensely than his Chelsea team. There will need to be an adjustment. But can a manager whose training methods at Chelsea were described by a well-placed source as “antiquated” get up to speed as quickly as United need?

Pochettino will adapt and his Premier League record commands the utmost respect. The relevance of his recent work to United in 2026-27 is less clear.

#943. AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership

Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can

When you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium.

AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.”

Kitcher was speaking before kick‑off in Saturday’s League One game at home against a Blackpool side dealing with a suspected norovirus outbreak in their squad. A superb arrowed strike from Alistair Smith and some vital late saves from Nathan Bishop ended Wimbledon’s winless run of 10 matches in all competitions. The 1-0 victory moved Johnnie Jackson’s side four points clear of the relegation zone and put a positive spin on a week that started with the fallout from the withdrawal of £87m of proposed investment, leaving the club’s finances even tighter.

Wimbledon made a £2.6m loss in the 2024-25 season – a figure expected to increase by £500,000 when they publish their accounts next month – which, as Kitcher pointed out, is not as loss-making as a number of other clubs in League One. Those clubs voted in the summer to reduce spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, but now many want to go further to curb the spiralling losses at this level. “It’s an ugly way of running a sport,” said Terry Hunt, a supporter who has been attending matches with his son Billy since AFC Wimbledon were founded in 2002 after the move to Milton Keynes.

Wimbledon returned home to Plough Lane in 2020, but had to create a bond to complete the move and the club still owe £7.5m in debts. In November 2025, the DTB warned that competing in the EFL at their new stadium was “not currently sustainable” under their structure at the time.

The makeup of the club has since changed. Supporters voted last April in favour of reducing their voting rights from 75% to 50.01% – the same 50+1 model that gives fans the final say on decisions at German clubs – and Wimbledon sought a cash injection. An £87m investment proposal from Sloane Street Capital, a venture including the sole funder, Omar Mir, and the former Chelsea and England defender Ryan Bertrand, was already being voted on by fans when Mir suddenly walked away last Sunday, citing a change in his investment priorities.

Mir passed Wimbledon’s due diligence tests, but the tech businessman was not a unifying figure. A Josimar report has detailed his “various connections to some of the most influential and controversial figures in football, technology and global security”. The 44-year-old did not attend either of the information evenings at Plough Lane after the proposal was first made in October, instead sending a two-minute video message, which meant fans could not directly ask him about his intention to purchase 90% of the economic rights of a fan‑owned football club.

“We really wanted to have some kind of knight in shining armour,” said Niall Couper, a former member of the DTB and author of three books on Wimbledon. “In this case, I personally wasn’t sure how shiny that armour was.” Couper, who raised questions about Mir’s background before his withdrawal, chose not to attend the Blackpool game owing to anger from some supporters at the deal collapsing.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

But the SSC deal is not completely dead. Bertrand and his remaining SSC partners Stuart Fiertz, Oliver Ward and Hugh Rosen – who would have owned 1.25% each of Wimbledon’s economic rights in the original proposal – have renamed themselves Sloane Street Football and are talking to other potential investors.

In the meantime, the board will seek approval from fans about taking out a loan of up to £3m to “manage the club’s cash position”, but they believe they are able to manage it through to the end of this season and into the next. Which division Wimbledon end up in next season remains to be seen – Jackson’s side survived relegation by four points last April and the manager will probably have his hands tied in January.

“I think we’ll probably go down, but bouncing between League Two and League One is absolutely fine by me,” Billy Hunt said. “The main goal is security and making sure we have a football club.”

#942. Where does Kane rank among all-time England greats?

Harry Kane is now England's most-capped men's player as well as his country's record goalscorer, but harder to quantify is where these achievements place him among the Three Lions' greatest ever players.

This is a tricky debate with so many variables and a timescale as old as the game itself and, to my mind, not merely a determination of a player's individual ability but also a measure of their impact upon the nation's psyche.

Ballon d'Or winners Stanley Matthews, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen would surely have a shout if the criteria was such, not to mention genius technicians such as Glenn Hoddle, Chris Waddle and John Barnes.

Likewise, if any England boss managed to extract the best from Paul Scholes, Steven Gerrard and Frank Lampard they would be surely making a classic late dart from midfield.

But to qualify as one of the greatest England players of all time, you need the above ability combined with an impactful overall contribution - those memorable moments and an element of longevity - in a Three Lions shirt.

It might be controversial then to leave out Geoff Hurst, who produced the most recognisable performance in England history, while the man he replaced, Jimmy Greaves, would be a shoo-in were it not for injury earlier in the tournament.

It is also hard to rank the contribution of those whose best football came outside of major tournaments and before the dawn of continental competitions - see Eddie Hapgood, Tom Finney, Nat Lofthouse, Dixie Dean et al.

There are only 10 spots, after all, so here we go.

Spice Boy. Celebrity. Galactico. There is no argument David Beckham is one of the most iconic England players of all time, but he backed it up on the pitch, too.

Beckham was the face of the Three Lions for a generation, and to his credit managed to overcome the vicious fallout of his red card against Argentina in 1998.

At times he seemed to single-handedly carry England, most notably scoring a 93rd-minute free-kick against Greece to qualify for the 2002 World Cup.

Beckham's former team-mate Gary Neville called him the "most influential player out of England in transforming football".

It's true. On top of 115 caps, Beckham was part of Manchester United's 1999 Treble-winning outfit - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up - before joining Real Madrid.

His profile was truly global with spells at LA Galaxy, AC Milan and Paris St-Germain.

David Beckham scored 17 goals for England, including five free-kicks

There's arguably no England star fans forged an emotional attachment with more than Gazza - crying with him in 1990, rejoicing in his spectacular effort against Scotland and desperately willing him to connect during that Euro 96 semi-final defeat by Germany.

Gascoigne won 57 caps and scored 10 goals. At his peak, he was captivating - transcending football as a cultural phenomenon during the summers of '90 and '96, having joined a star-studded Serie A between those tournaments.

Creative, unpredictable, vulnerable. He was a loveable but flawed genius.

He suffered long-term injuries, as England missed out on the World Cup in the USA, but helped the Three Lions qualify for France 98 before being dropped from the final squad, famously wrecking boss Glenn Hoddle's office.

Gascoigne, Poborsky , McCoist - Goals that defined Euro 96

Goalscorers often grab the headlines but I've tried to credit players across positions and eras. From a defensive point of view Ashley Cole, arguably England's best-ever full-back, was close to making it.

But instead it's the great Billy Wright, the first men's player to surpass a century of international caps, including a remarkable 70 successive appearances over eight years.

Wright captained his country on 90 occasions, a joint-record recently broken by Kane, taking in three World Cups with impressive longevity for his era.

He was a true one-club man, winning three league titles, the FA Cup and becoming unofficial "world champions" with Wolves in 1954 - helping inspire the birth of the European Cup - while finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up to Alfredo di Stefano in 1957.

Billy Wright captained England 90 times - a record shared with Bobby Moore until Harry Kane recently surpassed the pair

It feels a little premature to include a 23-year-old with the bulk of his England career ahead of him, but that shows the impact Jude Bellingham has already made for England and Real Madrid.

A Champions League winner, the midfielder has also appeared at four major tournaments for the Three Lions, becoming the youngest player to do so at the delayed Euro 2020, aged 17.

But his role in helping carry England to the final two years ago and a third-place finish at last summer's World Cup really make him stand out.

Bellingham has delivered those moments a nation collectively remembers. The last-gasp overhead kick against Slovakia in 2024, a quickfire double at the Azteca against Mexico this summer and 93rd-minute quarter-final winner against Norway.

His seven goals at this World Cup were more than any previous Three Lions player in a single edition, the solo effort against France a thing of beauty.

The former Birmingham and Dortmund man doesn't turn 24 until June but has already collected 61 England caps and netted 14 times. As Roy Keane put it, Bellingham has the potential to be one of the "greatest of all time".

Ten of Bellingham's 14 England goals have come at major tournaments

In terms of natural ability, Wayne Rooney is among England's greatest ever talents.

Bursting on to the scene at Euro 2004 as an electric 18-year-old, having become England's youngest player and scorer the previous year, convinced fans and media the teen sensation could carry the Three Lions to glory in Portugal.

He bounced World Cup winner Lilian Thuram around in England's opener against France in a glimpse of his precocious strength, before scoring twice against both Switzerland and Croatia.

Who knows how far England would have gone had Rooney not been injured against Portugal in the quarter-final?

He was unable to replicate the impact of his first Euros - a red card at World Cup 2006, suspension for the Euro 2012 group stage, seven goals across six major tournaments - but was an all-rounder who brought more than just goals.

Rooney also won it all with Manchester United, becoming the club's all-time top scorer, and finished his 15-year England career with 53 goals from 120 caps.

Rooney burst on to the scene as an 18-year-old at Euro 2004

There has to be a place for a goalkeeper, and Gordon Banks is the safest pair of hands.

A World Cup winner in 1966, his save from Pele four years later against Brazil is one of the most iconic of all time. Pele called him a "goalkeeper with magic".

Banks spent the majority of his career at Leicester and Stoke, winning a League Cup with each, and earned 73 England caps overall between 1963 and 1972.

His incredible athleticism and reflexes saw the shot-stopper named Fifa's best goalkeeper for five successive years between 1966 and 1971.

Banks and Pele became good friends following the goalkeeper's iconic save in 1970

Gary Lineker's early club career did not deliver the silverware as his goals deserved, netting 40 times but finishing league and FA Cup runner-up in his one season at Everton before joining Barcelona.

He scored a Clasico hat-trick and won the Copa del Rey and Cup Winner's Cup, however, before adding an FA Cup with Tottenham in 1991.

Lineker netted 283 club goals (and famously no cards) in total across spells with Leicester, Everton, Barcelona, Spurs and Nagoya Grampus Eight.

But as a player Lineker is most renowned for his contribution in an England shirt, winning the Golden Boot as they reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 1986 - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up that year - before netting another four as the Three Lions reached the semi-finals in 1990.

Lineker equalised against West Germany before England crashed out on penalties.

However, having missed a spot-kick against Brazil, he finished one short of Bobby Charlton's elusive goal record when his international career ended after Euro 92.

Gary Lineker scored 48 goals in 80 games for England

Harry Kane is undoubtedly England's most important and influential player of a generation - it is hard to imagine how this Three Lions side functions once the skipper hangs up his boots.

The Bayern Munich striker, complete with Ballon d'Or, has been scoring goals for his country for almost 12 years, the first just 79 seconds into his debut after coming off the bench against Lithuania in March 2015.

Rooney's goalscoring benchmark is long in his rear view mirror - you wouldn't bank against Kane doubling his nearest rival's figure once his England days are over.

They have come on the biggest stage, too - 21 in 36 appearances from three World Cups and European Championships apiece, winning the World Cup Golden Boot in 2018.

Kane has come closer to winning a major tournament than any England men's captain since Bobby Moore - losing two World Cup semi-finals and back-to-back Euros finals. Team-mate Bellingham called him the "greatest player that has ever played for England".

"I think we'll appreciate him even more in another 10, 15, 20 years when you look back and see what he has achieved," said ex-England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

In many ways, Bobby Moore would be the complete modern-day defender. Cool as you like under pressure, elegant in possession, a great passing range off both feet and, as his West Ham and England team-mate Geoff Hurst said: "Nobody out-ran him and nobody out-jumped him."

Moore's positioning and timing was perfect, that iconic tackle on Jairzinho at the 1970 World Cup the finest example of his poise and precision when defending.

He was also a composed and influential leader. A player built for the big occasions. England boss Sir Alf Ramsey called him: "My lieutenant on the field, a cool, calculated footballer I could trust with my life."

The Barking-born centre-back won the FA Cup and European Cup Winners' Cup with West Ham but his finest moment was leading England to glory in 1966. He was only 25 at the time, having become his country's youngest captain three years earlier.

In 1970, after the Bogota bracelet incident, Moore was imperious as England reached the quarter-finals before bowing out to West Germany.

It was, however, the final group game against Brazil, the most exciting side on the planet, that produced some of the most recognisable and renowned images in sporting history - not only Moore's tackle and Banks' save but the defender swapping shirts with Pele after the final whistle.

"The greatest defender I ever played against," was the Brazilian's verdict.

Bobby Moore is the only man to captain the Three Lions to World Cup glory

For more than a generation, Sir Bobby's England goalscoring record remained unmatched. It took 45 years from his 49th and final strike against Colombia in 1970 until Rooney surpassed him with his half century in 2015.

Charlton was, as Alan Shearer put it, "not only a great goalscorer but a scorer of great goals" and played a pivotal part of the Three Lions' World Cup success in 1966, netting three times on the way to the final.

A scampering run from the halfway line followed by a trademark long-range strike into the corner at Wembley gave England's campaign lift-off against Mexico, before he scored twice against Eusebio's Portugal in the semi-finals.

Manager Ramsey called the buccaneering midfielder his "lynchpin" as England triumphed over West Germany in the showpiece and those performances helped Charlton win the Ballon d'Or later that year.

He'd be runner-up in successive years after that, too.

Charlton won 106 England caps and was a star for Manchester United, with Rooney also the one to pip his club-record 249 goals for the Old Trafford outfit.

A survivor of the Munich air disaster on 6 February 1958, which killed 23 people including eight players and three members of the club's staff, Charlton won three league titles, an FA Cup and most poignantly the European Cup in 1968.

"England's greatest ever player," Lineker previously told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He was unique. Wherever you go in the world, even if they didn't speak the language, they knew two words - Bobby Charlton."

Charlton's England goal record stood for almost half a century

#941. Bethell ruled out of South Africa tour

Jacob Bethell has been ruled out of the tour of South Africa, with the England batter set to undergo knee surgery; Bethell has not featured since since July and suffered another setback with a flare-up after joining up with the white-ball squad in Australia

England batter Jacob Bethell has been ruled out of the tour of South Africa as he is set to undergo more surgery on a knee issue.

Bethell has not featured since July because of a right knee problem, which required an operation over the summer.

The 23-year-old had joined up with England's white-ball squad in Perth last week ahead of his planned comeback before the three-Test trip to South Africa in December.

However, following a flare-up in his knee, Bethell returned to England for assessment by a specialist and will now need another procedure.

An England and Wales Cricket Board spokesperson said: "Jacob Bethell will undergo surgery on his right knee this week and has been ruled out of the tour of South Africa."

There is understood to be no initial timeframe set on Bethell's return to action. A decision on a replacement will be made once England are in South Africa.

Left-hander Bethell had started 2026 with a fine century in the final Ashes Test in Sydney, but is now set to miss out on seven consecutive series across all formats.

With Bethell's continued absence, Tom Banton will have the chance to continue opening in the 50-over side while Emilio Gay and Jordan Cox remain in contention for the Test XI.
