#940. From postcards to texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack - Pulis

When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.

Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.

Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.

One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.

During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.

Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.

For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.

I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.

When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.

We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.

Michael Carrick was sacked by Manchester United this week, but the club opened talks with Mauricio Pochettino before Carrick's departure was decided or confirmed

When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.

One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.

During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.

When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!

Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.

My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.

I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.

I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.

Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.

I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.

That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.

As a player, Burrows helped third-tier Swindon Town shock Arsenal in the 1969 League Cup final. As a manager, he had spells in charge of Portsmouth, Cardiff City (both twice) and Swansea and was also assistant manager at West Brom

I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth, and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.

Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.

We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.

"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."

That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!

It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.

I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.

It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.

I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.

It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.

Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.

Gibson appointed Pulis as Boro boss in December 2017. They reached the play-offs that season, then missed out on sixth place in the Championship by a single point in 2018-19

I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.

When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.

I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.

Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.

I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.

After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.

Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.

After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.

My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.

I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.

My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

#938. 60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages

Harry Kane scored for a record-equalling seventh England away game

Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday.

In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions.

Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular."

To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of understatement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular.

It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations League final.

If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment.

The question being asked when England held a one-goal advantage through Harry Kane's penalty at half-time was 'what would theirs and Tuchel's reaction be?' Stick or twist?

Would Tuchel tell England to press their foot on the pedal for acceleration? Or would he take the approach of going into reverse gear, as he did to ill-fated effect against Argentina?

How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?

Who swaggered around like he owned the place? Spain v England ratings

England hold on to stun world champions Spain in thriller

The answer was delivered when they added goals from Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White in the first 12 minutes of the second half.

This being England, they then created a mess for themselves when Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the area after 65 minutes, although the main culprit was Jarell Quansah for initially conceding possession.

Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and, when Yamal set up Nico Williams for Spain's second with 15 minutes left, it looked like more than an hour of faultless England football might be wasted.

But not a bit of it, as goalkeeper James Trafford produced heroics and England defended with every fibre to close out this landmark win.

Was this the statement victory that was almost demanded of Tuchel as recompense for the World Cup disappointment, a performance to convince the doubters?

"We're fully aware what we put out there," said Tuchel afterwards. "What a performance we put out for 65 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up.

"Of course, the red card and the penalty changed the momentum and the characteristics of the game... but we know, and the players know very, very well, what they put out there. That is the statement - and that is the significance of this victory."

Simple details of the game barely touch the sides of a night filled with quality and glorious chaos, vindication for Tuchel and England's positive approach.

Spain opened with an ostentatious parade of the World Cup in front of England's players as the teams lined up, perhaps a psychological reminder of the superiority that has seen them dominate international football.

What followed, at times literally, reduced Spain's supporters to stunned silence and their players to a shell-shocked shambles chasing the shadows that were overpowering them.

England's white shirts were everywhere but Spain could not get near them. The tormentors had become the tormented.

It was alien territory for a Spain side that has carried all before them, while England's fans tucked away high in a corner of this vast arena were equally unbelieving as a dream unfolded in front of them.

England, for 65 minutes, were in a different class to Spain. And, yes, you have read that right.

From the first whistle, employing a suffocatingly high press, England ran all over Spain.

When White crowned a superb move with the third goal four minutes after Konsa's second, it looked, remarkably, to be a case of how big England's victory margin would be.

In the end, the margin was narrow but the stature and significance of England's victory was huge.

Tuchel labelled this meeting with Spain as "proof of concept at the highest level".

There was no doubt the German manager and England were under fierce scrutiny after the manner of the collapse, mentally and tactically, against Argentina at the World Cup.

Here they delivered the proof they can match the best then beat them.

Win over world champions Spain is a 'statement' - Tuchel

If the vital signs were being forensically examined for evidence Tuchel has learned lessons from a chastening World Cup, that England have improved after that harrowing experience, this game delivered these conclusions.

Of course, England must do it again. Do it when the pressure and expectation in at its highest.

The Nations League is competitive but cannot be compared to a World Cup and European Championship, both titles currently in the possession of the team they beat here.

But England's world-class players delivered - Kane inevitably with his 93rd international goal, but Jude Bellingham was on a level of his own, the outstanding performer on both sides with an individual display simply confirming he is the player with everything.

And Tuchel got his big calls right, especially selecting Trafford, who responded superbly in a frantic closing phase. White, making a strong claim for the right-back berth, not only scored a goal but produced crucial challenges in the face of relentless, albeit belated, Spain pressure.

"This was the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness," said Tuchel. "It was on the highest level football wise in all aspects of the game. We did everything that needs to be done together.

"The deep build-up. The high press. The counter-attack. The tracking. The defensive phases. This was an excellent performance and of course a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.

"We overcame some difficult moments in the end. That's how it is. But we are very well aware which steps we took now through after the World Cup."

England's win means they top their Nations League group, but the importance spreads much wider than simply a league table.

The first 65 minutes were simply breathtaking. Spain wilting under attack after attack. Spain rattled until they shook as England refused to allow them meaningful possession.

After Anderson's dismissal, bad memories were revisited as England were forced into a rearguard action, but any other result than the one that was eventually delivered would have been a huge injustice.

England survived 29 nervous minutes, including added time, to make a powerful statement about their current status, which is much healthier than when recriminations about Tuchel's approach provided the post-World Cup narrative.

"I'm very impressed with the steps that we took after the World Cup", said Tuchel. "We wanted to get better, better in a deep build-up, get better in defending in a low block and, on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play against every opponent.

"I think this was clearly visible throughout the whole group phase. The results followed with an excellent group phase."

Was this the finest performance of Tuchel's time in charge? Most observers felt so, but the head coach was best placed to answer.

"Yes, given the circumstances," he said, "and the pressure, the quality, where we played in this building against the reigning world champions, unbeaten in 43 matches. Putting a performance out there in Madrid, and in this environment, was a very complete performance."

Tuchel will, of course, need repeat performances - but the outstanding ability and character England displayed here to beat the World Cup holders will deliver a huge injection of confidence and self-belief.

#937. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

#936. Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

Meet the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contenders

Voting is now open for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.

Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-August 2026.

Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.

Sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Listen: Who is your BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026?

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Temwa Chawinga

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Ewa Pajor

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland and is the team's leading goalscorer.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alexia Putellas

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3â0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Alessia Russo

Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.

She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.

Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.

It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.

Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.

She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.

BBC Women's Footballer of the Year contender Khadija Shaw

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

#934. Tiger confirms date for fresh PGA Tour comeback

Tiger Woods has been added a tournament invite for the Hero World Challenge from December 3-6, hosted by his foundation; Woods has not featured in a competitive event since 2024; watch Woods' latest comeback live on Sky Sports Golf

Tiger Woods has confirmed he will return to competitive action at the Hero World Challenge next month, live on Sky Sports.

The invite-only tournament - hosted by Woods' foundation - has previously been used as a comeback event for Woods, who has played a limited schedule since suffering career-threatening injuries in a car crash in February 2021.

Woods has not appeared on the PGA Tour since missing the cut at The Open in July 2024, with the 15-time major champion missing the entire 2025 season after rupturing his Achilles tendon.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He underwent fresh back surgery last October and missed the 2026 campaign after "stepping away" from PGA Tour golf, following a car crash in March that saw him charged with reckless driving, but is now scheduled to return in Albany, Bahamas.

The 50-year-old is one of three sponsor's exemptions added to the field for the 20-man event, held from December 3-6, with 2019 US Open champion Gary Woodland and Rickie Fowler the others to be included.

Woods was a notable absentee from the initial line-up announcement last month, with Hideki Matsuyama returning as defending champion and Scottie Scheffler looking to win for a third time in four years, while Players champion Cameron Young and former US Open winner Matt Fitzpatrick also feature.

The former world No 1 is currently listed as 'unranked' in the OWGR standings, having only completed four 72-hole tournaments over the last six seasons and not had a worldwide top 10 since January 2020.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He last featured at the Hero World Challenge in 2023, his first appearance since withdrawing mid-tournament from The Masters earlier that year, although won the event in 2001, 2004, 2006, 2007 and 2011.

Woods was listed in Jupiter Links GC's expanded five-player roster for the 2026/27 TGL season, beginning December 27, with Kevin Kisner - replaced by Keith Mitchell in the line-up - expecting the five-time Masters champion to feature more frequently.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I'm not on the team anymore," Kisner told the Fore Play Podcast last month. "I had a two-year contract with Jupiter Links. Tiger wants to play and they wanted to sign Keith Mitchell, which is totally fine with me.

"Rob [McNamara], ​Tiger's guy, he texted me a long text last week. Just telling me what they did on their decisions, how they were moving around and what players were going to do and that Tiger wanted to play a full schedule."

Woods previously described the PNC Championship as his "fifth major", with the 36-hole team competition seeing a former winner of a major or The Players tee it up alongside a family member.

He featured in every edition since 2020 with his son, Charlie Woods, who fired a hole-in-one during the 2024 contest before they lost in a play-off to Bernhard Langer's team, although missed last year's contest due to injury.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Team Woods have yet to confirm their entry into this year's edition, held from December 19-20 and also live on Sky Sports, although there are spaces for them still to be included in the line-up.

"He plays there [at the Hero World Challenge] and PNC [Championship]," Kisner predicted. "He's going to play both.

"Come back, get your feet wet at the Hero, play with Charlie [Woods] in the Father/Son, play some TGL, get ready for Augusta."

#933. How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?

James Trafford (right) kept Spain out in the latter stages

England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group.

But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina.

So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look.

First of all the context of the two games was entirely different.

England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players.

Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on.

But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano.

Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford.

"Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners."

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages

England cling on to stun world champions Spain in thriller

Making defensive subs is fine when it works - but when it does not, boy will a manager hear about it.

In the World Cup last 16, England had been 2-1 up against Mexico in the Azteca when Jarell Quansah was sent off.

Tuchel brought on three defenders for a defender, a midfielder and a forward.

But England won 3-2 and Dan Burn's cameo was the stuff of legend.

However, nine days later with England 1-0 up against Argentina, Tuchel did the same again - three defenders on for a defender, midfielder and forward.

The first of those subs, with Konsa replacing Anthony Gordon, was in the 72nd minute.

And England just sat back until Argentina broke their resistance.

However, against Spain this time, despite England being down to 10 men and facing incessant pressure, Tuchel was not so quick with defensive subs.

Myles Lewis-Skelly, replacing Harry Kane, was the first on after 78 minutes - 15 minutes after Anderson's sending off. And then five minutes later he brought on two more players - but one of them was a striker in Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

Burn replaced fellow defender White in the 89th minute.

"Harry played 78 minutes, Jude [Bellingham] 83 minutes and then just defending and defending, it's tiring," explained Tuchel.

"So we needed fresh energy. I was asked yesterday what happens if there needs to be a critical or crucial substitution. And I said, I feel free enough to take any substitution if I think it is necessary to help the team and to influence the game.

"I feel free enough to do that and I think there was a lot of defending needed. So we just went for some fresh legs."

Win over world champions Spain is a 'statement' - Tuchel

England actually faced more of a siege this time than against the Argentines, the stats confirm.

In the final 30 minutes they faced 19 shots from Spain, with seven on target and an expected goals (xG) total of 2.53.

Argentina, in that time, had 10 shots, with four on target and an xG of 1.41.

In terms of passes from England the numbers were similar with 65 against Argentina and 61 against Spain - both times with an accuracy rate of about 64%.

In Thursday's 2-1 win against Croatia, as a comparison, they tried 557 passes with accuracy of 89%.

"For half an hour it was Mexico reloaded and it felt like we were back in the Azteca. We had to overcome 30 minutes which, against Spain, felt like three hours," Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"The difficult thing is it's not only a red card, it's a red card, and a goal so that makes a completely new game. Thirty minutes against the world champion feels like three hours. I said it before in the stadium and wave after wave after wave."

England were criticised for blowing a 2-1 half-time lead at Wembley in their first Nations League game with Spain.

But on that day their final 30-minute figurers were much better - with only five shots faced and 176 attempted passes with a 90% accuracy.

So what was different this time? Perhaps the team showed more resilience and unity?

After Spain had pulled one back England's players had a huddle.

"I love the fact the team went into a huddle and if anything the manager's stepped back because he wants to see the player reaction," said ex-England defender Matt Upson on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I almost think that the trauma from that sending off of Elliot Anderson has almost been a positive thing for England because it's given the team a chance to get together and cope in what is an incredibly difficult situation and come through the other side.

"There was so much going on in this game. England had to suffer and came through the other side."

Defender and goalscorer White was asked about the huddle after the game.

"Just stay calm, when you're one down it becomes more difficult and things change so it was all about managing that," he said.

Another factor was the performance of England keeper James Trafford, who made six saves - with four of them coming in the final 12 minutes of the game with the score at 3-2.

He made an incredible double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in injury time.

Upson said: "I think that double save was the moment for Spain and Trafford had the answers."

#932. Rihanna Addresses EJ Johnson Feud Rumors After Fashion Week Comment

Rihanna put rumors of a feud with EJ Johnson to bed over a month after the latter referenced her tardiness to a Dior show at Paris Fashion Week.

Rihanna always knows how to kiss it better.

After EJ Johnson raised eyebrows with a video detailing Rihanna’s tardiness to a Paris Fashion Week show—and when her apparent clap back raised eyebrows even higher—the “Umbrella” singer took a moment to confirm there’s no lingering bad blood.

“There’s no beef, you know there’s no beef,” she said in a video shared by TMZ. “I just felt bad for him, you know?”

In fact, she’s willing to put her best foot forward with EJ—or rather, allow them to.

When asked whether she’d ever let EJ walk in a Savage x Fenty show, the 38-year-old affirmed, “He deserves to.”

But while Rihanna proved it’s all loveeeeeee with EJ these days, there was a period when fans thought the pair had everything but love on the brain.

ICYMI, during Paris Fashion Week back in September, EJ shared a video recapping their experience at Dior’s Ready to Wear Spring/Summer 2027 collection.

“We just left the Dior show, getting out of there was crazy but the show itself was beautiful,” the Rich Kids of Beverly Hills alum said in the vlog. “It did start an hour late because Rihanna was late and, you know, like, we didn’t care to wait for her, but the show was beautiful nonetheless.”

Then, just a few days later, a video circulated on social media in which EJ could be seen posing for paparazzi in Paris, before making their way into their hotel. EJ’s way was soon blocked, however, by hotel staff, creating a kind of standstill witnessed by a crowd of fans and photographers.

And while Rihanna’s one-word response to the video (“Damn”) was originally interpreted as shade, garnering thousands of likes, her new comments reveal she just felt bad for the awkward moment EJ found themself in.

Besides, these days, Rihanna—mom to sons RZA, 4, Riot, 3, and daughter Rocki, 14 months, with A$AP Rocky—has been busy since she's been back in the studio, working on her first album in a decade.

It was A$AP who pulled back the proverbial curtain, revealing on The Jason Lee Show in August, “She in the studio right now.”

But even in the moments he said it, the rapper knew he’d just opened a massive can of worms.

“Yeah, I said it. Sorry, babe,” he joked. “Like, bro, she working. She cooking, no funny s--t.”

He then quipped, “Damn, I’ma get in trouble for this.”

As for EJ and Rihanna? While their rumored feud may have boiled down to nothing more than some misinterpreted comments, there are some Hollywood rivalries with much more heated waters. Read on for more.

The Sex and the City costars had dodged feud rumors for years, but they were reignited after Cattrall decided not to return for a third movie and made comments about her SLP that raised eyebrows.

"What was your reaction to Kim Cattrall telling Piers Morgan that you were never friends just colleagues?" Andy Cohen asked Parker on a September 2017 episode of Watch What Happens Live.

As she explained, "Just...heartbroken. I mean that whole week, you and I spoke about it because I was just...I don't know I found it really upsetting because that's, you know, that's not the way I recall our experience."

"So...it's sad but I'm kind of...I don't know, I always think that what ties us together is this singular experience is the thing," she continued. "It was a professional experience but it became personal because it was years and years of our lives. So I'm hoping that that sort of eclipses anything that's been recently spoken. That many years spent doing something so special that people had a connection with is such a privileged."

And though they didn't film scenes together, Cattrall did make a small appearance on And Just Like That.

During a 2022 TikTok challenge, JoJo Siwa described Candace Cameron Bure as the "rudest" celebrity, later explaining that she felt snubbed when Bure once refused to take a picture with her on a red carpet. Shortly after the dig, however, the Full House alum apologized: "I kind of broke your 11-year-old heart. I didn't take a picture with you. Ugh! I feel crummy, I feel—JoJo, I'm so sorry."

The two made amends. But months later, Cameron Bure was asked if she expects the Great American Family network, of which she serves as chief creative officer, to feature same-sex couples as leads in holiday movies. She said no, adding, "I think that Great American Family will keep traditional marriage at the core."

Siwa, who came out as a member of the LGBTQ+ community in 2021, wrote on Instagram that the actress' comment is "rude and hurtful to a whole community of people."

In August 2022, Morris and Pope traded harsh words with Aldean, wife of fellow country star Jason Aldean, after she shared an Instagram Reel of herself applying makeup, writing, "I'd really like to thank my parents for not changing my gender when I went through my tomboy phase. I love this girly life."

Berk (pictured second from left) addressed rumors of a falling out with France (middle) in January 2024, two months after he announced his exit from Queer Eye after eight seasons.

"I want people to know that Tan and I—we will be fine," he told Vanity Fair. "There was a situation, and that's between Tan and I, and it has nothing to do with the show. It was something personal that had been brewing—and nothing romantic, just to clarify that."

In March 2024, France responded to allegations that he had campaigned to replace Berk on Queer Eye with his friend Jeremiah Brent.

"Netflix and the production companies did a full-on casting. I didn't put my friend up for the job. They ended up getting it because they were the best person for the job," he said on Instagram. "But I didn't get them hired by getting rid of somebody else."

In September 2023, while playing a game called Stir the Pot with her daughter Kelly Osbourne on E! News, Sharon said the That '70s Show alum was the rudest celebrity she had ever met, branding him, a "rude, rude, rude, rude little boy" and a "dastardly little thing."

He did not respond to her remarks publicly.

Five years prior, Sharon told Larry King that when Ashton appeared on The Talk in 2014, he had an "attitude" after she got his name wrong.

"He goes, 'What are you, what have you done in this industry?'" she recalled. "And I was like, 'Kid, don't start with me, because I'm gonna eat you up and s--t you out.' So I was just like, 'You don't know what you're dealing with, kid.'"

Back in June 2021, the Hole frontwoman accused Rodrigo of copying her band's album cover for a promotional photo without giving credit, prompting the Disney alum to respond, "Love u and live through this sooooo much."

however, it seemed their hatchet was buried when Love replied, "Olivia - you're welcome. My favorite florist is in Notting Hill, London! Dm me for deets! I look forward to reading your note [winking face emoji]."

During a 2019 appearance on Watch What Happens Live, the Happy Days actor was asked why he didn't get along with the Forrest Gump star on the set of the 1989 flick Turner & Hooch.

"I was directing that movie for 13 days," Winkler recalled, "and then I was called into [producer] Jeff Katzenberg's office and he said, 'You have everything with you? Go home.'"

He did, however, seem to get along with Hanks' four-legged costar, quipping, "Love that dog."

Winkler later denied speculation that he still had beef with the Oscar winner, telling TMZ in 2020, "I don't have a feud with Tom Hanks."

Fans of The Hills will remember that iconic line, delivered by Conrad on the season three premiere. Their feud began when Montag started dating her now-husband Spencer Pratt, and hit its peak when Conrad accused her and Pratt of starting a rumor that she had made a sex tape with then-boyfriend Jason Wahler.

The costars reignited their ongoing feud in 2017 when Gibson publicly called out Johnson on Instagram after the Fast and Furious 9 release date was pushed back to April 2020. That same day, it was announced that a Fast and Furious spinoff starring Johnson and Jason Statham would hit theaters in 2019. The following month, Gibson threatened to quit Fast 9 if Johnson was in the movie.

Gibson then opened up about the feud, telling Van Lathan on The Red Pill podcast, "I have yet to talk to The Rock to this day, and we will have a conversation." He shared that he did have a chat with the former wrestler's producing partner, but not the actor himself.

"I found myself being the messenger on behalf of various people associated to the franchise, but stupid me was the only one who went public about those feelings, which is my own fault," gibson said. "It's not professional, it's not cool."

Swift and Perry had been in a feud for years, with their rift even allegedly inspiring the former's song "Bad Blood." The drama, which reportedly started over a backup dancer and competing tours, came to an end after Perry sent Swift a literal olive branch before her Reputation Tour kickoff in 2018.

"So I just got to my dressing room and found this actual olive branch," Swift said in an Instagram video. "This mean so much."

She captioned the video, "Thank you Katy."

The iconic singers have been feuding since 2004. While accepting the Classic Songwriter Award at the Q Awards that year, John said to attendees, "Madonna, best f--king live act? F--k off! Since when has lip-syncing been live? Sorry about that, but I think everyone who lip-syncs in public on stage, when you pay like 75 quid to see them, should be shot."

The former Grey's Anatomy star sparked a feud with the series creator in 2008 when she removed her name from the Emmy Awards consideration. Heigl stated that her reason for the move was because she wasn't "given the material to warrant a nomination."

Rhimes later opened up about Heigl's decision during an interview with Oprah Winfrey on Oprah's Next Chapter in 2012. "On some level it stung and on some level I was not surprised," she said. "When people show you who they are, believe them. I carry that [mantra] with me a lot. It has served me well."

It was the New York Fashion Week fight heard 'round the world when Nicki and Cardi got into a heated altercation at the Harper's Bazaar Icon party. The following month, Cardi opened up about the catalyst for the fight with Nicki.

"For a while now she's been taking a lot of shots at me," Cardi said in W magazine's Art Issue. "I spoke to her twice before, and we came to an understanding. But she kept it going."

The real spark of the fight came when Cardi saw that Nicki had allegedly liked and then unliked a tweet about Cardi's parenting skills, which Nicki has denied.

"I was going to make millions off my Bruno Mars tour, and I sacrificed that to stay with my daughter," Cardi continued. "I love my daughter. I'm a good-ass f--king mom. So for somebody that don't have a child to like that comment? So many people want to say that party wasn't the time or the place, but I'm not going to catch another artist in the grocery store or down the block."

Tension between Kanye and Taylor first started in 2009, when the "Stronger" rapper took the stage during her acceptance speech at the MTV Video Music Awards. Years later, the two would make up and even become friends, but that came to an end in 2016 after the release of his song "Famous," in which he name-checks the "End Game" singer.

In February 2025, one day before the Grammys, Kanye updated his Instagram to follow only Taylor. He added no further comment, and his fellow musician did not respond publicly to the move.

Carey and J.Lo's supposed feud started when the Queen of Christmas was asked to give her opinion on several singers during a 2003 German TV interview. When asked her opinion on Lopez, she replied, "I don't know her."

#930. Vinicius says transfer interest affected Real form

Vinicius Jr signed a new six-year contract with Real Madrid in August

Real Madrid forward Vinicius Jr says he felt "truly overwhelmed" by transfer speculation in the summer, which has contributed to his mixed form at the start of the season.

The Brazil international has scored just once and provided three assists in 12 appearances for Jose Mourinho's side this season.

He was linked with a move to Premier League champions Arsenal this summer as he entered the final year of his contract, before signing an extension at Real.

The 26-year-old also says he did not train as much as he should have following Brazil's last-16 exit at the World Cup.

"I don't think I prepared as well as I could have after the World Cup, because the impact of that tournament is so significant for all Brazilians," he said.

"Being knocked out so early was something we hadn't expected. So, I took advantage of my holidays to enjoy myself, rest, relax, and spend more time with my family. I ended up training less than in previous years.

"That may have affected my start to the season.

"On top of that, regarding my contract renewal, with so many clubs showing interest last summer, I felt truly overwhelmed, as with the situation at Real Madrid. But it's a very long season."

Vinicius received a red card for violent conduct in October when he pulled the hair of Villarreal midfielder Nathan Saliba, which led to a four-match suspension.

In his absence, record signing Yan Diomande has made the most of his opportunity on the left wing, scoring four goals.

Vinicius joined Real from Brazilian side Flamengo in 2018 and has scored more than 20 club goals in each of his past five seasons.

Mourinho's side are second in La Liga, three points behind rivals Barcelona, and return to league action when they host Celta Vigo on Saturday.

#929. Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson

Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013

For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking, consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

If following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a new farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, showed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

Here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata. Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess says Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como.

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

Carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United.

#927. As El Niño builds, studies of extreme marine heatwaves must start now

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alistair J. Hobday is a chief research scientist at CSIRO Environment, Hobart, Australia.

Kathryn E. Smith is a research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, Plymouth, UK.

Claire M. Spillman is a principal research scientist at the Bureau of Meteorology, Melbourne, Australia.

Karen Filbee-Dexter is a Future Fellow at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and a principal scientist at the Institute of Marine Research, Flødevigen Research Station, His, Norway.

Neil J. Holbrook is a professor of ocean and climate dynamics at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies and the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century, University of Tasmania, Hobart, Australia.

Caroline Rowland is head of ocean cryosphere and climate at the Met Office, Exeter, UK.

Dan A. Smale is a senior research fellow at the Marine Biological Association, Plymouth, UK.

Grant Smith is a senior research scientist at the Bureau of Meteorology, Melbourne, Australia.

Mads S. Thomsen is an adjunct professor at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and an associate professor in the School of Biological Sciences, University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand.

Thomas Wernberg is a laureate professor at the UWA Oceans Institute and School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia, and principal scientist at the Institute of Marine Research, Flødevigen Research Station, His, Norway.

Alex Sen Gupta is a professor in the Climate Change Research Centre and the Centre for Marine Science and Innovation, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia.

Coral nurseries, such as this one in French Polynesia, can be used to study the resilience of the organisms in real-world settings. Credit: Alexis Rosenfeld/Getty

With temperatures in the Pacific Ocean at record-high levels and forecasts of an extreme El Niño climate event, intense marine heatwaves are expected around the world in the coming year1,2. Scientists must prepare to study these extreme conditions now, so that managers of marine resources and decision makers can develop and implement response strategies and communities can plan for a hotter future.

The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?

The super El Niño is cooking coral reefs — can lullabies and probiotics save them?

El Niño is part of a recurring natural cycle in Earth’s climate in which warmer waters in the central and eastern Pacific alter ocean and atmospheric circulation, affecting weather worldwide. Marine heatwaves associated with El Niño provide opportunities to study ecosystems under real-world stress conditions and on scales that cannot be replicated in a laboratory.

Marine heatwaves can be forecast weeks or months ahead, giving researchers time to design field studies, deploy instruments and collect baseline data. Investigations can be designed to test theories and improve our understanding of ecological processes, thresholds and recovery mechanisms in a rapidly warming ocean.

Such knowledge can inform decisions about how to manage marine resources, such as whether to close fisheries. Much has been learnt about marine heatwaves since the last El Niño, in 2023–24 (see ‘Hot water’). But these lessons need to be consolidated and scaled up into consistent, long-term preparedness plans.

Source: Climate Reanalyzer (CC-BY-4.0); go.nature.com/4zae69a

Fortunately, effective approaches established in one place can be extended to others. Australia is a leader in developing early-warning systems and response plans for adaptation to a more extreme ocean climate. Other nations (including the United Kingdom, the United States, New Zealand and Peru) have improved their awareness of these events and put in place observation systems, forecasts and briefings, policy mechanisms and (in a few cases) adaptation measures.

But further action is needed, particularly in locations that have previously been unaffected by severe marine heatwaves. Here, we highlight seven priorities in increasing marine heatwave preparedness.

Seasonal forecasts with lead times of several months are now being delivered in various regions, including the United States3 and Australia4, and such systems are being developed in the United Kingdom and New Zealand5 and for the Mediterranean Sea6.

Forecasting relies on physical and statistical models to predict probable ocean temperatures7. Data from sustained surface and below-surface observations are essential for initializing models and verifying predictions, building users’ confidence in forecasts.

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

But managers want to know more precisely what the duration and intensity of a marine heatwave is expected to be. Forecasts become less accurate the further ahead they look and at fine spatial scales, such as along coasts. Improved ocean monitoring, a better understanding of the drivers of marine heatwaves and continued refinements of model physics are needed to improve forecast accuracy7.

Advances in machine learning are expected to be transformative. Next-generation models that incorporate ocean physics might be able to predict unprecedented marine heatwaves more accurately than current technologies can. Downscaling global climate models to inshore regions using machine-learning techniques could also increase the usefulness of forecasts in places where most marine-resource users operate.

Planning for and communication about impending marine heatwaves are also improving1. In 2023, engagement was piecemeal and often only in response to events that were already in progress. Activities are now more proactive and structured.

Coordinated briefings that translate forecasts into action provide ways of engaging with affected groups and planning ahead. Such communication strategies should be implemented around the world4,8. National briefings provide a broad overview of marine heatwave risks and impacts. Regional and industry specialists can provide further local advice.

For example, Australia’s national marine climate briefing series4 has been running since 2023. Similar meetings (led or contributed to by some of us) have taken place for the western Pacific Ocean (G.S.) and in the United Kingdom (C.R.), Brazil (K.E.S.), Singapore (C.M.S.) and New Zealand (C.M.S.).

Seafood-producing firms and conservation managers need a menu of actions to choose from when a marine heatwave looms. Options include adjusting collection strategies, temporarily closing fisheries and modifying aquaculture operations1.

Australia has developed regional and industry-specific response plans for marine heatwaves8. Response teams for fisheries are active during warming events and provide coordinated mechanisms for assessment, communication and management actions4,9.

Impacts of marine heatwaves are being monitored in restored giant kelp forests in Tasmania, Australia.Credit: Scott Ling/University of Tasmania

Early-warning systems and interagency coordination are key components of timely responses. Industry has also adopted operating protocols to reduce the impacts of marine heatwaves on animal health and food-product quality. For example, abalone fisheries in New South Wales have changed how sea snails (Haliotis spp.) are fished, handled and prepared for live export10. Other regions could benefit from similar plans4.

For example, fishing of Peruvian anchoveta (Engraulis ringens), the source of around 20% of fishmeal and fish oil globally, has already been curbed by the current El Niño. In 2023, the fishery had to be closed, resulting in an estimated loss11 of US$1.4 billion. This year, an alert in February prompted Peruvian authorities to bring the fishing season forwards by two weeks and reduce the total allowable catch of anchoveta and white anchovy (Anchoa nasus) by more than 30% to 1.9 million tonnes. This meant that fisheries could catch about 450,000 tonnes before the heatwave intensified and the season was ended in May.

In 2023, marine heatwave preparedness was recognized as inadequate in most regions. The emphasis then was mainly on raising risk awareness in sectors such as fisheries and aquaculture1. However, these and other industries need to adapt to a changing ocean, too.

Awareness has now grown among sectors and institutions, and behaviours have begun to change. For example, Australian marine climate briefings draw engagement from aquaculture and fishery managers, marine tourism operators, policymakers, researchers and individual fishers4.

In the United States, forecasts of marine heatwaves trigger advice to fishers regarding increases in interactions with marine mammals as the overlap between animals’ hunting grounds and deployed fishing gear expands, which can result in fishery closures. Coral-reef managers involved in restoration efforts can scale back replanting efforts and start collecting genetic material.

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

In the Mediterranean Sea, limiting diving tourism at coral reefs to minimize damage during marine heatwaves has been proposed, mirroring practices that were adopted in Asia during the 2023–24 marine heatwaves11.

In the Cook Islands’ black-pearl industry, seasonal forecasts have been proposed for supporting decisions around adaptive management aimed at reducing the thermal stress of oysters. These include increased reliance on hatchery production under controlled temperature conditions and preferential harvesting of pearls during cooler periods of the year.

In the United Kingdom, a national marine heatwave network and code of best practice have been established, enabling the exchange of transdisciplinary knowledge. Similar transfers of experience, capacity and lessons learnt between jurisdictions can accelerate preparedness globally and help to embed risk management into routine decision-making processes4.

The 2023 El Niño led to calls to strengthen monitoring and research capacity to improve the detection of, understanding of and response to marine heatwaves. Observation networks are now becoming a core component of preparedness and response plans, providing the information needed to support forecasting, impact assessment, management interventions and long-term adaptation strategies12.

Targeted uses of gliders and intensified monitoring strategies can bolster research, situational awareness and management decisions12. Research has expanded into understanding ecological resilience and adaptation. For example, genetic studies are identifying traits that might enhance the capacity of key fishery or habitat-forming species13 to persist under increasing thermal stress.

Researchers in Florida are studying corals obtained from local reefs as part of restoration efforts.Credit: Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty
